abstract: A new optimization strategy, Mean Field Annealing, is presented. Its application to MAP restoration of noisy range images is derived and experimentally verified.
originalAbstract: A new optimization strategy, Mean Field Annealing, is presented. Its application to MAP restoration of noisy range images is derived and experimentally verified.
title: Range Image Restoration Using Mean Field Annealing

abstract: Exact structure from motion is an ill-posed computation and therefore very sensitive to noise. In this work I describe how a qualitative shape representation, based on the sign of the Gaussian curvature, can be com(cid:173) puted directly from motion disparities, without the computation of an exact depth map or the directions of surface normals. I show that humans can judge the curvature sense of three points undergoing 3D motion from two, three and four views with success rate significantly above chance. A simple RBF net has been trained to perform the same task.
originalAbstract: Exact structure from motion is an ill-posed computation and therefore very sensitive to noise. In this work I describe how a qualitative shape representation, based on the sign of the Gaussian curvature, can be com(cid:173) puted directly from motion disparities, without the computation of an exact depth map or the directions of surface normals. I show that humans can judge the curvature sense of three points undergoing 3D motion from two, three and four views with success rate significantly above chance. A simple RBF net has been trained to perform the same task.

paragraphs: The paper studies how motion can reveal qualitative surface shape without reconstructing exact three-dimensional geometry. It starts from the observation that exact structure-from-motion estimation is ill-posed and highly sensitive to noise. The proposed representation instead uses the sign of Gaussian curvature, retaining a qualitative distinction about shape rather than a complete depth description.

The author describes computing this representation directly from motion disparities. The procedure does not require first estimating an exact depth map or the directions of surface normals. This changes the computational target: the method seeks the shape property needed for the judgment directly, avoiding the intermediate requirement to recover detailed geometry.

The paper also reports that people judge the curvature sense of three points undergoing three-dimensional motion above chance using two, three, or four views. A simple radial basis function network is trained on the same task. Together, the computational formulation and human judgments support the relevance of extracting qualitative curvature information from motion when exact reconstruction is unnecessarily demanding.
summary.tldr: Qualitative curvature can be inferred directly from motion without first recovering an exact depth map.

title: Qualitative structure from motion

abstract: Vector Quantization is useful for data compression. Competitive Learn(cid:173) ing which minimizes reconstruction error is an appropriate algorithm for vector quantization of unlabelled data. Vector quantization of labelled data for classification has a different objective, to minimize the number of misclassifications, and a different algorithm is appropriate. We show that a variant of Kohonen's LVQ2.1 algorithm can be seen as a multi(cid:173) class extension of an algorithm which in a restricted 2 class case can be proven to converge to the Bayes optimal classification boundary. We compare the performance of the LVQ2.1 algorithm to that of a modified version having a decreasing window and normalized step size, on a ten class vowel classification problem.
originalAbstract: Vector Quantization is useful for data compression. Competitive Learn(cid:173) ing which minimizes reconstruction error is an appropriate algorithm for vector quantization of unlabelled data. Vector quantization of labelled data for classification has a different objective, to minimize the number of misclassifications, and a different algorithm is appropriate. We show that a variant of Kohonen's LVQ2.1 algorithm can be seen as a multi(cid:173) class extension of an algorithm which in a restricted 2 class case can be proven to converge to the Bayes optimal classification boundary. We compare the performance of the LVQ2.1 algorithm to that of a modified version having a decreasing window and normalized step size, on a ten class vowel classification problem.

paragraphs: This paper distinguishes two purposes for vector quantization: compressing data and classifying labeled examples. For compression, the objective is to reconstruct inputs accurately from representative vectors. For classification, the objective is to assign the correct class. The authors argue that these different goals call for different learning algorithms, even though both use vector quantization.

They analyze a variant of Kohonen's LVQ2.1 algorithm by connecting it to a classification procedure with a theoretical guarantee. In a restricted two-class setting, that procedure can be proved to converge to the Bayes optimal classification boundary, the boundary that minimizes classification error. The LVQ variant is interpreted as a multiclass extension of this procedure.

The paper also compares LVQ2.1 with a modified version that uses a decreasing window and a normalized step size on a ten-class vowel classification task. The theoretical result is explicitly tied to the restricted two-class case. Its value is to give classification-oriented vector quantization a principled connection to optimal decision boundaries while motivating an empirical comparison of update rules.
summary.tldr: The paper connects an LVQ variant to a restricted optimal-classification result and compares update rules on vowel classification.

title: A Note on Learning Vector Quantization

The principle states that the input(cid:173) output mapping implemented by a processing stage should be cho(cid:173) sen so as to maximize the average mutual information between input and output patterns, subject to constraints and in the pres(cid:173) ence of processing noise. In the present work I show how infomax, when applied to a class of nonlinear input-output mappings, can under certain conditions generate optimal filters that have addi(cid:173) tional useful properties: (1) Output activity (for each input pat(cid:173) tern) tends to be concentrated among a relatively small number (2) The filters are sensitive to higher-order statistical of nodes. structure (beyond pairwise correlations). If the input features are localized, the filters' receptive fields tend to be localized as well. (3) Multiresolution sets of filters with subsampling at low spatial frequencies - related to pyramid coding and wavelet representations - emerge as favored solutions for certain types of input ensembles.

(3) Multiresolution sets of filters with subsampling at low spatial frequencies - related to pyramid coding and wavelet representations - emerge as favored solutions for certain types of input ensembles.

paragraphs: This paper asks what kinds of filters emerge when a processing stage is optimized to preserve information about its inputs. It uses infomax, which maximizes average mutual information between input and output while accounting for constraints and processing noise. The investigation applies this principle to a class of nonlinear mappings.

Under certain conditions, the resulting filters have several useful properties. For an individual input, activity tends to concentrate in a relatively small number of output nodes. The filters also respond to statistical structure beyond pairwise correlations. When the input features are localized, their receptive fields—the portions of the input to which they respond—also tend to become localized.

For some input ensembles, favored solutions include filters operating at multiple resolutions, with subsampling at low spatial frequencies. These solutions are related to pyramid and wavelet representations. The significance is that sparse activity, localized sensitivity, and multiresolution structure can arise from a common encoding objective. The stated conditions and dependence on input statistics are central to what the result establishes.
summary.tldr: Under suitable conditions, maximizing information preservation produces sparse responses, localized receptive fields, and multiresolution filters.

title: Deriving Receptive Fields Using an Optimal Encoding Criterion

abstract: A hint is any piece of side information about the target function to be learned. We consider the monotonicity hint, which states that the function to be learned is monotonic in some or all of the input variables. The application of mono tonicity hints is demonstrated on two real-world problems- a credit card application task, and a problem in medical diagnosis. A measure of the monotonicity error of a candidate function is defined and an objective function for the enforcement of monotonicity is derived from Bayesian principles. We report experimental results which show that using monotonicity hints leads to a statistically significant improvement in performance on both problems.
originalAbstract: A hint is any piece of side information about the target function to be learned. We consider the monotonicity hint, which states that the function to be learned is monotonic in some or all of the input variables. The application of mono tonicity hints is demonstrated on two real-world problems- a credit card application task, and a problem in medical diagnosis. A measure of the monotonicity error of a candidate function is defined and an objective function for the enforcement of monotonicity is derived from Bayesian principles. We report experimental results which show that using monotonicity hints leads to a statistically significant improvement in performance on both problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies how prior knowledge about a function's direction of change can help a learning system. A monotonicity hint says that increasing certain inputs should move the output consistently in one direction. Such knowledge supplements the training examples by describing a relationship the learned function is expected to respect.

The authors define a measure of monotonicity error for a candidate function. This makes violations of the hint something that can be assessed during learning. They then derive an objective for enforcing monotonicity from Bayesian principles, connecting the side information to a formal learning criterion rather than leaving it as an informal preference.

The approach is demonstrated on a credit card application task and a medical diagnosis problem. Using the hints produces statistically significant performance improvements on both. These findings show that directional knowledge can be useful training information in practical prediction tasks. The applicable premise is that the target function is monotonic in some or all of the relevant inputs; the hint expresses that substantive knowledge about the problem.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian objective incorporates monotonicity knowledge and significantly improves performance on two real-world prediction tasks.

title: Monotonicity Hints

abstract: How should we decide among competing explanations of a cognitive process given limited observations? The problem of model selection is at the heart of progress in cognitive science. In this paper, Minimum Description Length (MDL) is introduced as a method for selecting among computational models of cognition. We also show that differential geometry provides an intuitive understanding of what drives model selection in MDL. Finally, adequacy of MDL is demonstrated in two areas of cognitive modeling.
originalAbstract: How should we decide among competing explanations of a cognitive process given limited observations? The problem of model selection is at the heart of progress in cognitive science. In this paper, Minimum Description Length (MDL) is introduced as a method for selecting among computational models of cognition. We also show that differential geometry provides an intuitive understanding of what drives model selection in MDL. Finally, adequacy of MDL is demonstrated in two areas of cognitive modeling.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a basic problem in cognitive science: how to choose among computational explanations when observations are limited. Several models may offer accounts of the same cognitive process, so comparing them requires a selection principle. The authors introduce Minimum Description Length, or MDL, for making this choice among computational models of cognition.

A second contribution concerns understanding the selection principle itself. The authors use differential geometry to give an intuitive account of what drives MDL's decisions. This connects the formal model-selection method to a way of interpreting why it favors one candidate explanation over another, making the basis for selection part of the paper's focus.

The authors demonstrate the adequacy of MDL in two areas of cognitive modeling. These applications support its use in the settings examined. The work therefore combines a proposed selection method, an interpretation of its behavior, and demonstrations of its applicability, all directed at the problem of comparing explanations from limited observations.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces MDL for cognitive-model selection, explains its behavior geometrically, and demonstrates it in two modeling areas.

title: The Use of MDL to Select among Computational Models of Cognition

abstract: We show how a wavelet basis may be adapted to best represent natural images in terms of sparse coefficients. The wavelet basis, which may be either complete or overcomplete, is specified by a small number of spatial functions which are repeated across space and combined in a recursive fashion so as to be self-similar across scale. These functions are adapted to minimize the estimated code length under a model that assumes images are composed of a linear superposition of sparse, independent components. When adapted to natural images, the wavelet bases take on different orientations and they evenly tile the orientation domain, in stark contrast to the standard, non-oriented wavelet bases used in image compression. When the basis set is allowed to be overcomplete, it also yields higher coding efficiency than standard wavelet bases.
originalAbstract: We show how a wavelet basis may be adapted to best represent natural images in terms of sparse coefficients. The wavelet basis, which may be either complete or overcomplete, is specified by a small number of spatial functions which are repeated across space and combined in a recursive fashion so as to be self-similar across scale. These functions are adapted to minimize the estimated code length under a model that assumes images are composed of a linear superposition of sparse, independent components. When adapted to natural images, the wavelet bases take on different orientations and they evenly tile the orientation domain, in stark contrast to the standard, non-oriented wavelet bases used in image compression. When the basis set is allowed to be overcomplete, it also yields higher coding efficiency than standard wavelet bases.

paragraphs: This paper adapts wavelet representations to encode natural images with sparse coefficients. The representation is built from a small collection of spatial functions repeated across image locations and combined recursively across scales. This architecture preserves a self-similar structure while allowing the functions themselves to be learned from images.

Learning minimizes an estimated code length under a model in which images are linear combinations of sparse, independent components. The basis can be complete or overcomplete, allowing the study to examine both forms within the same architecture. The objective ties the learned visual structure to how efficiently the model represents the image data.

When trained on natural images, the functions develop different orientations that evenly cover the orientation domain. The authors contrast this with standard non-oriented wavelet bases used in image compression. When overcompleteness is allowed, the learned representation also achieves higher coding efficiency than standard wavelets. The findings connect adaptation to both the organization of image features and an improvement in the efficiency of their representation.
summary.tldr: Learning wavelet functions from natural images produces evenly distributed orientations and, with overcompleteness, better coding efficiency than standard wavelets.

title: Learning Sparse Image Codes using a Wavelet Pyramid Architecture

abstract: We are constructing caching policies that have 13-20% lower miss rates than the best of twelve baseline policies over a large variety of request streams. This represents an improvement of 49–63% over Least Recently Used, the most commonly implemented policy. We achieve this not by designing a speciﬁc new policy but by using on-line Machine Learning algorithms to dynamically shift between the standard policies based on their observed miss rates. A thorough experimental evaluation of our techniques is given, as well as a discussion of what makes caching an interesting on-line learning problem.
originalAbstract: We are constructing caching policies that have 13-20% lower miss rates than the best of twelve baseline policies over a large variety of request streams. This represents an improvement of 49–63% over Least Recently Used, the most commonly implemented policy. We achieve this not by designing a speciﬁc new policy but by using on-line Machine Learning algorithms to dynamically shift between the standard policies based on their observed miss rates. A thorough experimental evaluation of our techniques is given, as well as a discussion of what makes caching an interesting on-line learning problem.

paragraphs: No single cache-replacement policy is best for every request stream. This paper uses online learning to change among standard policies as their observed performance changes. The aim is to exploit existing policy strengths dynamically instead of designing one fixed replacement rule for all workloads.

The learner tracks miss rates and shifts its choices toward policies performing well on the current stream. This turns caching into an adaptive decision problem with repeated feedback. A broad experimental evaluation examines whether the combined behavior improves on simply committing to one baseline policy.

Reported miss rates are 13%–20% below the best of twelve baselines and 49%–63% below Least Recently Used. The contribution illustrates how learning at the policy-selection level can outperform the components considered individually. The size of the improvement depends on the evaluated request streams, but the mechanism is general: adapt the policy as evidence about the workload accumulates.
summary.tldr: Online learning adaptively combines cache policies, substantially reducing misses compared with fixed baselines on diverse request streams.

title: Adaptive Caching by Refetching

abstract: Adaptation is a ubiquitous neural and psychological phenomenon, with a wealth of instantiations and implications. Although a basic form of plasticity, it has, bar some notable exceptions, attracted computational theory of only one main variety. In this paper, we study adaptation from the perspective of factor analysis, a paradigmatic technique of unsuper- vised learning. We use factor analysis to re-interpret a standard view of adaptation, and apply our new model to some recent data on adaptation in the domain of face discrimination.
originalAbstract: Adaptation is a ubiquitous neural and psychological phenomenon, with a wealth of instantiations and implications. Although a basic form of plasticity, it has, bar some notable exceptions, attracted computational theory of only one main variety. In this paper, we study adaptation from the perspective of factor analysis, a paradigmatic technique of unsuper- vised learning. We use factor analysis to re-interpret a standard view of adaptation, and apply our new model to some recent data on adaptation in the domain of face discrimination.

paragraphs: The paper examines adaptation as a problem of unsupervised learning. Adaptation appears across neural activity and psychological experience, and the authors treat it as a basic form of plasticity. Their motivation is that computational accounts have largely followed one main theoretical approach, despite the variety of phenomena that adaptation encompasses.

Their alternative starts from factor analysis, a method for explaining observed variation through underlying factors. They use this perspective to reinterpret an established account of adaptation and develop a new model. This connects the question of how responses change with experience to the question of how a system represents patterns in its inputs.

The authors apply the model to data on adaptation in face discrimination. This gives the proposed interpretation a concrete perceptual setting: changes in the ability to distinguish faces. The contribution described is a new computational perspective and its application to those observations; the abstract does not establish that this perspective explains adaptation across all its forms.
summary.tldr: The paper uses factor analysis to reinterpret adaptation as unsupervised learning and applies the resulting model to face discrimination.

title: Adaptation and Unsupervised Learning

abstract: We describe a method for learning sparse multiscale image repre- sentations using a sparse prior distribution over the basis function coe(cid:14)cients. The prior consists of a mixture of a Gaussian and a Dirac delta function, and thus encourages coe(cid:14)cients to have exact zero values. Coe(cid:14)cients for an image are computed by sampling from the resulting posterior distribution with a Gibbs sampler. The learned basis is similar to the Steerable Pyramid basis, and yields slightly higher SNR for the same number of active coe(cid:14)cients. De- noising using the learned image model is demonstrated for some standard test images, with results that compare favorably with other denoising methods.
originalAbstract: We describe a method for learning sparse multiscale image repre- sentations using a sparse prior distribution over the basis function coe(cid:14)cients. The prior consists of a mixture of a Gaussian and a Dirac delta function, and thus encourages coe(cid:14)cients to have exact zero values. Coe(cid:14)cients for an image are computed by sampling from the resulting posterior distribution with a Gibbs sampler. The learned basis is similar to the Steerable Pyramid basis, and yields slightly higher SNR for the same number of active coe(cid:14)cients. De- noising using the learned image model is demonstrated for some standard test images, with results that compare favorably with other denoising methods.

paragraphs: The paper learns image representations that describe structure at multiple scales while using relatively few active coefficients. Sparsity is encouraged through a prior that mixes a Gaussian distribution with a Dirac delta function. The delta component places probability directly at zero, encouraging coefficients to be exactly inactive.

For a given image, coefficients are computed by sampling from the posterior distribution with a Gibbs sampler. This connects the sparse prior with the image evidence when estimating the representation. The learned basis resembles the Steerable Pyramid basis, and the authors report slightly higher signal-to-noise ratio for the same number of active coefficients.

The learned image model is also demonstrated in denoising standard test images, where results compare favorably with other methods. The representation result concerns a modest improvement at a matched level of coefficient activity; the denoising result shows another use of the learned model. Together, they support a probabilistic approach in which exact zeros are built into the prior and image structure is learned across scales.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-and-point-mass prior learns sparse multiscale image representations with exact zeros and favorable reported representation and denoising results.

title: Learning Sparse Multiscale Image Representations

abstract: Online mechanism design (MD) considers the problem of provid- ing incentives to implement desired system-wide outcomes in sys- tems with self-interested agents that arrive and depart dynami- cally. Agents can choose to misrepresent their arrival and depar- ture times, in addition to information about their value for di(cid:11)erent outcomes. We consider the problem of maximizing the total long- term value of the system despite the self-interest of agents. The online MD problem induces a Markov Decision Process (MDP), which when solved can be used to implement optimal policies in a truth-revealing Bayesian-Nash equilibrium.
originalAbstract: Online mechanism design (MD) considers the problem of provid- ing incentives to implement desired system-wide outcomes in sys- tems with self-interested agents that arrive and depart dynami- cally. Agents can choose to misrepresent their arrival and depar- ture times, in addition to information about their value for di(cid:11)erent outcomes. We consider the problem of maximizing the total long- term value of the system despite the self-interest of agents. The online MD problem induces a Markov Decision Process (MDP), which when solved can be used to implement optimal policies in a truth-revealing Bayesian-Nash equilibrium.

paragraphs: The paper considers systems in which self-interested agents arrive and leave over time. The designer wants decisions that maximize total long-term value, but agents may benefit from misreporting information. Their strategic choices include claims about when they arrive or depart, as well as how much they value different outcomes.

The approach expresses this online mechanism design problem as a Markov decision process. This connects the sequence of system decisions to a framework for optimizing value over time. The objective therefore accounts for the continuing operation of the system, rather than treating each interaction as a separate decision with only immediate consequences.

The stated result links the solution of that decision process to incentives: when the induced process is solved, its optimal policies can be implemented in a truth-revealing Bayesian-Nash equilibrium. Truthful reporting is thus supported in the specified equilibrium sense. The contribution is the connection between long-term optimization and strategic reporting in a system whose participants change dynamically.
summary.tldr: Solving an induced Markov decision process can support optimal long-term policies with truthful reporting in Bayesian-Nash equilibrium.

title: An MDP-Based Approach to Online Mechanism Design

abstract: We present a globally convergent method for regularized risk minimization prob- lems. Our method applies to Support Vector estimation, regression, Gaussian Processes, and any other regularized risk minimization setting which leads to a convex optimization problem. SVMPerf can be shown to be a special case of our approach. In addition to the uniﬁed framework we present tight convergence bounds, which show that our algorithm converges in O(1/) steps to  precision for general convex problems and in O(log(1/)) steps for continuously differen- tiable problems. We demonstrate in experiments the performance of our approach.
originalAbstract: We present a globally convergent method for regularized risk minimization prob- lems. Our method applies to Support Vector estimation, regression, Gaussian Processes, and any other regularized risk minimization setting which leads to a convex optimization problem. SVMPerf can be shown to be a special case of our approach. In addition to the uniﬁed framework we present tight convergence bounds, which show that our algorithm converges in O(1/) steps to  precision for general convex problems and in O(log(1/)) steps for continuously differen- tiable problems. We demonstrate in experiments the performance of our approach.

paragraphs: The paper presents a globally convergent optimization method for regularized risk minimization. This formulation combines the objective of fitting observations with a regularization term. The method applies when the resulting optimization problem is convex, providing a common framework for several learning tasks instead of requiring a separate optimization treatment for each.

The authors identify support vector estimation, regression, and Gaussian processes among the applications covered by this framework. They also show that SVMPerf is a special case. That relationship places an existing specialized approach inside a broader method and helps explain the scope of the proposed unification.

The theoretical results give tight bounds on the number of steps needed to reach a requested precision. For general convex problems, the bound grows in proportion to the inverse of that precision. For continuously differentiable problems, it grows logarithmically with the inverse precision. Thus, the stated guarantees distinguish between general convex objectives and the smoother case. Experiments demonstrate the method’s performance alongside this convergence analysis.
summary.tldr: A unified method for convex regularized risk minimization provides global convergence and stronger iteration bounds for continuously differentiable objectives.

title: Bundle Methods for Machine Learning

abstract: We propose a new fast Gaussian summation algorithm for high-dimensional datasets with high accuracy. First, we extend the original fast multipole-type methods to use approximation schemes with both hard and probabilistic error. Second, we utilize a new data structure called subspace tree which maps each data point in the node to its lower dimensional mapping as determined by any linear dimension reduction method such as PCA. This new data structure is suitable for reducing the cost of each pairwise distance computation, the most dominant cost in many kernel methods. Our algorithm guarantees probabilistic relative error on each kernel sum, and can be applied to high-dimensional Gaussian summations which are ubiquitous inside many kernel methods as the key computational bottleneck. We provide empirical speedup results on low to high-dimensional datasets up to 89 dimensions.
originalAbstract: We propose a new fast Gaussian summation algorithm for high-dimensional datasets with high accuracy. First, we extend the original fast multipole-type methods to use approximation schemes with both hard and probabilistic error. Second, we utilize a new data structure called subspace tree which maps each data point in the node to its lower dimensional mapping as determined by any linear dimension reduction method such as PCA. This new data structure is suitable for reducing the cost of each pairwise distance computation, the most dominant cost in many kernel methods. Our algorithm guarantees probabilistic relative error on each kernel sum, and can be applied to high-dimensional Gaussian summations which are ubiquitous inside many kernel methods as the key computational bottleneck. We provide empirical speedup results on low to high-dimensional datasets up to 89 dimensions.

paragraphs: Many kernel methods repeatedly add Gaussian contributions from data points, making these summations a computational bottleneck. This paper develops a fast summation algorithm for high-dimensional data. It targets both the number of calculations involved in approximation and the cost of computing individual distances between points.

The method extends multipole-style approximation to accommodate both hard and probabilistic error criteria. It also introduces a subspace tree, whose nodes represent their data through lower-dimensional mappings obtained with a linear dimension-reduction method such as PCA. These mappings reduce the cost of pairwise distance calculations, which the authors identify as a dominant expense in many kernel methods.

The algorithm provides a probabilistic relative-error guarantee for each kernel sum. That means its stated accuracy control is probabilistic and applies to the individual sums, rather than asserting error-free computation. Empirical speedups are reported across datasets ranging from low dimensionality to 89 dimensions. The contribution connects that accuracy control with a data structure designed to reduce a particularly expensive part of high-dimensional computation.
summary.tldr: A Monte Carlo multipole method uses lower-dimensional tree representations to accelerate Gaussian sums with probabilistic relative-error guarantees.

title: Fast High-dimensional Kernel Summations Using the Monte Carlo Multipole Method

abstract: The linear correlation coefficient is typically used to characterize and analyze dependencies of neural spike counts. Here, we show that the correlation coefficient is in general insufficient to characterize these dependencies. We construct two neuron spike count models with Poisson-like marginals and vary their dependence structure using copulas. To this end, we construct a copula that allows to keep the spike counts uncorrelated while varying their dependence strength. Moreover, we employ a network of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons to investigate whether weakly correlated spike counts with strong dependencies are likely to occur in real networks. We find that the entropy of uncorrelated but dependent spike count distributions can deviate from the corresponding distribution with independent components by more than 25% and that weakly correlated but strongly dependent spike counts are very likely to occur in biological networks. Finally, we introduce a test for deciding whether the dependence structure of distributions with Poisson-like marginals is well characterized by the linear correlation coefficient and verify it for different copula-based models.
originalAbstract: The linear correlation coefficient is typically used to characterize and analyze dependencies of neural spike counts. Here, we show that the correlation coefficient is in general insufficient to characterize these dependencies. We construct two neuron spike count models with Poisson-like marginals and vary their dependence structure using copulas. To this end, we construct a copula that allows to keep the spike counts uncorrelated while varying their dependence strength. Moreover, we employ a network of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons to investigate whether weakly correlated spike counts with strong dependencies are likely to occur in real networks. We find that the entropy of uncorrelated but dependent spike count distributions can deviate from the corresponding distribution with independent components by more than 25% and that weakly correlated but strongly dependent spike counts are very likely to occur in biological networks. Finally, we introduce a test for deciding whether the dependence structure of distributions with Poisson-like marginals is well characterized by the linear correlation coefficient and verify it for different copula-based models.

paragraphs: A small correlation between two neurons' spike counts can suggest that their activity is largely unrelated. This paper shows why that interpretation can fail: linear correlation does not generally capture the full dependence between counts. Two spike counts can be uncorrelated while still carrying substantial information about one another.

The authors construct paired spike-count models with Poisson-like individual distributions and control their dependence using copulas. One construction changes dependence strength while keeping correlation at zero. They find that the entropy of an uncorrelated but dependent distribution can differ by more than 25% from that of the corresponding independent distribution. Thus, matching correlation does not imply matching information content.

A network of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons is used to investigate whether this issue is plausible in biological networks. The findings suggest that weak correlation alongside strong dependence is very likely to occur there. The authors also introduce a test for whether linear correlation adequately describes dependence in Poisson-like counts, checking it on several copula-based models.
summary.tldr: Neural spike counts can have weak or zero linear correlation despite strong dependence, motivating a test of whether correlation is adequate.

title: Correlation Coefficients are Insufficient for Analyzing Spike Count Dependencies

abstract: Mixture distributions are often used to model complex data. In this paper, we develop a new method that jointly estimates mixture models over multiple data sets by exploiting the statistical dependencies between them. Specifically, we introduce a set of latent Dirichlet processes as sources of component models (atoms), and for each data set, we construct a nonparametric mixture model by combining sub-sampled versions of the latent DPs. Each mixture model may acquire atoms from different latent DPs, while each atom may be shared by multiple mixtures. This multi-to-multi association distinguishes the proposed method from prior constructions that rely on tree or chain structures, allowing mixture models to be coupled more flexibly. In addition, we derive a sampling algorithm that jointly infers the model parameters and present experiments on both document analysis and image modeling.
originalAbstract: Mixture distributions are often used to model complex data. In this paper, we develop a new method that jointly estimates mixture models over multiple data sets by exploiting the statistical dependencies between them. Specifically, we introduce a set of latent Dirichlet processes as sources of component models (atoms), and for each data set, we construct a nonparametric mixture model by combining sub-sampled versions of the latent DPs. Each mixture model may acquire atoms from different latent DPs, while each atom may be shared by multiple mixtures. This multi-to-multi association distinguishes the proposed method from prior constructions that rely on tree or chain structures, allowing mixture models to be coupled more flexibly. In addition, we derive a sampling algorithm that jointly infers the model parameters and present experiments on both document analysis and image modeling.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to fit mixture models to several related datasets together. A mixture describes complex data through component models, and related datasets may benefit from sharing some of those components. The challenge is to express their statistical connections without forcing every dataset into the same rigid sharing pattern.

The authors introduce latent Dirichlet processes that act as sources of components, called atoms. Each dataset’s mixture combines subsampled versions of these sources. A single mixture can draw atoms from multiple sources, and an individual atom can appear in several mixtures. This creates a many-to-many pattern of sharing across datasets and latent sources.

That flexibility distinguishes the construction from approaches organized around trees or chains. The authors also derive a sampling algorithm that jointly estimates the model parameters, providing a procedure for fitting the coupled mixtures. Experiments in document analysis and image modeling demonstrate the construction in two application areas, illustrating how the same sharing framework can support different kinds of data.
summary.tldr: Latent Dirichlet processes let related mixture models share components through flexible many-to-many relationships.

title: Coupling Nonparametric Mixtures via Latent Dirichlet Processes

abstract: Any reinforcement learning algorithm that applies to all Markov decision processes (MDPs) will suffer $\Omega(\sqrt{SAT})$ regret on some MDP, where $T$ is the elapsed time and $S$ and $A$ are the cardinalities of the state and action spaces. This implies $T = \Omega(SA)$ time to guarantee a near-optimal policy. In many settings of practical interest, due to the curse of dimensionality, $S$ and $A$ can be so enormous that this learning time is unacceptable. We establish that, if the system is known to be a \emph{factored} MDP, it is possible to achieve regret that scales polynomially in the number of \emph{parameters} encoding the factored MDP, which may be exponentially smaller than $S$ or $A$. We provide two algorithms that satisfy near-optimal regret bounds in this context: posterior sampling reinforcement learning (PSRL) and an upper confidence bound algorithm (UCRL-Factored).

In many settings of practical interest, due to the curse of dimensionality, $S$ and $A$ can be so enormous that this learning time is unacceptable. paragraphs: A reinforcement learning algorithm that covers arbitrary Markov decision processes must face difficult cases whose regret scales with the sizes of the state and action spaces. The abstract gives a lower bound proportional to the square root of SAT, where T is elapsed time. When states and actions are extremely numerous, the resulting learning requirement can be prohibitive.

The paper shows how known factored structure changes this picture. For a factored MDP, regret can scale polynomially with the number of parameters describing the system. That parameter count may be exponentially smaller than the number of states or actions, creating the possibility of much more favorable learning guarantees.

The key condition is that the system is known to be factored. The result therefore explains how exploiting an available compact representation can reduce the statistical burden of learning, even when the full state or action space is enormous.
summary.tldr: For known factored MDPs, two algorithms achieve near-optimal regret bounds governed by a potentially much smaller parameterization.

title: Near-optimal Reinforcement Learning in Factored MDPs

abstract: We consider the problem of sparse signal recovery from $m$ linear measurements quantized to $b$ bits. $b$-bit Marginal Regression is proposed as recovery algorithm. We study the question of choosing $b$ in the setting of a given budget of bits $B = m \cdot b$ and derive a single easy-to-compute expression characterizing the trade-off between $m$ and $b$. The choice $b = 1$ turns out to be optimal for estimating the unit vector corresponding to the signal for any level of additive Gaussian noise before quantization as well as for adversarial noise. For $b \geq 2$, we show that Lloyd-Max quantization constitutes an optimal quantization scheme and that the norm of the signal canbe estimated consistently by maximum likelihood.

paragraphs: When measurements must be stored using a fixed number of bits, there is a choice between collecting more coarse measurements and fewer precise ones. This paper studies that choice for sparse signal recovery from linear measurements. Each of the m measurements receives b bits, so the total budget is B = m × b.

The authors propose b-bit Marginal Regression and derive a single expression that characterizes the trade-off between measurement count and precision. For estimating the signal's direction, represented by its unit vector, one bit per measurement is optimal in the setting they analyze. This result covers any level of additive Gaussian noise before quantization, as well as adversarial noise.

The distinction between direction and magnitude matters. The one-bit conclusion concerns the unit vector, rather than full recovery of the signal's scale. For two or more bits per measurement, the paper establishes optimality of Lloyd-Max quantization and shows that maximum likelihood can consistently estimate the signal's norm. Together, these results connect allocation of a bit budget to the particular aspect of the signal being estimated.
summary.tldr: Under a fixed bit budget, one-bit measurements are optimal for estimating sparse signal direction in the analyzed setting.

title: b-bit Marginal Regression

abstract: Symmetry breaking is a technique for speeding up propositional satisfiability testing by adding constraints to the theory that restrict the search space while preserving satisfiability. In this work, we extend symmetry breaking to the problem of model finding in weighted and unweighted relational theories, a class of problems that includes MAP inference in Markov Logic and similar statistical-relational languages. We introduce term symmetries, which are induced by an evidence set and extend to symmetries over a relational theory. We provide the important special case of term equivalent symmetries, showing that such symmetries can be found in low-degree polynomial time. We show how to break an exponential number of these symmetries with added constraints whose number is linear in the size of the domain. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these techniques through experiments in two relational domains. We also discuss the connections between relational symmetry breaking and work on lifted inference in statistical-relational reasoning.

paragraphs: Symmetry can make a search procedure revisit configurations that differ in form but are equivalent for the problem being solved. Symmetry breaking reduces this redundancy by adding constraints. This paper extends that idea from propositional satisfiability to model finding in weighted and unweighted relational theories, including MAP inference in Markov Logic.

The authors introduce term symmetries, which arise from the evidence and extend to symmetries of the relational theory. They then identify a special class called term equivalent symmetries and show that these can be detected in low-degree polynomial time. This supplies a tractable way to find a useful class of redundancies before restricting the search.

The paper shows that a number of added constraints linear in domain size can break exponentially many of these symmetries. Experiments in two relational domains demonstrate the effectiveness of the techniques. The authors also relate this approach to lifted inference, connecting compact reasoning about relational structure with a concrete method for reducing redundant inference work.
summary.tldr: Efficiently detected relational symmetries can be broken with compact constraints to reduce redundant work in MAP inference.

title: Lifted Symmetry Detection and Breaking for MAP Inference

abstract: We propose a method for combining two sources of astronomical data, spectroscopy and photometry, that carry information about sources of light (e.g., stars, galaxies, and quasars) at extremely different spectral resolutions. Our model treats the spectral energy distribution (SED) of the radiation from a source as a latent variable that jointly explains both photometric and spectroscopic observations. We place a flexible, nonparametric prior over the SED of a light source that admits a physically interpretable decomposition, and allows us to tractably perform inference. We use our model to predict the distribution of the redshift of a quasar from five-band (low spectral resolution) photometric data, the so called ``photo-z'' problem. Our method shows that tools from machine learning and Bayesian statistics allow us to leverage multiple resolutions of information to make accurate predictions with well-characterized uncertainties.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to combine astronomical measurements that describe light at very different spectral resolutions. Spectroscopy provides one kind of observation, while photometry provides another. The model connects them through a shared, unobserved spectral energy distribution: the underlying pattern of radiation that is intended to explain both sources of data.

A Gaussian process supplies a flexible, nonparametric prior over that distribution. This lets the model represent variation without committing to a fixed parametric shape. The construction also admits a physically interpretable decomposition and keeps inference tractable. Those properties matter together: the representation can accommodate varied spectra while supporting both interpretation and computation.

The application is predicting a quasar’s redshift from photometric observations in five bands. The output is a distribution over redshift, making uncertainty part of the prediction itself. The reported findings show that combining information across resolutions through a Bayesian model can produce accurate predictions with well-characterized uncertainty.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model connects spectroscopy and photometry through a shared latent spectrum to predict quasar redshifts with characterized uncertainty.

title: A Gaussian Process Model of Quasar Spectral Energy Distributions

abstract: We present a derivation and theoretical investigation of the Adams-Bashforth and Adams-Moulton family of linear multistep methods for solving ordinary differential equations, starting from a Gaussian process (GP) framework. In the limit, this formulation coincides with the classical deterministic methods, which have been used as higher-order initial value problem solvers for over a century. Furthermore, the natural probabilistic framework provided by the GP formulation allows us to derive probabilistic versions of these methods, in the spirit of a number of other probabilistic ODE solvers presented in the recent literature. In contrast to higher-order Runge-Kutta methods, which require multiple intermediate function evaluations per step, Adams family methods make use of previous function evaluations, so that increased accuracy arising from a higher-order multistep approach comes at very little additional computational cost. We show that through a careful choice of covariance function for the GP, the posterior mean and standard deviation over the numerical solution can be made to exactly coincide with the value given by the deterministic method and its local truncation error respectively. We provide a rigorous proof of the convergence of these new methods, as well as an empirical investigation (up to fifth order) demonstrating their convergence rates in practice.

paragraphs: Numerical methods for ordinary differential equations approximate how a system evolves from an initial condition. This paper derives the Adams-Bashforth and Adams-Moulton families from a Gaussian process framework. The formulation recovers the classical deterministic methods in a limit and also supports probabilistic versions of these established solvers.

Adams methods reuse previous function evaluations when taking the next step. Consequently, increasing their order can improve accuracy with little additional computation, unlike higher-order Runge-Kutta methods that require multiple intermediate evaluations per step. The probabilistic construction adds a way to represent uncertainty around the numerical solution while retaining this reuse of earlier calculations.

With a carefully chosen Gaussian process covariance function, the posterior mean exactly matches the deterministic numerical value, and the posterior standard deviation matches its local truncation error. The authors prove convergence and empirically investigate convergence rates for methods up to fifth order. This connects the probabilistic output to a specific numerical-error quantity and supports the methods with both analysis and experiments.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian process formulation produces convergent probabilistic Adams solvers whose means and standard deviations can match classical solutions and local truncation errors.

title: Probabilistic Linear Multistep Methods

abstract: We propose a novel approach to reduce memory consumption of the backpropagation through time (BPTT) algorithm when training recurrent neural networks (RNNs). Our approach uses dynamic programming to balance a trade-off between caching of intermediate results and recomputation. The algorithm is capable of tightly fitting within almost any user-set memory budget while finding an optimal execution policy minimizing the computational cost. Computational devices have limited memory capacity and maximizing a computational performance given a fixed memory budget is a practical use-case. We provide asymptotic computational upper bounds for various regimes. The algorithm is particularly effective for long sequences. For sequences of length 1000, our algorithm saves 95\% of memory usage while using only one third more time per iteration than the standard BPTT.

paragraphs: Training recurrent neural networks with backpropagation through time requires managing intermediate results across a sequence. Keeping those results available consumes memory, while recreating them later consumes computation. This paper treats the choice between storage and recomputation as an optimization problem governed by a user-selected memory budget.

The proposed algorithm uses dynamic programming to choose an execution policy that minimizes computational cost within that budget. It can fit tightly within almost any specified memory allowance. This makes available device memory an explicit input to the training schedule, allowing the procedure to determine which intermediate results are worth retaining and which should be recomputed.

The authors provide asymptotic upper bounds on computation for several regimes and report particular benefits for long sequences. For sequences of length 1000, the method reduces memory use by 95% while increasing time per iteration by only one third relative to standard backpropagation through time. That example illustrates a substantial memory reduction at a measured computational cost, rather than a claim that memory savings come without extra work.
summary.tldr: Dynamic programming optimizes storage and recomputation for recurrent-network training under a user-set memory budget.

title: Memory-Efficient Backpropagation Through Time

abstract: With the recent success of embeddings in natural language processing, research has been conducted into applying similar methods to code analysis. Most works attempt to process the code directly or use a syntactic tree representation, treating it like sentences written in a natural language. However, none of the existing methods are sufficient to comprehend program semantics robustly, due to structural features such as function calls, branching, and interchangeable order of statements. In this paper, we propose a novel processing technique to learn code semantics, and apply it to a variety of program analysis tasks. In particular, we stipulate that a robust distributional hypothesis of code applies to both human- and machine-generated programs. Following this hypothesis, we define an embedding space, inst2vec, based on an Intermediate Representation (IR) of the code that is independent of the source programming language. We provide a novel definition of contextual flow for this IR, leveraging both the underlying data- and control-flow of the program. We then analyze the embeddings qualitatively using analogies and clustering, and evaluate the learned representation on three different high-level tasks. We show that even without fine-tuning, a single RNN architecture and fixed inst2vec embeddings outperform specialized approaches for performance prediction (compute device mapping, optimal thread coarsening); and algorithm classification from raw code (104 classes), where we set a new state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Programs contain relationships that are difficult to capture by treating source code like ordinary text. Function calls, branches, and statements that can change order complicate learning meaning from nearby tokens alone. This paper proposes inst2vec, an embedding approach built on a source-language-independent intermediate representation of code.

The authors formulate a distributional hypothesis intended to apply to both human-written and machine-generated programs. They define context using both data flow and control flow in the intermediate representation. This gives the embedding learner access to relationships involving how information moves and how execution proceeds. They examine the resulting representations through analogies and clustering.

The approach outperforms specialized methods for compute-device mapping and optimal thread coarsening, and establishes a new state of the art for classification into 104 algorithm classes. These results support the usefulness of one shared code representation across distinct program-analysis tasks.
summary.tldr: Inst2vec learns code embeddings from intermediate-representation data and control flow, supporting several program-analysis tasks with one fixed representation.

title: Neural Code Comprehension: A Learnable Representation of Code Semantics

abstract: We present a novel approach to probabilistic time series forecasting that combines state space models with deep learning. By parametrizing a per-time-series linear state space model with a jointly-learned recurrent neural network, our method retains desired properties of state space models such as data efficiency and interpretability, while making use of the ability to learn complex patterns from raw data offered by deep learning approaches. Our method scales gracefully from regimes where little training data is available to regimes where data from millions of time series can be leveraged to learn accurate models. We provide qualitative as well as quantitative results with the proposed method, showing that it compares favorably to the state-of-the-art.
originalAbstract: We present a novel approach to probabilistic time series forecasting that combines state space models with deep learning. By parametrizing a per-time-series linear state space model with a jointly-learned recurrent neural network, our method retains desired properties of state space models such as data efficiency and interpretability, while making use of the ability to learn complex patterns from raw data offered by deep learning approaches. Our method scales gracefully from regimes where little training data is available to regimes where data from millions of time series can be leveraged to learn accurate models. We provide qualitative as well as quantitative results with the proposed method, showing that it compares favorably to the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting can benefit from both structured statistical models and neural networks that learn complex patterns from data. This paper combines these approaches for probabilistic forecasting, where predictions describe uncertainty about future values. Its central design pairs a separate linear state-space model for each series with a jointly learned recurrent neural network.

The recurrent network supplies the parameters of the individual state-space models. This arrangement allows learning to draw on multiple time series while retaining a structured model for each one. The authors describe the resulting method as preserving useful state-space properties, including data efficiency and interpretability, while incorporating deep learning's ability to extract complicated patterns from raw observations.

The method is presented as working across a broad range of data availability, from limited training data to collections containing millions of time series. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations report favorable comparisons with state-of-the-art methods. The findings support the value of combining a shared neural learning component with individual structured forecasting models, particularly when the amount of available data varies substantially.
summary.tldr: A shared recurrent network parameterizes individual state-space models to combine flexible pattern learning with structured probabilistic forecasting.

title: Deep State Space Models for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: While statistics and machine learning offers numerous methods for ensuring generalization, these methods often fail in the presence of post selection ---the common practice in which the choice of analysis depends on previous interactions with the same dataset. A recent line of work has introduced powerful, general purpose algorithms that ensure a property called post hoc generalization (Cummings et al., COLT'16), which says that no person when given the output of the algorithm should be able to find any statistic for which the data differs significantly from the population it came from. In this work we show several limitations on the power of algorithms satisfying post hoc generalization. First, we show a tight lower bound on the error of any algorithm that satisfies post hoc generalization and answers adaptively chosen statistical queries, showing a strong barrier to progress in post selection data analysis. Second, we show that post hoc generalization is not closed under composition, despite many examples of such algorithms exhibiting strong composition properties.

In this work we show several limitations on the power of algorithms satisfying post hoc generalization. paragraphs: Analysts often choose their next question after seeing earlier results from the same dataset. This adaptive reuse can undermine ordinary generalization guarantees. Post hoc generalization addresses the problem by requiring that an algorithm's output not enable someone to identify a statistic whose dataset value differs substantially from its population value.

The paper establishes a tight lower bound on the error of algorithms that both satisfy this property and answer adaptively chosen statistical queries. This identifies a fundamental accuracy barrier within that class of algorithms. The result concerns what any qualifying method can achieve, rather than a weakness of a particular implementation.

The authors also show that post hoc generalization is not preserved under composition in general. Even though many individual algorithms with the property have strong composition behavior, the property alone does not ensure it. The two results clarify separate limits: how accurately adaptive queries can be answered under this guarantee, and whether guarantees for individual analyses can automatically be carried over when those analyses are combined.
summary.tldr: Post hoc generalization imposes a tight adaptive-query accuracy barrier and does not, by itself, survive composition.

title: The Limits of Post-Selection Generalization

abstract: The simple, elegant approach of training convolutional neural networks (CNNs) directly from RGB pixels has enjoyed overwhelming empirical success. But can more performance be squeezed out of networks by using different input representations? In this paper we propose and explore a simple idea: train CNNs directly on the blockwise discrete cosine transform (DCT) coefficients computed and available in the middle of the JPEG codec. Intuitively, when processing JPEG images using CNNs, it seems unnecessary to decompress a blockwise frequency representation to an expanded pixel representation, shuffle it from CPU to GPU, and then process it with a CNN that will learn something similar to a transform back to frequency representation in its first layers. Why not skip both steps and feed the frequency domain into the network directly? In this paper we modify \libjpeg to produce DCT coefficients directly, modify a ResNet-50 network to accommodate the differently sized and strided input, and evaluate performance on ImageNet. We find networks that are both faster and more accurate, as well as networks with about the same accuracy but 1.77x faster than ResNet-50.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether image classifiers can benefit from using the representation already present inside JPEG compression. Conventional convolutional networks receive RGB pixels after decompression. JPEG processing contains blockwise discrete cosine transform coefficients, which describe image information in a frequency representation. The authors propose feeding those coefficients directly to a network.

The motivation is to avoid expanding compressed image information into pixels, transferring that expanded representation, and then asking early network layers to learn frequency-like processing again. To implement the idea, the authors modify libjpeg to expose DCT coefficients and adapt ResNet-50 to the resulting input sizes and strides. The representation change therefore includes corresponding changes to the network’s input processing.

ImageNet experiments identify networks that are both faster and more accurate, as well as configurations with approximately the same accuracy as ResNet-50 at 1.77 times the speed. The findings show that the input representation can be an important source of efficiency. In this setting, computation can benefit from information already available within the image codec.
summary.tldr: Training adapted CNNs directly on JPEG frequency coefficients produces ImageNet models with improved speed, including 1.77× speed at similar ResNet-50 accuracy.

title: Faster Neural Networks Straight from JPEG

abstract: We present an approach for simultaneously separating and localizing multiple sound sources using recorded microphone data. Inspired by topic models, our approach is based on a probabilistic model of inter-microphone phase differences, and poses separation and localization as a Bayesian inference problem. We assume sound activity is locally smooth across time, frequency, and location, and use the known position of the microphones to obtain a consistent separation. We compare the performance of our method against existing algorithms on simulated anechoic voice data and find that it obtains high performance across a variety of input conditions.
originalAbstract: We present an approach for simultaneously separating and localizing multiple sound sources using recorded microphone data. Inspired by topic models, our approach is based on a probabilistic model of inter-microphone phase differences, and poses separation and localization as a Bayesian inference problem. We assume sound activity is locally smooth across time, frequency, and location, and use the known position of the microphones to obtain a consistent separation. We compare the performance of our method against existing algorithms on simulated anechoic voice data and find that it obtains high performance across a variety of input conditions.

paragraphs: The paper addresses two connected audio problems: separating several sound sources from microphone recordings and estimating where those sources are located. It treats these as a joint inference task. The observations used by the model are differences in sound phase between microphones, which provide information relevant to the spatial organization of the recorded sources.

Inspired by topic models, the authors construct a probabilistic model and formulate separation and localization as Bayesian inference. The approach assumes that sound activity varies smoothly within local neighborhoods of time, frequency, and location. It also uses the known microphone positions to obtain a consistent separation, linking statistical structure in the audio to the recording geometry.

The authors compare their method with existing algorithms using simulated voice recordings in anechoic conditions, where reverberation is absent. They report high performance across a variety of input conditions. The evidence therefore supports the joint modeling approach in the evaluated simulated setting, with local smoothness and known microphone positions serving as explicit ingredients of the method.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model combines microphone phase differences, known positions, and local activity smoothness to jointly separate and locate sound sources.

title: Latent Gaussian Activity Propagation: Using Smoothness and Structure to Separate and Localize Sounds in Large Noisy Environments

abstract: The standard margin-based structured prediction commonly uses a maximum loss over all possible structured outputs. The large-margin formulation including latent variables not only results in a non-convex formulation but also increases the search space by a factor of the size of the latent space. Recent work has proposed the use of the maximum loss over random structured outputs sampled independently from some proposal distribution, with theoretical guarantees. We extend this work by including latent variables. We study a new family of loss functions under Gaussian perturbations and analyze the effect of the latent space on the generalization bounds. We show that the non-convexity of learning with latent variables originates naturally, as it relates to a tight upper bound of the Gibbs decoder distortion with respect to the latent space. Finally, we provide a formulation using random samples and relaxations that produces a tighter upper bound of the Gibbs decoder distortion up to a statistical accuracy, which enables a polynomial time evaluation of the objective function. We illustrate the method with synthetic experiments and a computer vision application.

We extend this work by including latent variables. We study a new family of loss functions under Gaussian perturbations and analyze the effect of the latent space on the generalization bounds. We show that the non-convexity of learning with latent variables originates naturally, as it relates to a tight upper bound of the Gibbs decoder distortion with respect to the latent space. paragraphs: Structured prediction chooses outputs with multiple related parts. Standard margin-based training considers the maximum loss across possible outputs, and adding latent variables enlarges the search while introducing non-convexity. This paper extends an approach that replaces exhaustive output consideration with independently sampled structured outputs, bringing latent variables into that framework.

The authors study a family of loss functions under Gaussian perturbations and analyze how the latent space affects generalization bounds. They also connect non-convexity to a tight upper bound on Gibbs decoder distortion with respect to the latent space. This gives the difficult optimization structure a specific theoretical explanation within the proposed analysis.

A further formulation combines random samples and relaxations to produce a tighter upper bound on decoder distortion up to statistical accuracy. It permits polynomial-time evaluation of the objective function, addressing the cost of evaluating training criteria over large output and latent spaces. The authors illustrate the approach through synthetic experiments and a computer vision application; the computational claim specifically concerns objective evaluation.
summary.tldr: Gaussian perturbations, sampling, and relaxations support latent-variable structured prediction with analyzed bounds and polynomial-time objective evaluation.

title: Learning latent variable structured prediction models with Gaussian perturbations

abstract: A theoretical performance analysis of the graph neural network (GNN) is presented. For classification tasks, the neural network approach has the advantage in terms of flexibility that it can be employed in a data-driven manner, whereas Bayesian inference requires the assumption of a specific model. A fundamental question is then whether GNN has a high accuracy in addition to this flexibility. Moreover, whether the achieved performance is predominately a result of the backpropagation or the architecture itself is a matter of considerable interest. To gain a better insight into these questions, a mean-field theory of a minimal GNN architecture is developed for the graph partitioning problem. This demonstrates a good agreement with numerical experiments.

A fundamental question is then whether GNN has a high accuracy in addition to this flexibility. Moreover, whether the achieved performance is predominately a result of the backpropagation or the architecture itself is a matter of considerable interest. To gain a better insight into these questions, a mean-field theory of a minimal GNN architecture is developed for the graph partitioning problem. This demonstrates a good agreement with numerical experiments.

This paper asks how well that flexibility translates into accuracy and how much of the resulting performance comes from the architecture itself versus learning through backpropagation. These questions motivate a theoretical analysis of graph partitioning.

The authors develop a mean-field theory for a minimal GNN architecture on this problem. Choosing a minimal architecture makes a specific graph-learning system the object of analysis. The aim is to gain insight into its behavior and the sources of its performance, addressing questions that would be harder to disentangle from empirical accuracy alone.

The theoretical analysis agrees well with numerical experiments. This agreement supports the theory as a useful description of the studied architecture in graph partitioning. It provides an analytical foothold for examining why a GNN performs as it does. The stated finding is the match between theory and experiments; the abstract frames architecture versus backpropagation as a motivating question without assigning a universal share of performance to either.
summary.tldr: A mean-field analysis of a minimal graph neural network closely matches numerical experiments on graph partitioning.

title: Mean-field theory of graph neural networks in graph partitioning

abstract: Recently there has been a significant interest in learning disentangled representations, as they promise increased interpretability, generalization to unseen scenarios and faster learning on downstream tasks. In this paper, we investigate the usefulness of different notions of disentanglement for improving the fairness of downstream prediction tasks based on representations. We consider the setting where the goal is to predict a target variable based on the learned representation of high-dimensional observations (such as images) that depend on both the target variable and an unobserved sensitive variable. We show that in this setting both the optimal and empirical predictions can be unfair, even if the target variable and the sensitive variable are independent. Analyzing the representations of more than 12600 trained state-of-the-art disentangled models, we observe that several disentanglement scores are consistently correlated with increased fairness, suggesting that disentanglement may be a useful property to encourage fairness when sensitive variables are not observed.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate different factors underlying complex observations. This paper investigates whether that property helps make downstream predictions fairer. The setting involves observations, such as images, that depend on both a prediction target and a sensitive variable that is not observed during learning.

The authors show that both optimal predictions and predictions learned empirically can be unfair in this setting, even when the target and sensitive variable are independent. Independence between those variables therefore does not by itself settle the fairness of predictions made from the learned representation. This motivates examining the representation as part of the problem.

The empirical analysis covers representations from more than 12,600 trained disentanglement models. Several disentanglement scores consistently correlate with increased fairness. That finding suggests encouraging disentanglement may be useful when sensitive variables are unavailable. The evidence is an observed association between particular scores and fairness, preserving a distinction between a promising representation property and a guarantee that downstream predictions will be fair.
summary.tldr: Several disentanglement scores correlate with fairer downstream predictions, suggesting potential value when sensitive variables are unobserved.

title: On the Fairness of Disentangled Representations

abstract: The proliferation of automated inference algorithms in Bayesian statistics has provided practitioners newfound access to fast, reproducible data analysis and powerful statistical models. Designing automated methods that are also both computationally scalable and theoretically sound, however, remains a significant challenge. Recent work on Bayesian coresets takes the approach of compressing the dataset before running a standard inference algorithm, providing both scalability and guarantees on posterior approximation error. But the automation of past coreset methods is limited because they depend on the availability of a reasonable coarse posterior approximation, which is difficult to specify in practice. In the present work we remove this requirement by formulating coreset construction as sparsity-constrained variational inference within an exponential family. This perspective leads to a novel construction via greedy optimization, and also provides a unifying information-geometric view of present and past methods. The proposed Riemannian coreset construction algorithm is fully automated, requiring no problem-specific inputs aside from the probabilistic model and dataset. In addition to being significantly easier to use than past methods, experiments demonstrate that past coreset constructions are fundamentally limited by the fixed coarse posterior approximation; in contrast, the proposed algorithm is able to continually improve the coreset, providing state-of-the-art Bayesian dataset summarization with orders-of-magnitude reduction in KL divergence to the exact posterior.

This paper targets that dependency, which can be difficult to supply and limits how automatically such methods can be applied.

These findings link easier setup to better dataset summarization: removing the fixed approximation requirement also removes the particular restriction on refinement observed in the experiments.
