title: Sparse Variational Inference: Bayesian Coresets from Scratch

abstract: In a recent work, \cite{chierichetti2017fair} studied the following ``fair'' variants of classical clustering problems such as k-means and k-median: given a set of n data points in R^d and a binary type associated to each data point, the goal is to cluster the points while ensuring that the proportion of each type in each cluster is roughly the same as its underlying proportion. Subsequent work has focused on either extending this setting to when each data point has multiple, non-disjoint sensitive types such as race and gender \cite{bera2019fair}, or to address the problem that the clustering algorithms in the above work do not scale well. The main contribution of this paper is an approach to clustering with fairness constraints that involve {\em multiple, non-disjoint} attributes, that is {\em also scalable}. Our approach is based on novel constructions of coresets: for the k-median objective, we construct an \eps-coreset of size O(\Gamma k^2 \eps^{-d}) where \Gamma is the number of distinct collections of groups that a point may belong to, and for the k-means objective, we show how to construct an \eps-coreset of size O(\Gamma k^3\eps^{-d-1}). The former result is the first known coreset construction for the fair clustering problem with the k-median objective, and the latter result removes the dependence on the size of the full dataset as in~\cite{schmidt2018fair} and generalizes it to multiple, non-disjoint attributes. Importantly, plugging our coresets into existing algorithms for fair clustering such as \cite{backurs2019scalable} results in the fastest algorithms for several cases. Empirically, we assess our approach over the \textbf{Adult} and \textbf{Bank} dataset, and show that the coreset sizes are much smaller than the full dataset; applying coresets indeed accelerates the running time of computing the fair clustering objective while ensuring that the resulting objective difference is small.

In the setting described here, clusters should approximately reflect the underlying proportions of sensitive groups. Handling multiple overlapping attributes complicates this requirement because one person or point can belong to several groups simultaneously. The paper addresses scalability while retaining this richer group structure.

The method constructs coresets that summarize the dataset for fairness-constrained clustering. For k-median, the stated size is O(Γk²ε⁻ᵈ); for k-means, it is O(Γk³ε⁻ᵈ⁻¹). Here Γ counts distinct combinations of group memberships. These bounds avoid dependence on the full dataset size, although they still depend on dimension, approximation precision, cluster count, and membership combinations.

Combining the summaries with existing algorithms yields the fastest algorithms for several cases. Experiments on Adult and Bank find substantially smaller summaries and faster fair-clustering objective computation, with a small difference in the resulting objective.
summary.tldr: Compact coresets accelerate clustering with fairness constraints across multiple overlapping groups while controlling changes to the clustering objective.

title: Coresets for Clustering with Fairness Constraints

abstract: We introduce in this paper a novel strategy for efficiently approximating the Sinkhorn distance between two discrete measures. After identifying neglectable components of the dual solution of the regularized Sinkhorn problem, we propose to screen those components by directly setting them at that value before entering the Sinkhorn problem. This allows us to solve a smaller Sinkhorn problem while ensuring approximation with provable guarantees. More formally, the approach is based on a new formulation of dual of Sinkhorn divergence problem and on the KKT optimality conditions of this problem, which enable identification of dual components to be screened. This new analysis leads to the Screenkhorn algorithm. We illustrate the efficiency of Screenkhorn on complex tasks such as dimensionality reduction and domain adaptation involving regularized optimal transport.

paragraphs: Screenkhorn aims to approximate the Sinkhorn distance between two discrete measures more efficiently. The computational problem comes from regularized optimal transport, which compares measures by optimizing a transport relationship between them. The paper's strategy is to identify parts of the optimization that can be fixed before running the main Sinkhorn computation.

The authors reformulate the dual problem and use its Karush-Kuhn-Tucker optimality conditions to identify negligible dual components. They screen these components by assigning them their selected negligible values in advance. The remaining variables form a smaller Sinkhorn problem, reducing the work required while retaining provable guarantees for the resulting approximation.

The paper illustrates the algorithm's efficiency on dimensionality reduction and domain adaptation tasks involving regularized optimal transport. The contribution is therefore both an analytical rule for deciding what to screen and an algorithm that uses that rule. Its guarantee concerns a controlled approximation, so the reduction in problem size does not require claiming that every screened variable is exactly irrelevant.
summary.tldr: Screenkhorn fixes negligible dual components to solve a smaller Sinkhorn problem with provable approximation guarantees.

title: Screening Sinkhorn Algorithm for Regularized Optimal Transport

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating a vector from its noisy measurements using a prior specified only through a denoising function. Recent work on plug-and-play priors (PnP) and regularization-by-denoising (RED) has shown the state-of-the-art performance of estimators under such priors in a range of imaging tasks. In this work, we develop a new block coordinate RED algorithm that decomposes a large-scale estimation problem into a sequence of updates over a small subset of the unknown variables. We theoretically analyze the convergence of the algorithm and discuss its relationship to the traditional proximal optimization. Our analysis complements and extends recent theoretical results for RED-based estimation methods. We numerically validate our method using several denoiser priors, including those based on convolutional neural network (CNN) denoisers.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering an unknown vector from noisy measurements when prior knowledge is available only as a denoising function. Instead of requiring a separately specified mathematical model of plausible solutions, the estimator uses the denoiser to supply that information. This setting builds on plug-and-play priors and regularization by denoising, which have performed strongly in imaging tasks.

The proposed algorithm brings block coordinate updates to regularization by denoising. It divides a large estimation problem into steps that update only a small subset of the unknown variables. This changes the organization of the computation: progress is made through smaller updates rather than requiring every step to address the full vector together.

The authors analyze convergence and explain connections to traditional proximal optimization, extending existing theoretical work on denoising-based estimation. They also validate the algorithm numerically with several denoiser priors, including convolutional neural network denoisers. The contribution combines a strategy for handling large problems with analysis of how that strategy relates to established optimization methods.
summary.tldr: Block coordinate RED tackles large denoising-based estimation problems through smaller variable updates, supported by convergence analysis and numerical validation.

title: Block Coordinate Regularization by Denoising

abstract: We study the problem of finding low-cost {\em fair clusterings} in data where each data point may belong to many protected groups. Our work significantly generalizes the seminal work of Chierichetti \etal (NIPS 2017) as follows. - We allow the user to specify the parameters that define fair representation. More precisely, these parameters define the maximum over- and minimum under-representation of any group in any cluster. - Our clustering algorithm works on any $\ell_p$-norm objective (e.g. $k$-means, $k$-median, and $k$-center). Indeed, our algorithm transforms any vanilla clustering solution into a fair one incurring only a slight loss in quality. - Our algorithm also allows individuals to lie in multiple protected groups. In other words, we do not need the protected groups to partition the data and we can maintain fairness across different groups simultaneously. Our experiments show that on established data sets, our algorithm performs much better in practice than what our theoretical results suggest.

paragraphs: Clustering groups similar data points, but a low-cost grouping may represent protected groups unevenly. This paper studies clusterings that balance the usual clustering objective with explicit representation requirements. Users specify bounds controlling how much each protected group may be overrepresented or underrepresented within any cluster.

The proposed algorithm transforms an ordinary clustering solution into a fair one with only a slight loss in quality under the paper's guarantees. It applies across objectives based on any l_p norm, including k-means, k-median, and k-center. This breadth makes the fairness framework applicable to several different ways of measuring the quality of a grouping.

The method also allows a person or data point to belong to multiple protected groups simultaneously. Fairness constraints therefore do not require assigning everyone to exactly one mutually exclusive category. Experiments on established datasets perform substantially better than the theoretical results suggest. The contribution is a flexible, explicitly parameterized representation framework whose observed clustering costs are more favorable than its theoretical guarantees alone would indicate.
summary.tldr: A general clustering method enforces user-specified representation bounds for overlapping protected groups with a slight loss in clustering quality.

title: Fair Algorithms for Clustering

abstract: Maximum target coverage by adjusting the orientation of distributed sensors is an important problem in directional sensor networks (DSNs). This problem is challenging as the targets usually move randomly but the coverage range of sensors is limited in angle and distance. Thus, it is required to coordinate sensors to get ideal target coverage with low power consumption, e.g. no missing targets or reducing redundant coverage. To realize this, we propose a Hierarchical Target-oriented Multi-Agent Coordination (HiT-MAC), which decomposes the target coverage problem into two-level tasks: targets assignment by a coordinator and tracking assigned targets by executors. Specifically, the coordinator periodically monitors the environment globally and allocates targets to each executor. In turn, the executor only needs to track its assigned targets. To effectively learn the HiT-MAC by reinforcement learning, we further introduce a bunch of practical methods, including a self-attention module, marginal contribution approximation for the coordinator, goal-conditional observation filter for the executor, etc. Empirical results demonstrate the advantage of HiT-MAC in coverage rate, learning efficiency, and scalability, comparing to baselines. We also conduct an ablative analysis on the effectiveness of the introduced components in the framework.

paragraphs: Directional sensors observe only a limited angle and distance, so their orientations must be coordinated to cover moving targets. Random target movement makes this difficult: sensors can miss targets or redundantly cover the same ones. The paper seeks effective coverage while motivating the need to avoid unnecessary power consumption.

HiT-MAC divides the problem into two levels. A coordinator periodically observes the overall environment and assigns targets to individual executors. Each executor then focuses on tracking its assigned targets. This separation gives the coordinator responsibility for allocation while simplifying the local tracking decisions that executors must learn.

The reinforcement learning framework includes self-attention, an approximation of marginal contributions for the coordinator, and an observation filter conditioned on the executor’s goal. Experiments report advantages over baselines in coverage rate, learning efficiency, and scalability, with ablations examining the introduced components. The stated results support the hierarchical division of coordination and tracking; although low power consumption motivates the problem, the abstract’s reported comparative findings specifically concern coverage, learning, and scaling.
summary.tldr: HiT-MAC separates global target assignment from local sensor tracking, improving coverage, learning efficiency, and scalability in experiments.

title: Learning Multi-Agent Coordination for Enhancing Target Coverage in Directional Sensor Networks

abstract: Learning causal effects from data is a fundamental problem across the sciences. Determining the identifiability of a target effect from a combination of the observational distribution and the causal graph underlying a phenomenon is well-understood in theory. However, in practice, it remains a challenge to apply the identification theory to estimate the identified causal functionals from finite samples. Although a plethora of effective estimators have been developed under the setting known as the back-door (also called conditional ignorability), there exists still no systematic way of estimating arbitrary causal functionals that are both computationally and statistically attractive. This paper aims to bridge this gap, from causal identification to causal estimation. We note that estimating functionals from limited samples based on the empirical risk minimization (ERM) principle has been pervasive in the machine learning literature, and these methods have been extended to causal inference under the back-door setting. In this paper, we develop a learning framework that marries two families of methods, benefiting from the generality of the causal identification theory and the effectiveness of the estimators produced based on the principle of ERM. Specifically, we develop a sound and complete algorithm that generates causal functionals in the form of weighted distributions that are amenable to the ERM optimization. We then provide a practical procedure for learning causal effects from finite samples and a causal graph. Finally, experimental results support the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Causal identification asks whether a target effect can be determined from an observational distribution and a causal graph. Even when theory answers that question, estimating the resulting expression from finite data can remain difficult. This paper addresses the gap between identifying an effect and building a practical estimator, extending beyond the well-developed back-door setting.

The authors connect causal identification with empirical risk minimization, the principle of fitting a model by optimizing a loss on observed samples. They develop a sound and complete algorithm that expresses causal functionals as weighted distributions suitable for ERM optimization. The weights provide the interface between the causal expression and a learning procedure.

The framework then supplies a practical method for learning causal effects from finite samples together with a causal graph. Experiments support the approach's effectiveness. Its significance is the systematic translation from identification theory into estimation machinery: effects handled by the framework can be approached through weighted learning objectives. The graph remains part of the supplied information, and the identification result and finite-sample estimation procedure serve distinct roles.
summary.tldr: A sound and complete identification algorithm expresses causal functionals as weighted distributions that support practical estimation through empirical risk minimization.

title: Learning Causal Effects via Weighted Empirical Risk Minimization

abstract: Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have shown promising results in processing graph data by extracting structure-aware features. This gave rise to extensive work in geometric deep learning, focusing on designing network architectures that ensure neuron activations conform to regularity patterns within the input graph. However, in most cases the graph structure is only accounted for by considering the similarity of activations between adjacent nodes, which limits the capabilities of such methods to discriminate between nodes in a graph. Here, we propose to augment conventional GCNs with geometric scattering transforms and residual convolutions. The former enables band-pass filtering of graph signals, thus alleviating the so-called oversmoothing often encountered in GCNs, while the latter is introduced to clear the resulting features of high-frequency noise. We establish the advantages of the presented Scattering GCN with both theoretical results establishing the complementary benefits of scattering and GCN features, as well as experimental results showing the benefits of our method compared to leading graph neural networks for semi-supervised node classification, including the recently proposed GAT network that typically alleviates oversmoothing using graph attention mechanisms.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks use graph structure to learn features, often encouraging neighboring nodes to have similar activations. Too much similarity can make different nodes difficult to distinguish, a problem called oversmoothing. This paper augments conventional graph convolution with geometric scattering transforms and residual convolutions to preserve more informative variation.

The scattering component provides band-pass filtering of graph signals, giving the model access to information that ordinary smoothing can suppress. Residual convolutions then help remove high-frequency noise from the resulting features. The two additions serve related but distinct purposes: retaining useful differences among nodes and cleaning up unwanted variation.

The authors provide theoretical results establishing complementary benefits of scattering and conventional GCN features. Experiments on semi-supervised node classification show advantages over leading graph neural networks, including a graph attention network that also addresses oversmoothing. The findings support combining different ways of processing graph signals so that structural regularity can aid classification without erasing distinctions that matter for identifying nodes.
summary.tldr: Scattering GCN combines band-pass graph features with residual convolutions to reduce oversmoothing and improve semi-supervised node classification.

title: Scattering GCN: Overcoming Oversmoothness in Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: We study the reinforcement learning problem in the setting of finite-horizon1episodic Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with S states, A actions, and episode length H. We propose a model-free algorithm UCB-ADVANTAGE and prove that it achieves \tilde{O}(\sqrt{H^2 SAT}) regret where T=KH and K is the number of episodes to play. Our regret bound improves upon the results of [Jin et al., 2018] and matches the best known model-based algorithms as well as the information theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. We also show that UCB-ADVANTAGE achieves low local switching cost and applies to concurrent reinforcement learning, improving upon the recent results of [Bai et al., 2019].

We propose a model-free algorithm UCB-ADVANTAGE and prove that it achieves \tilde{O}(\sqrt{H^2 SAT}) regret where T=KH and K is the number of episodes to play. paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning in episodes of a fixed length, with a finite number of states and actions. Its central question is how efficiently a model-free learner can improve through interaction. Performance is measured by regret: the accumulated shortfall from acting optimally while the agent is still learning.

The authors propose UCB-ADVANTAGE and prove a regret bound of order square root of H squared times S times A times T, ignoring logarithmic factors. Here, H is episode length, S and A count states and actions, and T is the total number of interaction steps. This improves the earlier model-free result identified in the abstract and matches the best known model-based bounds and the information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

The algorithm also has low local switching cost and applies to concurrent reinforcement learning. These additional results address how learning proceeds when policy changes matter or experience is gathered concurrently. Together, the guarantees establish that model-free learning can approach the fundamental regret limit in this finite-horizon setting.
summary.tldr: UCB-ADVANTAGE brings model-free episodic reinforcement learning within logarithmic factors of the optimal regret bound.

title: Almost Optimal Model-Free Reinforcement Learningvia Reference-Advantage Decomposition

abstract: Owing to their stability and convergence speed, extragradient methods have become a staple for solving large-scale saddle-point problems in machine learning. The basic premise of these algorithms is the use of an extrapolation step before performing an update; thanks to this exploration step, extra-gradient methods overcome many of the non-convergence issues that plague gradient descent/ascent schemes. On the other hand, as we show in this paper, running vanilla extragradient with stochastic gradients may jeopardize its convergence, even in simple bilinear models. To overcome this failure, we investigate a double stepsize extragradient algorithm where the exploration step evolves at a more aggressive time-scale compared to the update step. We show that this modification allows the method to converge even with stochastic gradients, and we derive sharp convergence rates under an error bound condition.

The basic premise of these algorithms is the use of an extrapolation step before performing an update; thanks to this exploration step, extra-gradient methods overcome many of the non-convergence issues that plague gradient descent/ascent schemes. On the other hand, as we show in this paper, running vanilla extragradient with stochastic gradients may jeopardize its convergence, even in simple bilinear models. To overcome this failure, we investigate a double stepsize extragradient algorithm where the exploration step evolves at a more aggressive time-scale compared to the update step. We show that this modification allows the method to converge even with stochastic gradients, and we derive sharp convergence rates under an error bound condition.

This extra look ahead helps avoid convergence failures that can affect ordinary gradient descent and ascent. The paper examines what happens when those gradient calculations are stochastic, so the directions used by the algorithm contain noise.

The authors show that ordinary extragradient can lose its convergence behavior under stochastic gradients, even in simple bilinear problems. Their remedy gives the exploratory step and the final update different step sizes. Exploration proceeds on a more aggressive timescale, while the update changes the current solution more conservatively.

The analysis shows that this separation allows convergence with stochastic gradients and provides sharp convergence rates under an error-bound condition. That condition is part of the stated rate result. The contribution explains why adding an exploratory step alone may be insufficient in a noisy setting and shows how the relative scaling of exploration and updating can restore convergence.
summary.tldr: Using more aggressive exploration than updating restores stochastic extragradient convergence, with sharp rates under an error-bound condition.

title: Explore Aggressively, Update Conservatively: Stochastic Extragradient Methods with Variable Stepsize Scaling

abstract: We present a randomized approximation scheme for the permanent of a matrix with nonnegative entries. Our scheme extends a recursive rejection sampling method of Huber and Law (SODA 2008) by replacing the permanent upper bound with a linear combination of the subproblem bounds at a moderately large depth of the recursion tree. This method, we call deep rejection sampling, is empirically shown to outperform the basic, depth-zero variant, as well as a related method by Kuck et al. (NeurIPS 2019). We analyze the expected running time of the scheme on random $(0, 1)$-matrices where each entry is independently $1$ with probability $p$. Our bound is superior to a previous one for $p$ less than $1/5$, matching another bound that was only known to hold when every row and column has density exactly $p$.

Its starting point is an existing recursive rejection sampling procedure. The central change concerns the upper bound used within that procedure: the authors incorporate information from deeper levels of the recursion.

Their method, called deep rejection sampling, replaces the original permanent upper bound with a linear combination of bounds for subproblems at a moderately large recursion depth. This makes the depth of the recursive calculation an explicit part of the approximation strategy. The theoretical improvement therefore applies to a specifically defined random-matrix setting.
summary.tldr: Deep rejection sampling uses bounds from deeper recursive subproblems to improve permanent approximation empirically and strengthen running-time bounds for certain random matrices.

title: Approximating the Permanent with Deep Rejection Sampling

abstract: Finding neural network weights that generalize well from small datasets is difficult. A promising approach is to learn a weight initialization such that a small number of weight changes results in low generalization error. We show that this form of meta-learning can be improved by letting the learning algorithm decide which weights to change, i.e., by learning where to learn. We find that patterned sparsity emerges from this process, with the pattern of sparsity varying on a problem-by-problem basis. This selective sparsity results in better generalization and less interference in a range of few-shot and continual learning problems. Moreover, we find that sparse learning also emerges in a more expressive model where learning rates are meta-learned. Our results shed light on an ongoing debate on whether meta-learning can discover adaptable features and suggest that learning by sparse gradient descent is a powerful inductive bias for meta-learning systems.

paragraphs: Meta-learning can prepare a neural network to adapt from a small dataset by learning a useful starting set of weights. This paper extends that idea by allowing the learning algorithm to decide which weights should change during adaptation. The learned adaptation procedure therefore includes where learning takes place, alongside the initial parameter values.

The authors find that structured patterns of sparse updates emerge, and that these patterns differ between problems. This means the method does not impose one universally preferred subset of adaptable weights. In a range of few-shot and continual learning problems, the resulting selectivity improves generalization and reduces interference.

Sparse learning also emerges in a more expressive model that meta-learns learning rates. That observation supports the broader relevance of selective adaptation beyond the initial formulation. The findings contribute to the question of whether meta-learning can discover adaptable features, and suggest sparse gradient descent as a useful inductive bias. Their practical meaning is that restricting updates in a learned, problem-dependent way can improve adaptation in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Learning which weights to update produces problem-dependent sparsity that improves tested few-shot and continual learning outcomes.

title: Learning where to learn: Gradient sparsity in meta and continual learning

abstract: Training Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) has been challenging for a long time due to the difficulty of computing precisely the log-likelihood gradient. Over the past decades, many works have proposed more or less successful recipes but without studying systematically the crucial quantity of the problem: the mixing time i.e. the number of MCMC iterations needed to sample completely new configurations from a model. In this work, we show that this mixing time plays a crucial role in the behavior and stability of the trained model, and that RBMs operate in two well-defined distinct regimes, namely equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium, depending on the interplay between this mixing time of the model and the number of MCMC steps, $k$, used to approximate the gradient. We further show empirically that this mixing time increases along the learning, which often implies a transition from one regime to another as soon as $k$ becomes smaller than this time.In particular, we show that using the popular $k$ (persistent) contrastive divergence approaches, with $k$ small, the dynamics of the fitted model are extremely slow and often dominated by strong out-of-equilibrium effects. On the contrary, RBMs trained in equilibrium display much faster dynamics, and a smooth convergence to dataset-like configurations during the sampling.Finally, we discuss how to exploit in practice both regimes depending on the task one aims to fulfill: (i) short $k$s can be used to generate convincing samples in short learning times, (ii) large $k$ (or increasingly large) must be used to learn the correct equilibrium distribution of the RBM. Finally, the existence of these two operational regimes seems to be a general property of energy based models trained via likelihood maximization.

paragraphs: Training restricted Boltzmann machines requires approximating a likelihood gradient through sampling. This paper focuses on mixing time: how many sampling iterations are needed to obtain genuinely new configurations from the model. The authors show that the relationship between this time and the number of sampling steps used for each gradient approximation strongly affects learning and model behavior.

They distinguish equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium training regimes. Empirically, mixing time increases during learning, so a fixed sampling budget can eventually become too short. With small step counts in contrastive divergence or persistent contrastive divergence, fitted models often have very slow dynamics dominated by nonequilibrium effects. Models trained in equilibrium instead show faster dynamics and smoothly approach configurations resembling the data during sampling.

The practical choice depends on the goal. Short sampling runs can produce convincing samples after brief training, whereas learning the correct equilibrium distribution requires large or increasing step counts. The authors also suggest that these two regimes may occur more generally in energy-based models trained by likelihood maximization.
summary.tldr: The balance between mixing time and sampling budget separates RBM training into regimes suited to different modeling goals.

title: Equilibrium and non-Equilibrium regimes in the learning of Restricted Boltzmann Machines

abstract: Adversarial training is a powerful type of defense against adversarial examples. Previous empirical results suggest that adversarial training requires wider networks for better performances. However, it remains elusive how does neural network width affect model robustness. In this paper, we carefully examine the relationship between network width and model robustness. Specifically, we show that the model robustness is closely related to the tradeoff between natural accuracy and perturbation stability, which is controlled by the robust regularization parameter λ. With the same λ, wider networks can achieve better natural accuracy but worse perturbation stability, leading to a potentially worse overall model robustness. To understand the origin of this phenomenon, we further relate the perturbation stability with the network's local Lipschitzness. By leveraging recent results on neural tangent kernels, we theoretically show that wider networks tend to have worse perturbation stability. Our analyses suggest that: 1) the common strategy of first fine-tuning λ on small networks and then directly use it for wide model training could lead to deteriorated model robustness; 2) one needs to properly enlarge λ to unleash the robustness potential of wider models fully. Finally, we propose a new Width Adjusted Regularization (WAR) method that adaptively enlarges λ on wide models and significantly saves the tuning time.

paragraphs: Wider neural networks have been associated with better adversarial-training performance, but this paper asks when extra width actually improves robustness. Its analysis separates accuracy on ordinary inputs from stability under perturbations. Robustness depends on their tradeoff, which is controlled by the strength of the robust regularization parameter, lambda.

With lambda held fixed, wider models can improve ordinary accuracy while becoming less stable to perturbations. Overall robustness can therefore worsen. The authors connect this instability to local Lipschitzness, which describes how sensitively network outputs change near an input. Using neural tangent kernel results, they theoretically show a tendency for wider networks to have worse perturbation stability.

This explains why tuning lambda on a small network and reusing it unchanged for a wider one can be problematic. The analysis indicates that increasing regularization appropriately is needed to realize the wider model's robustness potential. The proposed Width Adjusted Regularization method adaptively increases lambda for wide models and substantially reduces tuning time. The central finding is a relationship between width and regularization, rather than an unconditional advantage from adding width.
summary.tldr: Wider networks can become less robust at fixed regularization, motivating an adaptive increase in regularization strength as width grows.

title: Do Wider Neural Networks Really Help Adversarial Robustness?

abstract: A structural equation model (SEM) is an effective framework to reason over causal relationships represented via a directed acyclic graph (DAG).Recent advances have enabled effective maximum-likelihood point estimation of DAGs from observational data. However, a point estimate may not accurately capture the uncertainty in inferring the underlying graph in practical scenarios, wherein the true DAG is non-identifiable and/or the observed dataset is limited.We propose Bayesian Causal Discovery Nets (BCD Nets), a variational inference framework for estimating a distribution over DAGs characterizing a linear-Gaussian SEM.Developing a full Bayesian posterior over DAGs is challenging due to the the discrete and combinatorial nature of graphs.We analyse key design choices for scalable VI over DAGs, such as 1) the parametrization of DAGs via an expressive variational family, 2) a continuous relaxation that enables low-variance stochastic optimization, and 3) suitable priors over the latent variables.We provide a series of experiments on real and synthetic data showing that BCD Nets outperform maximum-likelihood methods on standard causal discovery metrics such as structural Hamming distance in low data regimes.

However, a point estimate may not accurately capture the uncertainty in inferring the underlying graph in practical scenarios, wherein the true DAG is non-identifiable and/or the observed dataset is limited.We propose Bayesian Causal Discovery Nets (BCD Nets), a variational inference framework for estimating a distribution over DAGs characterizing a linear-Gaussian SEM.Developing a full Bayesian posterior over DAGs is challenging due to the the discrete and combinatorial nature of graphs.We analyse key design choices for scalable VI over DAGs, such as 1) the parametrization of DAGs via an expressive variational family, 2) a continuous relaxation that enables low-variance stochastic optimization, and 3) suitable priors over the latent variables.We provide a series of experiments on real and synthetic data showing that BCD Nets outperform maximum-likelihood methods on standard causal discovery metrics such as structural Hamming distance in low data regimes.

paragraphs: Causal discovery seeks a directed graph describing relationships among variables. Returning a single graph can hide uncertainty, particularly when observations are scarce or cannot uniquely identify the true causal structure. This paper develops BCD Nets to estimate a distribution over possible directed acyclic graphs within a linear-Gaussian structural equation model.

The approach uses variational inference to approximate that distribution. Graphs are discrete objects with many possible configurations, making Bayesian inference difficult to scale. The authors examine three design choices: an expressive family for representing candidate graph distributions, a continuous relaxation that supports low-variance stochastic optimization, and suitable prior distributions over the underlying latent variables.

These choices make uncertainty over causal graphs part of the learning target rather than reducing the result to one maximum-likelihood estimate. Experiments on real and synthetic data show better performance than maximum-likelihood methods on standard causal-discovery measures, including structural Hamming distance, when data are limited. The stated evidence supports the framework particularly in those low-data settings, where committing to one graph can obscure uncertainty in the inferred relationships.
summary.tldr: BCD Nets approximate distributions over causal graphs and outperform maximum-likelihood methods in the reported low-data experiments.

title: BCD Nets: Scalable Variational Approaches for Bayesian Causal Discovery

abstract: Regret-based algorithms are highly efficient at finding approximate Nash equilibria in sequential games such as poker games. However, most regret-based algorithms, including counterfactual regret minimization (CFR) and its variants, rely on iterate averaging to achieve convergence. Inspired by recent advances on last-iterate convergence of optimistic algorithms in zero-sum normal-form games, we study this phenomenon in sequential games, and provide a comprehensive study of last-iterate convergence for zero-sum extensive-form games with perfect recall (EFGs), using various optimistic regret-minimization algorithms over treeplexes. This includes algorithms using the vanilla entropy or squared Euclidean norm regularizers, as well as their dilated versions which admit more efficient implementation. In contrast to CFR, we show that all of these algorithms enjoy last-iterate convergence, with some of them even converging exponentially fast. We also provide experiments to further support our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Algorithms for sequential games often learn useful strategies through regret minimization. Many, including counterfactual regret minimization and its variants, obtain convergence by averaging the strategies produced across iterations. This paper asks whether the latest strategy itself can converge, removing the need for averaging as the basis of the convergence guarantee.

The analysis concerns zero-sum extensive-form games with perfect recall. It studies optimistic regret-minimization algorithms over treeplexes, the structured strategy spaces used in the analysis. The algorithms use entropy or squared Euclidean norm regularizers, including dilated versions that allow more efficient implementation. This brings several algorithmic choices into a common study of last-iterate behavior.

The authors prove last-iterate convergence for all the algorithms they examine, with exponential convergence for some of them. Experiments provide additional support for the theoretical findings. The key outcome is that convergence can apply directly to the current strategy in this game setting, while the strongest speed claim belongs only to a subset of the studied algorithms.
summary.tldr: For zero-sum extensive-form games with perfect recall, the studied optimistic algorithms converge in their latest strategies, with some converging exponentially fast.

title: Last-iterate Convergence in Extensive-Form Games

abstract: We present a joint deep neural system identification model for two major sources of neural variability: stimulus-driven and stimulus-conditioned fluctuations. To this end, we combine (1) state-of-the-art deep networks for stimulus-driven activity and (2) a flexible, normalizing flow-based generative model to capture the stimulus-conditioned variability including noise correlations. This allows us to train the model end-to-end without the need for sophisticated probabilistic approximations associated with many latent state models for stimulus-conditioned fluctuations. We train the model on the responses of thousands of neurons from multiple areas of the mouse visual cortex to natural images. We show that our model outperforms previous state-of-the-art models in predicting the distribution of neural population responses to novel stimuli, including shared stimulus-conditioned variability. Furthermore, it successfully learns known latent factors of the population responses that are related to behavioral variables such as pupil dilation, and other factors that vary systematically with brain area or retinotopic location. Overall, our model accurately accounts for two critical sources of neural variability while avoiding several complexities associated with many existing latent state models. It thus provides a useful tool for uncovering the interplay between different factors that contribute to variability in neural activity.

paragraphs: Neural responses vary both because the image being viewed changes and because brain activity fluctuates even for a given image. This paper builds a joint model of these two sources of variability. Its goal is to predict the distribution of activity across a population of neurons, including fluctuations that neurons share.

The approach combines a deep network for stimulus-driven activity with a generative model based on normalizing flows for variability conditional on the stimulus. The flow component gives the model flexibility to represent correlated responses. The combined system can be trained end to end while avoiding sophisticated probabilistic approximations required by many latent-state approaches.

Trained on thousands of neurons from multiple mouse visual areas, the model improves predictions for previously unseen images over earlier leading models. It also recovers latent factors associated with pupil dilation and factors that vary with brain area or retinotopic location. These findings make it useful for examining how stimulus information, behavior, and population fluctuations jointly shape neural activity.
summary.tldr: A joint neural-network and normalizing-flow model predicts image-driven neural activity and shared fluctuations while recovering behavior-related latent factors.

title: A flow-based latent state generative model of neural population responses to natural images

abstract: Several performance measures can be used for evaluating classification results: accuracy, F-measure, and many others. Can we say that some of them are better than others, or, ideally, choose one measure that is best in all situations? To answer this question, we conduct a systematic analysis of classification performance measures: we formally define a list of desirable properties and theoretically analyze which measures satisfy which properties. We also prove an impossibility theorem: some desirable properties cannot be simultaneously satisfied. Finally, we propose a new family of measures satisfying all desirable properties except one. This family includes the Matthews Correlation Coefficient and a so-called Symmetric Balanced Accuracy that was not previously used in classification literature. We believe that our systematic approach gives an important tool to practitioners for adequately evaluating classification results.

paragraphs: Classification results can be summarized by accuracy, F-measure, and many other scores. Choosing among them raises a deeper question than which number looks best: what behavior should an evaluation measure have? This paper approaches that question by formally specifying desirable properties and examining which existing measures satisfy them.

The analysis establishes an impossibility result: some of the desired properties cannot hold simultaneously. Within this framework, selecting a measure therefore requires accepting a tradeoff. The theorem gives a precise reason why searching for a score with every listed virtue cannot succeed, rather than treating disagreements between measures as merely a matter of taste.

The authors then propose a family of measures satisfying every desired property except one. It contains the Matthews Correlation Coefficient and Symmetric Balanced Accuracy, which they identify as previously unused in classification literature. The practical contribution is a systematic basis for choosing evaluation measures. Users can relate a score’s mathematical behavior to their evaluation needs, while recognizing the unavoidable compromise established by the analysis.
summary.tldr: A formal analysis reveals unavoidable tradeoffs among classification metrics and proposes a family satisfying all but one of the specified desirable properties.

title: Good Classification Measures and How to Find Them

abstract: Many modern machine learning applications come with complex and nuanced design goals such as minimizing the worst-case error, satisfying a given precision or recall target, or enforcing group-fairness constraints. Popular techniques for optimizing such non-decomposable objectives reduce the problem into a sequence of cost-sensitive learning tasks, each of which is then solved by re-weighting the training loss with example-specific costs. We point out that the standard approach of re-weighting the loss to incorporate label costs can produce unsatisfactory results when used to train over-parameterized models. As a remedy, we propose new cost- sensitive losses that extend the classical idea of logit adjustment to handle more general cost matrices. Our losses are calibrated, and can be further improved with distilled labels from a teacher model. Through experiments on benchmark image datasets, we showcase the effectiveness of our approach in training ResNet models with common robust and constrained optimization objectives.

paragraphs: Some learning goals concern the behavior of a model across a dataset rather than an independent error for each example. Examples include reducing worst-case error, meeting precision or recall targets, and enforcing group fairness. Common optimization methods handle these goals through a sequence of cost-sensitive learning problems.

A standard way to solve each problem is to multiply individual training losses by example-specific costs. This paper shows that such reweighting can yield unsatisfactory results with over-parameterized models. The authors propose alternative cost-sensitive losses that extend logit adjustment to more general cost matrices, changing how costs enter the learning objective.

The proposed losses are calibrated, providing a theoretical connection between the loss and the intended cost-sensitive decision problem. The authors also find that labels distilled from a teacher model can further improve them. Experiments on benchmark image datasets demonstrate effectiveness for ResNet training with common robust and constrained objectives. The contribution addresses the learning step inside these broader optimization procedures, showing why the choice of cost-sensitive loss matters when the model has substantial capacity.
summary.tldr: Calibrated losses based on generalized logit adjustment improve cost-sensitive training of over-parameterized models for robust and constrained objectives.

title: Training Over-parameterized Models with Non-decomposable Objectives

abstract: Given a neural network, training data, and a threshold, finding weights for the neural network such that the total error is below the threshold is known to be NP-hard. We determine the algorithmic complexity of this fundamental problem precisely, by showing that it is $\exists\mathbb R$-complete. This means that the problem is equivalent, up to polynomial time reductions, to deciding whether a system of polynomial equations and inequalities with integer coefficients and real unknowns has a solution. If, as widely expected, $\exists\mathbb R$ is strictly larger than NP, our work implies that the problem of training neural networks is not even in NP.Neural networks are usually trained using some variation of backpropagation. The result of this paper gives an explanation why techniques commonly used to solve big instances of NP-complete problems (such as SAT solvers, IP solvers, local search, dynamic programming, etc.) seem to be of no use to this task.

paragraphs: This paper studies a precise decision version of neural-network training: given a network, training examples, and an error threshold, do weights exist that make total error fall below that threshold? The problem was already known to be NP-hard. The authors establish a more specific classification of its algorithmic complexity.

They prove that the problem is complete for the existential theory of the reals, written ∃R. This means it is equivalent, through polynomial-time reductions, to deciding whether polynomial equations and inequalities with integer coefficients have a solution in real-valued unknowns. The result places the training problem alongside this broader class of real-number feasibility problems.

The implication about NP remains conditional. If ∃R is strictly larger than NP, as widely expected, then the training decision problem is not in NP. The paper presents this classification as an explanation for why techniques successful on large NP-complete problems may be ill-suited to neural-network training. It characterizes the computational difficulty of the stated threshold problem rather than establishing that every practical training instance is intractable.
summary.tldr: Deciding whether neural-network weights can achieve a specified error threshold is ∃R-complete, sharpening the known NP-hardness result.

title: Training Neural Networks is ER-complete

abstract: We present an end-to-end differentiable training method for retrieval-augmented open-domain question answering systems that combine information from multiple retrieved documents when generating answers. We model retrieval decisions as latent variables over sets of relevant documents. Since marginalizing over sets of retrieved documents is computationally hard, we approximate this using an expectation-maximization algorithm. We iteratively estimate the value of our latent variable (the set of relevant documents for a given question) and then use this estimate to update the retriever and reader parameters. We hypothesize that such end-to-end training allows training signals to flow to the reader and then to the retriever better than staged-wise training. This results in a retriever that is able to select more relevant documents for a question and a reader that is trained on more accurate documents to generate an answer. Experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms all existing approaches of comparable size by 2-3% absolute exact match points, achieving new state-of-the-art results. Our results also demonstrate the feasibility of learning to retrieve to improve answer generation without explicit supervision of retrieval decisions.

We model retrieval decisions as latent variables over sets of relevant documents. Since marginalizing over sets of retrieved documents is computationally hard, we approximate this using an expectation-maximization algorithm. We iteratively estimate the value of our latent variable (the set of relevant documents for a given question) and then use this estimate to update the retriever and reader parameters. We hypothesize that such end-to-end training allows training signals to flow to the reader and then to the retriever better than staged-wise training. This results in a retriever that is able to select more relevant documents for a question and a reader that is trained on more accurate documents to generate an answer. Experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms all existing approaches of comparable size by 2-3% absolute exact match points, achieving new state-of-the-art results. Our results also demonstrate the feasibility of learning to retrieve to improve answer generation without explicit supervision of retrieval decisions.

paragraphs: Open-domain question answering can combine a retriever that finds documents with a reader that uses them to generate an answer. This paper develops an end-to-end differentiable training method for systems whose reader combines information across multiple documents. The central challenge is learning which collection of documents will support a useful answer.

The method treats the relevant document set as a latent variable: something the model must infer during training. Accounting for all possible sets is computationally difficult, so the authors approximate this process with expectation-maximization. Training alternates between estimating a relevant set for each question and using that estimate to update both the retriever and the reader.

The authors hypothesize that this joint process passes learning signals through the two components more effectively than staged training. Across three benchmarks, they report improvements of 2–3 absolute exact-match percentage points over existing approaches of comparable size. The results also demonstrate that retrieval can be learned to improve answer generation without explicit supervision identifying the correct retrieval decisions.
summary.tldr: An expectation-maximization approach jointly trains a multi-document retriever and reader, improving question answering without explicit retrieval supervision.

title: End-to-End Training of Multi-Document Reader and Retriever for Open-Domain Question Answering

abstract: Deep learning has been successful in automating the design of features in machine learning pipelines. However, the algorithms optimizing neural network parameters remain largely hand-designed and computationally inefficient. We study if we can use deep learning to directly predict these parameters by exploiting the past knowledge of training other networks. We introduce a large-scale dataset of diverse computational graphs of neural architectures - DeepNets-1M - and use it to explore parameter prediction on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. By leveraging advances in graph neural networks, we propose a hypernetwork that can predict performant parameters in a single forward pass taking a fraction of a second, even on a CPU. The proposed model achieves surprisingly good performance on unseen and diverse networks. For example, it is able to predict all 24 million parameters of a ResNet-50 achieving a 60% accuracy on CIFAR-10. On ImageNet, top-5 accuracy of some of our networks approaches 50%. Our task along with the model and results can potentially lead to a new, more computationally efficient paradigm of training networks. Our model also learns a strong representation of neural architectures enabling their analysis.

paragraphs: Training a neural network typically relies on a hand-designed optimization procedure to find its parameters. This paper asks whether experience from other networks can instead support directly predicting useful parameters for a new architecture. The authors introduce DeepNets-1M, a large dataset of diverse architectural computation graphs, and study this problem on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

Their hypernetwork uses graph neural-network advances to process architectures and predict parameters in a single forward pass. The reported prediction takes a fraction of a second even on a CPU. This makes the architecture itself an input to a learned parameter-producing model, allowing the method to address previously unseen networks with varied structures.

For example, the method predicts all 24 million parameters of a ResNet-50 that achieves 60% accuracy on CIFAR-10. Some evaluated networks approach 50% top-5 accuracy on ImageNet. The model also learns representations useful for analyzing architectures. These findings suggest a possible route toward more computationally efficient network training, while the paper presents that broader shift as a potential outcome.
summary.tldr: A graph-based hypernetwork predicts useful parameters for unseen neural architectures in a single fast forward pass.

title: Parameter Prediction for Unseen Deep Architectures

abstract: Standard meta-learning for representation learning aims to find a common representation to be shared across multiple tasks. The effectiveness of these methods is often limited when the nuances of the tasks’ distribution cannot be captured by a single representation. In this work we overcome this issue by inferring a conditioning function, mapping the tasks’ side information (such as the tasks’ training dataset itself) into a representation tailored to the task at hand. We study environments in which our conditional strategy outperforms standard meta-learning, such as those in which tasks can be organized in separate clusters according to the representation they share. We then propose a meta-algorithm capable of leveraging this advantage in practice. In the unconditional setting, our method yields a new estimator enjoying faster learning rates and requiring less hyper-parameters to tune than current state-of-the-art methods. Our results are supported by preliminary experiments.

paragraphs: Representation meta-learning usually searches for one representation that many tasks can share. That arrangement can be restrictive when different kinds of tasks need different features. This paper studies a conditional alternative in which the representation itself changes according to information available about the task being solved.

The method learns a conditioning function that maps task side information, potentially the task's own training dataset, to a tailored linear representation. The authors analyze environments where this strategy improves over standard meta-learning. One example is an environment with separate task clusters, where tasks within each cluster share a representation but a single representation does not capture all clusters equally well.

The paper then proposes a meta-algorithm intended to realize this conditional advantage in practice. It also obtains a benefit in the unconditional setting: a new estimator with faster learning rates and fewer hyperparameters to tune than the state-of-the-art methods considered. Preliminary experiments support the results. The contribution links task-dependent representations to identifiable task structure while also improving the shared-representation case.
summary.tldr: Learning a task-conditioned linear representation can improve meta-learning in structured task environments, with preliminary experiments supporting the theory.

title: Conditional Meta-Learning of Linear Representations

abstract: Extreme Multi-label Text Classification (XMC) involves learning a classifier that can assign an input with a subset of most relevant labels from millions of label choices. Recent approaches, such as XR-Transformer and LightXML, leverage a transformer instance to achieve state-of-the-art performance. However, in this process, these approaches need to make various trade-offs between performance and computational requirements. A major shortcoming, as compared to the Bi-LSTM based AttentionXML, is that they fail to keep separate feature representations for each resolution in a label tree. We thus propose CascadeXML, an end-to-end multi-resolution learning pipeline, which can harness the multi-layered architecture of a transformer model for attending to different label resolutions with separate feature representations. CascadeXML significantly outperforms all existing approaches with non-trivial gains obtained on benchmark datasets consisting of up to three million labels. Code for CascadeXML will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xmc-aalto/cascadexml.

paragraphs: Extreme multi-label text classification requires selecting relevant labels from a collection that can contain millions of possibilities. A label tree organizes this enormous choice space into different resolutions. The paper examines how transformer-based classifiers represent text when making decisions across those resolutions, where computational demands and prediction quality both matter.

The authors identify a shortcoming in existing transformer approaches: they do not maintain separate feature representations for each resolution in the label tree. CascadeXML addresses this through an end-to-end training pipeline that uses the transformer's multiple layers to attend to different label resolutions. Each resolution can therefore use a separate representation within the same overall model.

The reported experiments show substantial improvements over existing approaches on benchmark datasets containing up to three million labels. These findings support matching the model's internal representations to the multiple resolutions of the classification problem. The contribution is a way to organize transformer learning around that structure while training the complete pipeline together.
summary.tldr: CascadeXML uses different transformer representations for different label-tree resolutions, improving classification on benchmarks with millions of labels.

title: CascadeXML: Rethinking Transformers for End-to-end Multi-resolution Training in Extreme Multi-label Classification

abstract: Improving the generalization of deep networks is an important open challenge, particularly in domains without plentiful data. The mixup algorithm improves generalization by linearly interpolating a pair of examples and their corresponding labels. These interpolated examples augment the original training set. Mixup has shown promising results in various classification tasks, but systematic analysis of mixup in regression remains underexplored. Using mixup directly on regression labels can result in arbitrarily incorrect labels. In this paper, we propose a simple yet powerful algorithm, C-Mixup, to improve generalization on regression tasks. In contrast with vanilla mixup, which picks training examples for mixing with uniform probability, C-Mixup adjusts the sampling probability based on the similarity of the labels. Our theoretical analysis confirms that C-Mixup with label similarity obtains a smaller mean square error in supervised regression and meta-regression than vanilla mixup and using feature similarity. Another benefit of C-Mixup is that it can improve out-of-distribution robustness, where the test distribution is different from the training distribution. By selectively interpolating examples with similar labels, it mitigates the effects of domain-associated information and yields domain-invariant representations. We evaluate C-Mixup on eleven datasets, ranging from tabular to video data. Compared to the best prior approach, C-Mixup achieves 6.56%, 4.76%, 5.82% improvements in in-distribution generalization, task generalization, and out-of-distribution robustness, respectively. Code is released at https://github.com/huaxiuyao/C-Mixup.

C-Mixup addresses this problem by changing which examples are likely to be paired, rather than abandoning interpolation as a training strategy.

Its theoretical analysis finds smaller mean squared error than ordinary mixup and feature-similarity pairing in supervised regression and meta-regression. These findings support label-aware pair selection as a useful modification of mixup for regression, including settings where the test distribution differs from training.
summary.tldr: C-Mixup improves regression generalization by making examples with similar labels more likely to be mixed.

title: C-Mixup: Improving Generalization in Regression

abstract: Model-based offline reinforcement learning approaches generally rely on bounds of model error. Estimating these bounds is usually achieved through uncertainty estimation methods. In this work, we combine parametric and nonparametric methods for uncertainty estimation through a novel latent space based metric. In particular, we build upon recent advances in Riemannian geometry of generative models to construct a pullback metric of an encoder-decoder based forward model. Our proposed metric measures both the quality of out-of-distribution samples as well as the discrepancy of examples in the data. We leverage our combined method for uncertainty estimation in a pessimistic model-based framework, showing a significant improvement upon contemporary model-based offline approaches on continuous control and autonomous driving benchmarks.

paragraphs: Model-based offline reinforcement learning relies on a learned dynamics model while using previously collected data. Uncertainty estimates help assess model error, which matters when the learned model encounters examples outside the data distribution. This paper proposes combining parametric and nonparametric uncertainty methods through a metric defined in latent space.

The metric uses Riemannian geometry associated with an encoder-decoder forward model. Specifically, the authors construct a pullback metric, tying the latent-space measurement to the learned model. Their proposed measure captures both the quality of out-of-distribution samples and discrepancies among examples in the data, bringing these two sources of information into one uncertainty estimate.

They integrate the combined estimate into a pessimistic model-based reinforcement-learning framework, where uncertainty informs cautious treatment of model predictions. Experiments on continuous-control and autonomous-driving benchmarks show significant improvements over contemporary model-based offline approaches. The findings support using model-informed latent geometry for uncertainty estimation in the evaluated settings, connecting a geometric construction to the practical quality of learned decision-making.
summary.tldr: A geometry-based latent metric combines uncertainty estimates and improves pessimistic model-based offline reinforcement learning on evaluated benchmarks.

title: Uncertainty Estimation Using Riemannian Model Dynamics for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Humans naturally use verbal utterances and nonverbal gestures to refer to various objects (known as $\textit{referring expressions}$) in different interactional scenarios. As collecting real human interaction datasets are costly and laborious, synthetic datasets are often used to train models to unambiguously detect relationships among objects. However, existing synthetic data generation tools that provide referring expressions generally neglect nonverbal gestures. Additionally, while a few small-scale datasets contain multimodal cues (verbal and nonverbal), these datasets only capture the nonverbal gestures from an exo-centric perspective (observer). As models can use complementary information from multimodal cues to recognize referring expressions, generating multimodal data from multiple views can help to develop robust models. To address these critical issues, in this paper, we present a novel embodied simulator, CAESAR, to generate multimodal referring expressions containing both verbal utterances and nonverbal cues captured from multiple views. Using our simulator, we have generated two large-scale embodied referring expression datasets, which we have released publicly. We have conducted experimental analyses on embodied spatial relation grounding using various state-of-the-art baseline models. Our experimental results suggest that visual perspective affects the models' performance; and that nonverbal cues improve spatial relation grounding accuracy. Finally, we will release the simulator publicly to allow researchers to generate new embodied interaction datasets.

paragraphs: People refer to objects through combinations of speech and gestures. Learning to interpret these combinations requires data that captures both signals and the viewpoints from which they are observed. Collecting real interactions is costly, while existing synthetic tools often omit gestures and available multimodal datasets may cover only an outside observer’s view.

CAESAR is an embodied simulator designed to generate referring expressions with verbal and nonverbal information from multiple views. The authors use it to create two large-scale datasets, which they report having released publicly. This makes viewpoint and gesture information part of the generated interaction data available for studying how expressions connect to objects and spatial relationships.

Experiments evaluate spatial relation grounding with several state-of-the-art baseline models. The results suggest that visual perspective affects performance and that nonverbal information improves grounding accuracy. These findings support studying language alongside gesture and viewpoint. The abstract also states an intention to release the simulator so researchers can generate additional embodied interaction datasets.
summary.tldr: CAESAR generates multiview language-and-gesture datasets, with experiments suggesting gestures improve spatial relation grounding.

title: CAESAR: An Embodied Simulator for Generating Multimodal Referring Expression Datasets

abstract: Video-language modeling has attracted much attention with the rapid growth of web videos. Most existing methods assume that the video frames and text description are semantically correlated, and focus on video-language modeling at video level. However, this hypothesis often fails for two reasons: (1) With the rich semantics of video contents, it is difficult to cover all frames with a single video-level description; (2) A raw video typically has noisy/meaningless information (e.g., scenery shot, transition or teaser). Although a number of recent works deploy attention mechanism to alleviate this problem, the irrelevant/noisy information still makes it very difficult to address. To overcome such challenge, we thus propose an efficient and effective model, termed Language-Guided Denoising Network (LGDN), for video-language modeling. Different from most existing methods that utilize all extracted video frames, LGDN dynamically filters out the misaligned or redundant frames under the language supervision and obtains only 2--4 salient frames per video for cross-modal token-level alignment. Extensive experiments on five public datasets show that our LGDN outperforms the state-of-the-arts by large margins. We also provide detailed ablation study to reveal the critical importance of solving the noise issue, in hope of inspiring future video-language work.

paragraphs: A video's text description rarely explains every frame. Some frames show other content, and others contain transitions, teasers, or information irrelevant to the description. This paper argues that treating all extracted frames as semantically aligned with the text introduces noise into video-language modeling, even when attention mechanisms are used.

The Language-Guided Denoising Network uses language supervision to dynamically remove frames that are misaligned or redundant. It retains only two to four salient frames per video for token-level alignment between video and language. Frame selection therefore becomes part of the modeling approach, focusing the cross-modal comparison on a small set of relevant visual observations.

Experiments on five public datasets report large improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The authors also use ablation studies to examine the importance of addressing noise. The findings support explicitly filtering the visual material used for alignment: a compact selection guided by language can provide a stronger basis for video-language modeling than retaining every extracted frame in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: LGDN uses language to select two to four relevant video frames, improving video-language modeling by removing misaligned and redundant content.

title: LGDN: Language-Guided Denoising Network for Video-Language Modeling

abstract: While vision-and-language models perform well on tasks such as visual question answering, they struggle when it comes to basic human commonsense reasoning skills. In this work, we introduce WinoGAViL: an online game of vision-and-language associations (e.g., between werewolves and a full moon), used as a dynamic evaluation benchmark. Inspired by the popular card game Codenames, a spymaster gives a textual cue related to several visual candidates, and another player tries to identify them. Human players are rewarded for creating associations that are challenging for a rival AI model but still solvable by other human players. We use the game to collect 3.5K instances, finding that they are intuitive for humans (>90% Jaccard index) but challenging for state-of-the-art AI models, where the best model (ViLT) achieves a score of 52%, succeeding mostly where the cue is visually salient. Our analysis as well as the feedback we collect from players indicate that the collected associations require diverse reasoning skills, including general knowledge, common sense, abstraction, and more. We release the dataset, the code and the interactive game, allowing future data collection that can be used to develop models with better association abilities.

paragraphs: WinoGAViL evaluates whether vision-and-language models can recognize associations that people find intuitive. A textual cue must be linked to several candidate images, as in connecting werewolves with a full moon. The task probes reasoning beyond cases where the cue is directly visible in the image.

The benchmark is collected through an online game inspired by Codenames. One player supplies a cue and another identifies the associated images. Players receive rewards for creating associations that challenge a rival AI while remaining solvable by other humans. This process produces examples shaped by both model difficulty and human understandability.

The authors collect 3.5K instances. Humans exceed a 90% Jaccard index, while the strongest evaluated model, ViLT, scores 52% and succeeds mostly when cues are visually salient. Analysis and player feedback indicate that the associations draw on general knowledge, common sense, abstraction, and other reasoning skills. summary.tldr: WinoGAViL uses a human association game to collect image–text reasoning challenges that expose a large gap between people and evaluated models.

title: WinoGAViL: Gamified Association Benchmark to Challenge Vision-and-Language Models

abstract: Deep Neural Networks inherit spurious correlations embedded in training data and hence may fail to predict desired labels on unseen domains (or environments), which have different distributions from the domain to provide training data. Invariance Learning (IL) has been developed recently to overcome this shortcoming; using training data in many domains, IL estimates such a predictor that is invariant to a change of domain. However, the requirement of training data in multiple domains is a strong restriction of using IL, since it demands expensive annotation. We propose a novel IL framework to overcome this problem. Assuming the availability of data from multiple domains for a higher level of classification task, for which the labeling cost is lower, we estimate an invariant predictor for the target classification task with training data gathered in a single domain. Additionally, we propose two cross-validation methods for selecting hyperparameters of invariance regularization, which has not been addressed properly in existing IL methods. The effectiveness of the proposed framework, including the cross-validation, is demonstrated empirically. Theoretical analysis reveals that our framework can estimate the desirable invariant predictor with a hyperparameter fixed correctly, and that such a preferable hyperparameter is chosen by the proposed CV methods under some conditions.

paragraphs: A model can learn accidental associations that work in its training environment but fail elsewhere. Invariance learning aims to find predictors that remain useful across environments, usually by requiring training data from several domains. This paper reduces the demand for expensive target-task annotations by making use of a hierarchy of classification labels.

The framework assumes that data from multiple domains are available for a higher-level classification task whose labels cost less to obtain. For the target task, training examples need come from only one domain. The method uses the broader task's cross-domain information to estimate an invariant predictor for the more specific task, connecting annotation availability across levels of the hierarchy.

The authors also propose two cross-validation procedures for choosing the strength of invariance regularization. Experiments demonstrate the framework's effectiveness, including this model-selection component. The theory shows that the desired invariant predictor can be estimated when the hyperparameter is correctly fixed, and that the proposed cross-validation methods select a suitable value under stated conditions. Thus both the learning result and parameter-selection result retain explicit qualifications.
summary.tldr: Label hierarchies enable invariant learning with target-task data from one domain, provided higher-level labeled data span multiple domains.

title: Invariance Learning based on Label Hierarchy

abstract: Nowadays self-paced learning (SPL) is an important machine learning paradigm that mimics the cognitive process of humans and animals. The SPL regime involves a self-paced regularizer and a gradually increasing age parameter, which plays a key role in SPL but where to optimally terminate this process is still non-trivial to determine. A natural idea is to compute the solution path w.r.t. age parameter (i.e., age-path). However, current age-path algorithms are either limited to the simplest regularizer, or lack solid theoretical understanding as well as computational efficiency. To address this challenge, we propose a novel Generalized Age-path Algorithm (GAGA) for SPL with various self-paced regularizers based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and sets control, which can learn the entire solution spectrum w.r.t. a range of age parameters. To the best of our knowledge, GAGA is the first exact path-following algorithm tackling the age-path for general self-paced regularizer. Finally the algorithmic steps of classic SVM and Lasso are described in detail. We demonstrate the performance of GAGA on real-world datasets, and find considerable speedup between our algorithm and competing baselines.
