paragraphs: Self-paced learning controls the progression of training through a regularizer and a gradually increasing parameter called age. Choosing where to stop this progression is difficult. One way to understand the choice is to trace the age-path: the sequence of learned solutions obtained as the age parameter changes over a range.

GAGA provides a path-following algorithm for various self-paced regularizers. It combines ordinary differential equations with set control to track the solution across age values. This broadens the scope beyond earlier algorithms that were restricted to the simplest regularizer or lacked a strong combination of theoretical understanding and computational efficiency.

The authors describe GAGA as, to their knowledge, the first exact age-path algorithm for general self-paced regularizers. They give concrete algorithmic steps for support vector machines and Lasso, and report considerable speedups over competing baselines on real-world datasets. Computing the path makes the effect of the age parameter accessible across a range; the stated contribution is this exact and efficient tracking, rather than a claimed universal stopping rule.
summary.tldr: GAGA uses differential equations and set control to efficiently trace exact solution paths across age parameters for general self-paced regularizers.

title: GAGA: Deciphering Age-path of Generalized Self-paced Regularizer

abstract: Previous works show global covariance pooling (GCP) has great potential to improve deep architectures especially on visual recognition tasks, where post-normalization of GCP plays a very important role in final performance. Although several post-normalization strategies have been studied, these methods pay more close attention to effect of normalization on covariance representations rather than the whole GCP networks, and their effectiveness requires further understanding. Meanwhile, existing effective post-normalization strategies (e.g., matrix power normalization) usually suffer from high computational complexity (e.g., $O(d^{3})$ for $d$-dimensional inputs). To handle above issues, this work first analyzes the effect of post-normalization from the perspective of training GCP networks. Particularly, we for the first time show that \textit{effective post-normalization can make a good trade-off between representation decorrelation and information preservation for GCP, which are crucial to alleviate over-fitting and increase representation ability of deep GCP networks, respectively}. Based on this finding, we can improve existing post-normalization methods with some small modifications, providing further support to our observation. Furthermore, this finding encourages us to propose a novel pre-normalization method for GCP (namely DropCov), which develops an adaptive channel dropout on features right before GCP, aiming to reach trade-off between representation decorrelation and information preservation in a more efficient way. Our DropCov only has a linear complexity of $O(d)$, while being free for inference. Extensive experiments on various benchmarks (i.e., ImageNet-1K, ImageNet-C, ImageNet-A, Stylized-ImageNet, and iNat2017) show our DropCov is superior to the counterparts in terms of efficiency and effectiveness, and provides a simple yet effective method to improve performance of deep architectures involving both deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision transformers (ViTs).

paragraphs: Global covariance pooling summarizes relationships among feature channels and can improve visual recognition networks. Its performance depends strongly on how the resulting representation is normalized. This paper examines normalization through its effect on training the whole network, while also addressing the high computational cost of effective existing methods.

The analysis identifies a useful balance between reducing correlations in the representation and preserving information. These serve different purposes: decorrelation helps reduce overfitting, while information preservation supports representational capacity. Small changes to existing normalization methods improve them and provide additional support for this explanation.

The authors then introduce DropCov, which adaptively drops feature channels immediately before covariance pooling. This places the intervention before pooling and aims to achieve the same balance more efficiently. The method has linear complexity in the feature dimension and adds no inference cost, whereas some existing normalization methods have cubic complexity. Experiments across several visual benchmarks report advantages in effectiveness and efficiency, with improvements for architectures involving both convolutional networks and vision transformers.
summary.tldr: DropCov uses adaptive channel dropout before covariance pooling to balance decorrelation and information preservation with low computational overhead.

title: DropCov: A Simple yet Effective Method for Improving Deep Architectures

abstract: This paper presents new projection-free algorithms for Online Convex Optimization (OCO) over a convex domain $\mathcal{K} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$. Classical OCO algorithms (such as Online Gradient Descent) typically need to perform Euclidean projections onto the convex set $\mathcal{K}$ to ensure feasibility of their iterates. Alternative algorithms, such as those based on the Frank-Wolfe method, swap potentially-expensive Euclidean projections onto $\mathcal{K}$ for linear optimization over $\mathcal{K}$. However, such algorithms have a sub-optimal regret in OCO compared to projection-based algorithms. In this paper, we look at a third type of algorithms that output approximate Newton iterates using a self-concordant barrier for the set of interest. The use of a self-concordant barrier automatically ensures feasibility without the need of projections. However, the computation of the Newton iterates requires a matrix inverse, which can still be expensive. As our main contribution, we show how the stability of the Newton iterates can be leveraged to only compute the inverse Hessian a vanishing fractions of the rounds, leading to a new efficient projection-free OCO algorithm with a state-of-the-art regret bound.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization requires repeated decisions that remain inside a convex feasible set. Standard methods often enforce this by projecting each update back onto the set, which can be expensive. Methods based on Frank-Wolfe replace projections with linear optimization, but the abstract identifies a disadvantage in their regret guarantees relative to projection-based approaches.

The authors investigate another route: approximate Newton updates using a self-concordant barrier for the domain. The barrier keeps updates feasible without explicit projection. However, computing Newton steps introduces its own costly operation, because the method requires an inverse of the Hessian matrix associated with the update.

The paper’s main contribution uses stability in the Newton iterates to avoid recomputing that inverse on most rounds. The fraction of rounds requiring an inverse computation vanishes, reducing this recurring computational burden. The resulting algorithm combines projection-free feasibility with a state-of-the-art regret bound. Its significance lies in addressing both the quality of sequential decisions and the expensive matrix operations needed to produce them.
summary.tldr: Stable approximate Newton updates reduce matrix inversions while delivering projection-free online optimization with a state-of-the-art regret bound.

title: Projection-Free Online Convex Optimization via Efficient Newton Iterations

abstract: Multilabel ranking is a central task in machine learning. However, the most fundamental question of learnability in a multilabel ranking setting with relevance-score feedback remains unanswered. In this work, we characterize the learnability of multilabel ranking problems in both batch and online settings for a large family of ranking losses. Along the way, we give two equivalence classes of ranking losses based on learnability that capture most losses used in practice.

paragraphs: Multilabel ranking concerns ordering labels according to their relevance. This paper studies the fundamental question of when such a ranking problem is learnable when feedback consists of relevance scores. Its focus is on the possibility of learning across a broad family of ranking losses, the criteria used to judge ranking errors.

The authors characterize learnability in both batch and online settings. Addressing both settings makes the analysis relevant to learning from a collected dataset and to learning as examples arrive over time. The central contribution is a theoretical characterization across these settings, connecting the ranking task and its evaluation loss to whether learning is possible.

The work also identifies two equivalence classes of losses based on learnability, covering most ranking losses used in practice. This groups different ways of scoring ranking mistakes according to their learnability behavior. Such a classification gives a common theoretical organization to losses that may otherwise appear separate. The stated result concerns these learnability relationships under relevance-score feedback, rather than an empirical comparison of particular ranking systems.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes multilabel-ranking learnability with relevance-score feedback and organizes practical ranking losses into two learnability equivalence classes.

title: On the Learnability of Multilabel Ranking

abstract: This paper studies delayed stochastic algorithms for weakly convex optimization in a distributed network with workers connected to a master node. Recently, Xu~et~al.~2022 showed that an inertial stochastic subgradient method converges at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(\tau_{\text{max}}/\sqrt{K})$ which depends on the maximum information delay $\tau_{\text{max}}$. In this work, we show that the delayed stochastic subgradient method ($\texttt{DSGD}$) obtains a tighter convergence rate which depends on the expected delay $\bar{\tau}$. Furthermore, for an important class of composition weakly convex problems, we develop a new delayed stochastic prox-linear ($\texttt{DSPL}$) method in which the delays only affect the high-order term in the rate and hence, are negligible after a certain number of $\texttt{DSPL}$ iterations. In addition, we demonstrate the robustness of our proposed algorithms against arbitrary delays. By incorporating a simple safeguarding step in both methods, we achieve convergence rates that depend solely on the number of workers, eliminating the effect of delays. Our numerical experiments further confirm the empirical superiority of our proposed methods.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization can involve workers sending information to a central node after delays, so updates may use stale information. This paper studies that problem for stochastic weakly convex optimization. It improves the understanding of how delay affects convergence and develops algorithms that reduce its influence under the settings analyzed.

For delayed stochastic subgradient descent, the authors obtain a tighter convergence rate governed by expected delay rather than maximum delay. This distinction matters when unusually late messages make the worst case much larger than typical delays. For an important class of composition problems, their delayed stochastic prox-linear method places delay effects only in a higher-order term, which becomes negligible after enough iterations.

The paper also adds a simple safeguarding step to both methods to handle arbitrary delays. With this safeguard, the convergence rates depend on the number of workers rather than delay quantities. Numerical experiments support the proposed methods’ empirical advantages. Together, the results show several ways to reduce the theoretical penalty from stale information, with the strongest conclusions tied to the corresponding algorithm and problem structure.
summary.tldr: The paper sharpens convergence guarantees for delayed distributed optimization and introduces methods that reduce or remove delay dependence from those guarantees.

title: Delayed Algorithms for Distributed Stochastic Weakly Convex Optimization

abstract: Pseudo-labeling has emerged as a popular and effective approach for utilizing unlabeled data. However, in the context of semi-supervised multi-label learning (SSMLL), conventional pseudo-labeling methods encounter difficulties when dealing with instances associated with multiple labels and an unknown label count. These limitations often result in the introduction of false positive labels or the neglect of true positive ones. To overcome these challenges, this paper proposes a novel solution called Class-Aware Pseudo-Labeling (CAP) that performs pseudo-labeling in a class-aware manner. The proposed approach introduces a regularized learning framework incorporating class-aware thresholds, which effectively control the assignment of positive and negative pseudo-labels for each class. Notably, even with a small proportion of labeled examples, our observations demonstrate that the estimated class distribution serves as a reliable approximation. Motivated by this finding, we develop a class-distribution-aware thresholding strategy to ensure the alignment of pseudo-label distribution with the true distribution. The correctness of the estimated class distribution is theoretically verified, and a generalization error bound is provided for our proposed method. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets confirm the efficacy of CAP in addressing the challenges of SSMLL problems.

paragraphs: Pseudo-labeling uses a model’s predictions as training labels for otherwise unlabeled examples. In multi-label learning, an example may belong to several classes, and the number of applicable labels is unknown. Conventional pseudo-labeling can therefore assign labels that should be absent or overlook labels that should be present. This paper proposes Class-Aware Pseudo-Labeling, or CAP, to address those errors.

CAP places class-specific thresholds inside a regularized learning framework to control positive and negative pseudo-label assignments. Its central idea is to use estimated class frequencies to guide those thresholds, aligning the distribution of pseudo-labels with the true class distribution. The authors observe that even a small labeled portion can provide a reliable approximation of class frequencies.

The paper supplies theoretical support for the distribution estimate and a generalization error bound for CAP. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets also support the method’s effectiveness. Together, these results suggest that class prevalence is useful information when selecting pseudo-labels: prediction confidence can be interpreted alongside how frequently a class is expected to occur.
summary.tldr: CAP uses estimated class frequencies to set class-specific pseudo-label thresholds for learning from partially labeled multi-label data.

title: Class-Distribution-Aware Pseudo-Labeling for Semi-Supervised Multi-Label Learning

abstract: Variational inference (VI) is a method to approximate the computationally intractable posterior distributions that arise in Bayesian statistics. Typically, VI fits a simple parametric distribution to be close to the target posterior, optimizing an appropriate objective such as the evidence lower bound (ELBO). In this work, we present a new approach to VI. Our method is based on the principle of score matching---namely, that if two distributions are equal then their score functions (i.e., gradients of the log density) are equal at every point on their support. With this principle, we develop score-matching VI, an iterative algorithm that seeks to match the scores between the variational approximation and the exact posterior. At each iteration, score-matching VI solves an inner optimization, one that minimally adjusts the current variational estimate to match the scores at a newly sampled value of the latent variables. We show that when the variational family is a Gaussian, this inner optimization enjoys a closed-form solution, which we call Gaussian score matching VI (GSM-VI). GSM-VI is a ``black box'' variational algorithm in that it only requires a differentiable joint distribution, and as such it can be applied to a wide class of models. We compare GSM-VI to black box variational inference (BBVI), which has similar requirements but instead optimizes the ELBO. We first study how GSM-VI behaves as a function of the problem dimensionality, the condition number of the target covariance matrix (when the target is Gaussian), and the degree of mismatch between the approximating and exact posterior distribution. We then study GSM-VI on a collection of real-world Bayesian inference problems from the posteriorDB database of datasets and models. We find that GSM-VI is faster than BBVI and equally or more accurate. Specifically, over a wide range of target posteriors, GSM-VI requires 10-100x fewer gradient evaluations than BBVI to obtain a comparable quality of approximation.

This paper develops an approach based on matching score functions, the gradients of log densities. Its starting principle is that equal distributions have equal scores at every point on their support.

At each iteration, the algorithm samples latent variables and minimally adjusts the current approximation to match the posterior’s score at that sample. When the approximation is Gaussian, this inner optimization has a closed-form solution. The resulting Gaussian score-matching method, GSM-VI, requires only a differentiable joint distribution, enabling application across a broad class of Bayesian models.

Compared with black-box variational inference that optimizes the evidence lower bound, GSM-VI is faster and equally or more accurate in the reported experiments. Across a wide range of target posteriors, it reaches comparable approximation quality using 10–100 times fewer gradient evaluations.
summary.tldr: Gaussian score-matching variational inference uses closed-form local updates and reaches comparable posterior approximation quality with substantially fewer gradient evaluations in reported experiments.

title: Variational Inference with Gaussian Score Matching

abstract: In structured prediction, target objects have rich internal structure which does not factorize into independent components and violates common i.i.d. assumptions. This challenge becomes apparent through the exponentially large output space in applications such as image segmentation or scene graph generation.We present a novel PAC-Bayesian risk bound for structured prediction wherein the rate of generalization scales not only with the number of structured examples but also with their size.The underlying assumption, conforming to ongoing research on generative models, is that data are generated by the Knothe-Rosenblatt rearrangement of a factorizing reference measure. This allows to explicitly distill the structure between random output variables into a Wasserstein dependency matrix. Our work makes a preliminary step towards leveraging powerful generative models to establish generalization bounds for discriminative downstream tasks in the challenging setting of structured prediction.

This challenge becomes apparent through the exponentially large output space in applications such as image segmentation or scene graph generation.We present a novel PAC-Bayesian risk bound for structured prediction wherein the rate of generalization scales not only with the number of structured examples but also with their size.The underlying assumption, conforming to ongoing research on generative models, is that data are generated by the Knothe-Rosenblatt rearrangement of a factorizing reference measure. paragraphs: Structured prediction produces outputs whose parts depend on one another, as in image segmentation or scene graphs. Treating those parts as independent misses this internal structure, while the number of possible complete outputs can grow exponentially. This paper develops a PAC-Bayesian risk bound to reason about generalization in that setting.

The bound's generalization rate depends on both the number of structured examples and their size. Its key assumption concerns how the data are generated: a Knothe-Rosenblatt rearrangement transforms a factorizing reference measure into the data distribution. In plain terms, the analysis starts from an independent reference distribution and uses a specified transformation to represent the dependencies in the observed outputs.

This construction allows the authors to summarize relationships among output variables in a Wasserstein dependency matrix. That representation connects the assumed generative process to a guarantee for a discriminative prediction task. The paper presents this as a preliminary step toward using powerful generative models to certify generalization, with the stated generation assumption central to the proposed bound.
summary.tldr: A new structured-prediction generalization bound accounts for example size under a specified generative assumption that represents output dependencies.

title: On Certified Generalization in Structured Prediction

abstract: Recently, the Deep Learning community has become interested in evolutionary optimization (EO) as a means to address hard optimization problems, e.g. meta-learning through long inner loop unrolls or optimizing non-differentiable operators. One core reason for this trend has been the recent innovation in hardware acceleration and compatible software -- making distributed population evaluations much easier than before. Unlike for gradient descent-based methods though, there is a lack of hyperparameter understanding and best practices for EO – arguably due to severely less `graduate student descent' and benchmarking being performed for EO methods. Additionally, classical benchmarks from the evolutionary community provide few practical insights for Deep Learning applications. This poses challenges for newcomers to hardware-accelerated EO and hinders significant adoption. Hence, we establish a new benchmark of EO methods (NEB) tailored toward Deep Learning applications and exhaustively evaluate traditional and meta-learned EO. We investigate core scientific questions including resource allocation, fitness shaping, normalization, regularization & scalability of EO. The benchmark is open-sourced at https://github.com/neuroevobench/neuroevobench under Apache-2.0 license.

paragraphs: Evolutionary optimization is attracting interest for deep-learning problems such as non-differentiable operations and meta-learning with long inner loops. Hardware acceleration and compatible software have made distributed evaluation of candidate populations easier. However, the paper identifies a shortage of practical hyperparameter knowledge and benchmarking tailored to these applications.

NeuroEvoBench addresses that gap with a benchmark designed specifically for deep-learning uses of evolutionary optimization. It evaluates both traditional optimizers and meta-learned alternatives. Its investigation covers resource allocation, fitness shaping, normalization, regularization, and scalability, connecting optimizer evaluation to practical choices involved in running these methods.

The contribution is a shared basis for studying evolutionary optimizers in settings where classical evolutionary benchmarks offer limited guidance. The abstract does not name a universally best optimizer; its emphasis is systematic evaluation of the methods and their configuration. The benchmark is released under the Apache-2.0 license, making the evaluation resource available for further use and investigation.
summary.tldr: NeuroEvoBench benchmarks traditional and meta-learned evolutionary optimizers on deep-learning applications and investigates practical configuration choices.

title: NeuroEvoBench: Benchmarking Evolutionary Optimizers for Deep Learning Applications

abstract: We propose and deploy an approach to continually train an instruction-following agent from feedback provided by users during collaborative interactions. During interaction, human users instruct an agent using natural language, and provide realtime binary feedback as they observe the agent following their instructions. We design a contextual bandit learning approach, converting user feedback to immediate reward. We evaluate through thousands of human-agent interactions, demonstrating 15.4% absolute improvement in instruction execution accuracy over time. We also show our approach is robust to several design variations, and that the feedback signal is roughly equivalent to the learning signal of supervised demonstration data.

paragraphs: An instruction-following agent can receive useful teaching signals while people are interacting with it. This paper proposes and deploys a system that continually learns from those signals. Users give natural-language instructions and then provide binary feedback in real time as they watch the agent attempt to carry them out.

The learning method uses a contextual bandit formulation, converting feedback into immediate reward. This makes the feedback part of the training process rather than merely an evaluation collected after interaction. The approach connects what users observe during collaboration with subsequent improvement in instruction execution, using a simple feedback format that does not itself require a full demonstration.

Across thousands of human-agent interactions, instruction execution accuracy improves by 15.4 percentage points over time. The authors also report robustness to several design variations and find that the feedback provides a learning signal roughly equivalent to supervised demonstration data. These results support continual learning from realtime feedback in the evaluated setting, with the comparison to demonstrations remaining approximate.
summary.tldr: An instruction-following agent learns continually from realtime binary user feedback, improving execution accuracy by 15.4 percentage points in the evaluation.

title: Continual Learning for Instruction Following from Realtime Feedback

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are ubiquitous in computer vision and natural language processing, but suffer from high inference cost. This problem can be addressed by quantization, which consists in converting floating point operations into a lower bit-width format. With the growing concerns on privacy rights, we focus our efforts on data-free methods. However, such techniques suffer from their lack of adaptability to the target devices, as a hardware typically only supports specific bit widths. Thus, to adapt to a variety of devices, a quantization method shall be flexible enough to find good accuracy v.s. speed trade-offs for every bit width and target device. To achieve this, we propose REx, a quantization method that leverages residual error expansion, along with group sparsity. We show experimentally that REx enables better trade-offs (in terms of accuracy given any target bit-width) on both convnets and transformers for computer vision, as well as NLP models. In particular, when applied to large language models, we show that REx elegantly solves the outlier problem that hinders state-of-the-art quantization methods.In addition, REx is backed off by strong theoretical guarantees on the preservation of the predictive function of the original model. Lastly, we show that REx is agnostic to the quantization operator and can be used in combination with previous quantization work.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces neural-network inference cost by replacing floating-point computation with lower-bit formats. Deploying one approach across devices is difficult because hardware supports particular bit widths. REx addresses this flexibility problem in the data-free setting, where quantization does not depend on access to training data.

The method combines residual quantization error expansion with group sparsity. Its goal is to provide useful accuracy–speed trade-offs across target bit widths and devices. It is also independent of the particular quantization operator, allowing it to work alongside earlier quantization techniques rather than requiring a single fixed conversion rule.

Experiments show better accuracy trade-offs at target bit widths for vision convolutional networks, transformers, and natural-language models. For large language models, the authors report resolving the outlier problem that hampers leading quantization approaches. They also provide theoretical guarantees concerning preservation of the original model’s predictive function. These results connect practical compression flexibility with a formal account of how quantization affects predictions, while supporting use across several model families.
summary.tldr: REx combines residual error expansion and group sparsity for flexible data-free quantization across bit widths and model families.

title: REx: Data-Free Residual Quantization Error Expansion

abstract: Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DPMs) have recently shown remarkable performance in image generation tasks, which are capable of generating highly realistic images. When adopting DPMs for image restoration tasks, the crucial aspect lies in how to integrate the conditional information to guide the DPMs to generate accurate and natural output, which has been largely overlooked in existing works. In this paper, we present a unified conditional framework based on diffusion models for image restoration. We leverage a lightweight UNet to predict initial guidance and the diffusion model to learn the residual of the guidance. By carefully designing the basic module and integration module for the diffusion model block, we integrate the guidance and other auxiliary conditional information into every block of the diffusion model to achieve spatially-adaptive generation conditioning. To handle high-resolution images, we propose a simple yet effective inter-step patch-splitting strategy to produce arbitrary-resolution images without grid artifacts. We evaluate our conditional framework on three challenging tasks: extreme low-light denoising, deblurring, and JPEG restoration, demonstrating its significant improvements in perceptual quality and the generalization to restoration tasks. The code will be released at https://zhangyi-3.github.io/project/UCDIR/.

paragraphs: Image restoration requires an output that looks natural while remaining faithful to the image being repaired. A diffusion model’s ability to generate realistic images does not by itself solve that problem. This paper focuses on how restoration information should guide the generation process throughout the network.

The framework first uses a lightweight UNet to produce an initial estimate. The diffusion model then learns the residual: the correction needed relative to that estimate. Specially designed modules introduce both the initial guidance and additional conditioning information into every diffusion block. This allows the influence of the guidance to vary across image locations.

For high-resolution inputs, the authors introduce a patch-splitting strategy applied between sampling steps, reporting arbitrary-resolution outputs without grid artifacts. They evaluate the framework on extreme low-light denoising, deblurring, and JPEG restoration. The reported perceptual improvements across these tasks support the usefulness of combining an initial restoration estimate with spatially adaptive guidance throughout diffusion.
summary.tldr: The framework restores images by guiding every diffusion block with an initial estimate and learning the corrections that estimate needs.

title: A Unified Conditional Framework for Diffusion-based Image Restoration

abstract: We study the problem of generating arbitrarily large environments to improve the throughput of multi-robot systems. Prior work proposes Quality Diversity (QD) algorithms as an effective method for optimizing the environments of automated warehouses. However, these approaches optimize only relatively small environments, falling short when it comes to replicating real-world warehouse sizes. The challenge arises from the exponential increase in the search space as the environment size increases. Additionally, the previous methods have only been tested with up to 350 robots in simulations, while practical warehouses could host thousands of robots. In this paper, instead of optimizing environments, we propose to optimize Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) environment generators via QD algorithms. We train a collection of NCA generators with QD algorithms in small environments and then generate arbitrarily large environments from the generators at test time. We show that NCA environment generators maintain consistent, regularized patterns regardless of environment size, significantly enhancing the scalability of multi-robot systems in two different domains with up to 2,350 robots. Additionally, we demonstrate that our method scales a single-agent reinforcement learning policy to arbitrarily large environments with similar patterns. We include the source code at https://github.com/lunjohnzhang/warehouse_env_gen_nca_public.

paragraphs: Designing an environment for many robots becomes difficult as its size grows, because the number of possible layouts increases exponentially. Earlier quality diversity approaches optimized relatively small warehouse environments directly. This paper instead optimizes generators, aiming to carry useful layout patterns from manageable training environments into much larger spaces.

The generators are neural cellular automata, and quality diversity algorithms train a collection of them on small environments. At test time, those learned generators produce environments of arbitrary size. The central change is the object being optimized: a reusable process for constructing layouts replaces the search for each individual large layout.

The authors find that generated environments retain consistent, regularized patterns across sizes. They report improved scalability in two multi-robot domains, with experiments reaching 2,350 robots. They also demonstrate that a single-agent reinforcement learning policy can operate in arbitrarily large environments with similar patterns. These findings connect scalable generation with behavioral reuse, while the concrete multi-robot evidence extends to the tested system sizes.
summary.tldr: Optimizing neural cellular automata on small environments produces reusable generators that scale layouts to larger robot systems.

title: Arbitrarily Scalable Environment Generators via Neural Cellular Automata

abstract: Most existing methods for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) rely on a shared network to extract domain-invariant features. However, when facing multiple source domains, optimizing such a network involves updating the parameters of the entire network, making it both computationally expensive and challenging, particularly when coupled with min-max objectives. Inspired by recent advances in prompt learning that adapts high-capacity models for downstream tasks in a computationally economic way, we introduce Multi-Prompt Alignment (MPA), a simple yet efficient framework for multi-source UDA. Given a source and target domain pair, MPA first trains an individual prompt to minimize the domain gap through a contrastive loss. Then, MPA denoises the learned prompts through an auto-encoding process and aligns them by maximizing the agreement of all the reconstructed prompts. Moreover, we show that the resulting subspace acquired from the auto-encoding process can easily generalize to a streamlined set of target domains, making our method more efficient for practical usage. Extensive experiments show that MPA achieves state-of-the-art results on three popular datasets with an impressive average accuracy of 54.1% on DomainNet.

paragraphs: Multi-source unsupervised domain adaptation uses several source domains to help a model work on a target domain without target labels. Updating an entire shared network to reconcile those domains can be expensive and difficult. Multi-Prompt Alignment instead builds on prompt learning as a computationally economical way to adapt a high-capacity model.

For each source–target pair, the method learns an individual prompt using a contrastive loss to reduce the domain gap. It then passes the learned prompts through an auto-encoding process to denoise them. Maximizing agreement among the reconstructed prompts aligns what the different source domains contribute, connecting pair-specific adaptation with a shared result.

The authors also show that the subspace learned by auto-encoding can generalize to a streamlined set of target domains, improving practical efficiency. Experiments report state-of-the-art results on three datasets, including average accuracy of 54.1% on DomainNet. These findings support prompt alignment as an effective approach in the evaluated multi-source setting, where adapting and reconciling prompts replaces the expensive emphasis on updating a full shared feature network.
summary.tldr: Multi-Prompt Alignment learns, denoises, and reconciles domain-specific prompts for efficient multi-source unsupervised adaptation.

title: Multi-Prompt Alignment for Multi-Source Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: Gradient estimation is critical in zeroth-order optimization methods, which aims to obtain the descent direction by sampling update directions and querying function evaluations. Extensive research has been conducted including smoothing and linear interpolation. The former methods smooth the objective function, causing a biased gradient estimation, while the latter often enjoys more accurate estimates, at the cost of large amounts of samples and queries at each iteration to update variables. This paper resorts to the linear interpolation strategy and proposes to reduce the complexity of gradient estimation by reusing queries in the prior iterations while maintaining the sample size unchanged. Specifically, we model the gradient estimation as a quadratically constrained linear program problem and manage to derive the analytical solution. It innovatively decouples the required sample size from the variable dimension without extra conditions required, making it able to leverage the queries in the prior iterations. Moreover, part of the intermediate variables that contribute to the gradient estimation can be directly indexed, significantly reducing the computation complexity. Experiments on both simulation functions and real scenarios (black-box adversarial attacks neural architecture search, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning for large language models), show its efficacy and efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/Thinklab-SJTU/ReLIZO.git.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization searches for better solutions using function evaluations rather than directly available gradients. Estimating a useful descent direction can require many queries. Linear interpolation can provide accurate estimates, but its sampling cost is often high. ReLIZO aims to reduce that cost by reusing function queries from earlier iterations.

The authors formulate gradient estimation as a linear optimization problem with a quadratic constraint and derive an analytical solution. Their formulation separates the required sample count from the number of optimization variables without requiring extra conditions. This makes previous queries usable while keeping the sample size unchanged, reducing the need for fresh evaluations at every iteration.

The method also allows some intermediate quantities used in gradient estimation to be retrieved directly by indexing, lowering computational complexity. Experiments cover simulation functions, black-box adversarial attacks, neural architecture search, and parameter-efficient language-model fine-tuning. They report effectiveness and efficiency across these settings. The contribution is therefore both query reuse and cheaper computation for extracting an update direction from the available observations.
summary.tldr: ReLIZO reduces zeroth-order gradient-estimation costs by reusing earlier function queries through an analytically solved interpolation formulation.

title: ReLIZO: Sample Reusable Linear Interpolation-based Zeroth-order Optimization

abstract: Push-Relabel is one of the most celebrated network flow algorithms. Maintaining a pre-flow that saturates a cut, it enjoys better theoretical and empirical running time than other flow algorithms, such as Ford-Fulkerson. In practice, Push-Relabel is even faster than what theoretical guarantees can promise, in part because of the use of good heuristics for seeding and updating the iterative algorithm. However, it remains unclear how to run Push-Relabel on an arbitrary initialization that is not necessarily a pre-flow or cut-saturating. We provide the first theoretical guarantees for warm-starting Push-Relabel with a predicted flow, where our learning-augmented version benefits from fast running time when the predicted flow is close to an optimal flow, while maintaining robust worst-case guarantees. Interestingly, our algorithm uses the gap relabeling heuristic, which has long been employed in practice, even though prior to our work there was no rigorous theoretical justification for why it can lead to run-time improvements. We then show our algorithmic framework works well in practice, as our warm-start version of Push-Relabel improves over the cold-start version by a larger and larger percentage as the size of the image increases.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to initialize the Push-Relabel network-flow algorithm using a predicted flow. Standard Push-Relabel relies on a particular intermediate structure: a pre-flow that saturates a cut. An arbitrary prediction need not satisfy those conditions, making it unclear how to use potentially helpful prior information while retaining algorithmic guarantees.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for a learning-augmented version that accepts a predicted initialization. Its running time benefits when that prediction is close to an optimal flow, while robust worst-case guarantees remain available. This makes the acceleration conditional on prediction quality without making the algorithm's worst-case protection depend on a good prediction.

The framework uses gap relabeling, a heuristic long employed in practice. The analysis supplies a rigorous explanation for how this heuristic can improve running time within the proposed method. Practical results also favor warm-starting: the percentage improvement over cold-start Push-Relabel grows as image size increases. The paper thus connects prediction-assisted initialization, established implementation heuristics, and formal running-time analysis.
summary.tldr: A warm-start Push-Relabel algorithm exploits accurate flow predictions for speed while retaining robust worst-case guarantees.

title: Warm-starting Push-Relabel

abstract: Methods of computational quantum chemistry provide accurate approximations of molecular properties crucial for computer-aided drug discovery and other areas of chemical science. However, high computational complexity limits the scalability of their applications.Neural network potentials (NNPs) are a promising alternative to quantum chemistry methods, but they require large and diverse datasets for training.This work presents a new dataset and benchmark called $\nabla^2$DFT that is based on the nablaDFT.It contains twice as much molecular structures, three times more conformations, new data types and tasks, and state-of-the-art models.The dataset includes energies, forces, 17 molecular properties, Hamiltonian and overlap matrices, and a wavefunction object.All calculations were performed at the DFT level ($\omega$B97X-D/def2-SVP) for each conformation. Moreover, $\nabla^2$DFT is the first dataset that contains relaxation trajectories for a substantial number of drug-like molecules. We also introduce a novel benchmark for evaluating NNPs in molecular property prediction, Hamiltonian prediction, and conformational optimization tasks. Finally, we propose an extendable framework for training NNPs and implement 10 models within it.

paragraphs: Quantum chemistry calculations provide useful approximations of molecular properties, but their computational cost limits large-scale use. Neural network potentials offer a promising alternative, provided they have sufficiently large and varied training data. This paper introduces an expanded dataset and benchmark for developing these models on drug-like molecules.

Building on nablaDFT, the new dataset doubles the molecular structures and triples the conformations, which are different spatial arrangements of molecules. It supplies energies, forces, 17 molecular properties, Hamiltonian and overlap matrices, and a wavefunction object. Each conformation is calculated using the stated density functional theory setup, ωB97X-D/def2-SVP. The dataset also includes relaxation trajectories for a substantial number of drug-like molecules.

The benchmark evaluates molecular property prediction, Hamiltonian prediction, and conformational optimization, connecting the data to several distinct modeling tasks. The authors additionally provide an extensible training framework with ten implemented models. Together, these resources support both learning molecular quantities and evaluating how neural potentials perform when used to improve molecular configurations.
summary.tldr: An expanded quantum chemistry dataset and ten-model framework support benchmarking neural potentials for molecular prediction and conformational optimization.

title: $\nabla^2$DFT: A Universal Quantum Chemistry Dataset of Drug-Like Molecules and a Benchmark for Neural Network Potentials

abstract: We present a comprehensive study of surrogate loss functions for learning to defer. We introduce a broad family of surrogate losses, parameterized by a non-increasing function $\Psi$, and establish their realizable $H$-consistency under mild conditions. For cost functions based on classification error, we further show that these losses admit $H$-consistency bounds when the hypothesis set is symmetric and complete, a property satisfied by common neural network and linear function hypothesis sets. Our results also resolve an open question raised in previous work [Mozannar et al., 2023] by proving the realizable $H$-consistency and Bayes-consistency of a specific surrogate loss. Furthermore, we identify choices of $\Psi$ that lead to $H$-consistent surrogate losses for *any general cost function*, thus achieving Bayes-consistency, realizable $H$-consistency, and $H$-consistency bounds *simultaneously*. We also investigate the relationship between $H$-consistency bounds and realizable $H$-consistency in learning to defer, highlighting key differences from standard classification. Finally, we empirically evaluate our proposed surrogate losses and compare them with existing baselines.

paragraphs: Learning to defer requires a model to learn when to make its own prediction and when to pass the decision elsewhere. Training commonly uses a surrogate loss that is easier to optimize than the actual decision cost. This paper studies when minimizing such losses is theoretically aligned with the intended deferral objective, including when the available hypothesis class is restricted.

The authors introduce a broad loss family controlled by a non-increasing function, Psi, and prove realizable H-consistency under mild conditions. For costs based on classification error, they also establish H-consistency bounds when the hypothesis class is symmetric and complete. The abstract notes that common neural-network and linear-function classes satisfy this property.

Certain choices of Psi provide H-consistent losses for arbitrary general cost functions, combining Bayes-consistency, realizable H-consistency, and H-consistency bounds. The paper also resolves a previously open consistency question for a particular loss and explains how relationships among these guarantees differ from standard classification. Empirical comparisons accompany the theory, making the contribution both a family of training objectives and a characterization of their guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper develops surrogate losses for learning to defer and proves multiple consistency guarantees under specified conditions, including results for general costs.

title: Realizable $H$-Consistent and Bayes-Consistent Loss Functions for Learning to Defer

abstract: Robust estimation of the essential matrix, which encodes the relative position and orientation of two cameras, is a fundamental step in structure from motion pipelines. Recent deep-based methods achieved accurate estimation by using complex network architectures that involve graphs, attention layers, and hard pruning steps. Here, we propose a simpler network architecture based on Deep Sets. Given a collection of point matches extracted from two images, our method identifies outlier point matches and models the displacement noise in inlier matches. A weighted DLT module uses these predictions to regress the essential matrix. Our network achieves accurate recovery that is superior to existing networks with significantly more complex architectures.

Here, we propose a simpler network architecture based on Deep Sets. Given a collection of point matches extracted from two images, our method identifies outlier point matches and models the displacement noise in inlier matches. paragraphs: Recovering the relationship between two cameras is an important step in reconstructing a scene from images. The essential matrix encodes their relative position and orientation, and estimating it depends on matches between points in the two images. This paper proposes a simpler neural architecture for that estimation problem using Deep Sets, taking the collection of point matches as its input.

The network handles two different sources of error. It identifies outlier matches, where the proposed correspondence is unreliable, and models displacement noise in inlier matches, where the correspondence is valid but its location is imperfect. A weighted DLT module then uses those predictions to estimate the essential matrix. This gives both match reliability and positional noise an explicit role in the geometric calculation.

The authors report more accurate recovery than existing networks with substantially more complex architectures. The result supports the usefulness of this direct combination of learned match assessment and geometric estimation, without making architectural complexity the central source of accuracy.
summary.tldr: A Deep Sets network improves essential matrix estimation by identifying bad point matches and modeling noise in valid ones.

title: Consensus Learning with Deep Sets for Essential Matrix Estimation

abstract: We present a new random walk for uniformly sampling high-dimensional convex bodies. It achieves state-of-the-art runtime complexity with stronger guarantees on the output than previously known, namely in Rényi divergence (which implies TV, $\mathcal{W}_2$, KL, $\chi^2$). The proof departs from known approaches for polytime algorithms for the problem - we utilize a stochastic diffusion perspective to show contraction to the target distribution with the rate of convergence determined by functional isoperimetric constants of the stationary density.
originalAbstract: We present a new random walk for uniformly sampling high-dimensional convex bodies. It achieves state-of-the-art runtime complexity with stronger guarantees on the output than previously known, namely in Rényi divergence (which implies TV, $\mathcal{W}_2$, KL, $\chi^2$). The proof departs from known approaches for polytime algorithms for the problem - we utilize a stochastic diffusion perspective to show contraction to the target distribution with the rate of convergence determined by functional isoperimetric constants of the stationary density.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a random walk for drawing uniform samples from high-dimensional convex bodies. The objective is to produce samples whose distribution approaches the uniform target while keeping the computation efficient. The authors report state-of-the-art runtime complexity together with stronger guarantees about the distribution of the output than were previously known.

Those guarantees are expressed in Rényi divergence, a way of measuring the discrepancy between distributions. In the stated result, this control also implies guarantees in total variation, Wasserstein-2 distance, KL divergence, and chi-squared divergence. The significance is that the analysis establishes accuracy in a form that supports several other measures of sampling error.

The proof uses a stochastic diffusion perspective rather than the approaches previously used for polynomial-time algorithms for this problem. It establishes contraction toward the target distribution, with the convergence rate governed by functional isoperimetric constants of the stationary density. The contribution therefore combines an efficient sampling procedure with an analytical approach linking convergence to properties of the target distribution.
summary.tldr: A new random walk samples convex bodies with state-of-the-art runtime complexity and stronger distributional guarantees proved through a diffusion perspective.

title: In-and-Out: Algorithmic Diffusion for Sampling Convex Bodies

abstract: Medical Imaging (MI) datasets are fundamental to artificial intelligence in healthcare. The accuracy, robustness, and fairness of diagnostic algorithms depend on the data (and its quality) used to train and evaluate the models. MI datasets used to be proprietary, but have become increasingly available to the public, including on community-contributed platforms (CCPs) like Kaggle or HuggingFace. While open data is important to enhance the redistribution of data's public value, we find that the current CCP governance model fails to uphold the quality needed and recommended practices for sharing, documenting, and evaluating datasets. In this paper, we conduct an analysis of publicly available machine learning datasets on CCPs, discussing datasets' context, and identifying limitations and gaps in the current CCP landscape. We highlight differences between MI and computer vision datasets, particularly in the potentially harmful downstream effects from poor adoption of recommended dataset management practices. We compare the analyzed datasets across several dimensions, including data sharing, data documentation, and maintenance. We find vague licenses, lack of persistent identifiers and storage, duplicates, and missing metadata, with differences between the platforms. Our research contributes to efforts in responsible data curation and AI algorithms for healthcare.

paragraphs: Public medical imaging datasets make it easier to develop and evaluate healthcare AI, but availability alone does not establish data quality. This paper examines how datasets are shared and maintained on community-contributed platforms such as Kaggle and HuggingFace. Its concern is the connection between dataset management and the reliability of downstream diagnostic algorithms.

The authors analyze publicly available datasets across dimensions including sharing practices, documentation, and maintenance. They identify unclear licenses, absent persistent identifiers and storage, duplicate datasets, and missing metadata. The patterns differ between platforms, but collectively reveal gaps in how these resources are governed and documented.

The study also distinguishes medical imaging from broader computer vision by emphasizing the potentially harmful consequences of poor dataset practices in healthcare. Its finding is that current platform governance does not uphold the needed quality and recommended practices for sharing, documenting, and evaluating these datasets. The contribution is evidence for improving responsible curation while preserving the public value that open data can provide.
summary.tldr: An analysis of public medical imaging datasets finds documentation, licensing, duplication, and maintenance problems that weaken responsible healthcare AI data curation.

title: Copycats: the many lives of a publicly available medical imaging dataset

abstract: Supervised multi-modal learning involves mapping multiple modalities to a target label. Previous studies in this field have concentrated on capturing in isolation either the inter-modality dependencies (the relationships between different modalities and the label) or the intra-modality dependencies (the relationships within a single modality and the label). We argue that these conventional approaches that rely solely on either inter- or intra-modality dependencies may not be optimal in general. We view the multi-modal learning problem from the lens of generative models where we consider the target as a source of multiple modalities and the interaction between them. Towards that end, we propose inter- \& intra-modality modeling (I2M2) framework, which captures and integrates both the inter- and intra-modality dependencies, leading to more accurate predictions. We evaluate our approach using real-world healthcare and vision-and-language datasets with state-of-the-art models, demonstrating superior performance over traditional methods focusing only on one type of modality dependency. The code is available at https://github.com/divyam3897/I2M2.

Useful information can come from relationships within one modality or from interactions across modalities. This paper argues that approaches concentrating exclusively on either kind of dependency may miss information needed for accurate prediction, and therefore may not be optimal in general.

The authors develop I2M2, a framework that captures and integrates both kinds of dependency. Their reasoning starts from a generative view in which the target is treated as a source of the modalities and their interactions. This perspective motivates representing the information each modality contributes individually together with the information available through their relationships.

Experiments use healthcare and vision-and-language datasets with state-of-the-art models. The reported results show better performance than traditional methods focused on only one dependency type. These findings support the framework’s central claim in the tested settings: multimodal prediction can benefit from jointly modeling individual sources of evidence and the interactions that connect them to the target.
summary.tldr: I2M2 improves multimodal prediction by jointly modeling label-related dependencies within modalities and across them.

title: Jointly Modeling Inter- & Intra-Modality Dependencies for Multi-modal Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of recovering the support of a sparse signal using noisy projections. While extensive work has been done on the dense measurement matrix setting, the sparse setting remains less explored. In this work, we establish sufficient conditions on the sample size for successful sparse recovery using sparse measurement matrices. Bringing together our result with previously known necessary conditions, we discover that, in the regime where $ds/p \rightarrow +\infty$, sparse recovery using a sparse design exhibits a phase transition at an information-theoretic threshold of $n_{\text{INF}}^{\text{SP}} = \Theta\left(s\log\left(p/s\right)/\log\left(ds/p\right)\right)$ for the number of measurements, where \(p\) denotes the signal dimension, $s$ the number of non-zero components of the signal, and $d$ the expected number of non-zero components per row of measurement. This expression makes the price of sparsity explicit: restricting each measurement to $d$ non‑zeros inflates the required sample size by a factor of $\log{s}/\log\left(ds/p\right)$, revealing a precise trade‑off between sampling complexity and measurement sparsity. Additionally, we examine the effect of sparsifying an originally dense measurement matrix on sparse signal recovery. We prove in the regime of $s = \alpha p$ and $d = \psi p$ with $\alpha, \psi \in \left(0,1\right)$ and $\psi$ small that a sample of size $n^{\text{Sp-ified}}_{\text{INF}} = \Theta\left(p / \psi^2\right)$ is sufficient for recovery, subject to a certain uniform integrability conjecture, the proof of which is work in progress.

paragraphs: Sparse support recovery identifies which entries of a mostly zero signal are nonzero using noisy measurements. title: The Price of Sparsity: Sufficient Conditions for Sparse Recovery using Sparse and Sparsified Measurements

abstract: Policy optimization (PO) is a cornerstone of modern reinforcement learning (RL), with diverse applications spanning robotics, healthcare, and large language model training. The increasing deployment of PO in sensitive domains, however, raises significant privacy concerns. In this paper, we initiate a theoretical study of differentially private policy optimization, focusing explicitly on its sample complexity. We first formalize an appropriate definition of differential privacy (DP) tailored to PO, addressing the inherent challenges arising from on-policy learning dynamics and the subtlety involved in defining the unit of privacy. We then systematically analyze the sample complexity of widely-used PO algorithms, including policy gradient (PG), natural policy gradient (NPG) and more, under DP constraints and various settings, via a unified framework. Our theoretical results demonstrate that privacy costs can often manifest as lower-order terms in the sample complexity, while also highlighting subtle yet important observations in private PO settings. These offer valuable practical insights for privacy-preserving PO algorithms.

paragraphs: Policy optimization improves an agent’s behavior through experience, making privacy relevant when that experience contains sensitive information. This paper studies the amount of data needed to optimize a policy under differential privacy. Its focus is theoretical sample complexity: how privacy requirements change the learning resources an algorithm needs.

The first step is defining privacy appropriately for policy optimization. On-policy learning is challenging because the current policy influences the data collected next, and the unit being protected requires careful specification. The authors formalize a privacy definition that addresses these issues, then build a unified framework for analyzing algorithms under it.

The analysis covers policy gradient, natural policy gradient, and additional methods across different settings. A central finding is that privacy costs can often appear as lower-order terms in sample complexity. In those cases, privacy changes the bound without determining its leading scaling behavior. The claim is qualified across settings rather than universal. The framework clarifies when privacy may add a comparatively modest statistical cost and identifies subtleties relevant to designing private policy optimization algorithms.
summary.tldr: A unified theoretical framework shows that differential privacy can often add only lower-order sample-complexity costs to policy optimization.

title: On the Sample Complexity of Differentially Private Policy Optimization

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are equipped with increasingly extended context windows recently, yet their long context understanding capabilities over long dependency tasks remain fundamentally limited and underexplored. This gap is especially significant in many real-world long-context applications that were rarely benchmarked. In this paper, we introduce $\textbf{LooGLE v2}$, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' long context ability in real-world applications and scenarios. Our benchmark consists of automatically collected real-world long texts, ranging from 16k to 2M tokens, encompassing domains in law, finance, game and code. Accordingly, we delicately design 10 types of domain-specific long-dependency tasks and generate 1,934 QA instances with various diversity and complexity in a scalable data curation pipeline for further practical needs. We conduct a comprehensive assessment of 6 locally deployed and 4 API-based LLMs. The evaluation results show that even the best-performing model achieves only a 59.2\% overall score on our benchmark. Despite the extensive context windows, popular LLMs are only capable of understanding a much shorter length of context than they claim to be, revealing significant limitations in their ability to handle real-world tasks with long dependencies and highlighting substantial room for model improvement in practical long-context understanding.

paragraphs: LooGLE v2 examines whether large language models can use information spread across long real-world texts. Larger context windows allow models to accept more text, but that capacity does not establish that they can understand dependencies throughout it. The benchmark focuses on practical tasks where answering requires handling such long-range relationships.

They conclude that the evaluated models effectively understand much shorter contexts than their advertised windows suggest. The result highlights a practical gap between accepting lengthy inputs and successfully solving tasks that depend on information across those inputs.
summary.tldr: LooGLE v2 exposes a gap between large advertised context windows and effective long-dependency reasoning, with the best evaluated model scoring 59.2% overall.

title: LooGLE v2: Are LLMs Ready for Real World Long Dependency Challenges?

abstract: This paper firstly addresses the challenge of few-shot universal cross-domain retrieval (FS-UCDR), enabling machines trained with limited data to generalize to novel retrieval scenarios, with queries from entirely unknown domains and categories. To achieve this, we first formally define the FS-UCDR task and propose the Multi-Modal Interactive Agent Layer (MAIL), which enhances the cross-modal interaction in vision-language models (VLMs) by aligning the parameter updates of target layer pairs across modalities. Specifically, MAIL freezes the selected target layer pair and introduces a trainable agent layer pair to approximate localized parameter updates. A bridge function is then introduced to couple the agent layer pair, enabling gradient communication across modalities to facilitate update alignment. The proposed MAIL offers four key advantages: 1) its cross-modal interaction mechanism improves knowledge acquisition from limited data, making it highly effective in low-data scenarios; 2) during inference, MAIL integrates seamlessly into the VLM via reparameterization, preserving inference complexity; 3) extensive experiments validate the superiority of MAIL, which achieves substantial performance gains over data-efficient UCDR methods while requiring significantly fewer training samples; 4) beyond UCDR, MAIL also performs competitively on few-shot classification tasks, underscoring its strong generalization ability. Code.

paragraphs: This paper defines a retrieval setting in which a model learns from limited examples and must later handle queries from previously unknown domains and categories. The challenge is to make useful adaptation possible with little data while retaining the ability to transfer beyond the training scenarios.

The proposed Multi-Modal Interactive Agent Layer, or MAIL, coordinates updates across the visual and language components of a vision-language model. Selected original layers are frozen, while paired trainable agent layers approximate their local parameter updates. A bridge function couples the agent layers so that gradients communicate across modalities, encouraging their updates to align.

At inference time, reparameterization integrates the learned changes into the vision-language model while preserving inference complexity. Experiments report substantial retrieval gains over data-efficient universal cross-domain retrieval methods using significantly fewer training samples. MAIL also performs competitively on few-shot classification. These findings support coordinated cross-modal adaptation as a way to learn effectively from small datasets, with evidence extending beyond the retrieval task that motivated the method.
summary.tldr: MAIL aligns visual and language parameter updates to improve few-shot retrieval while preserving inference complexity.

title: Multi-Modal Interactive Agent Layer for Few-Shot Universal Cross-Domain Retrieval and Beyond

abstract: This work studies a novel subset selection problem called *max-min diversification with monotone submodular utility* (MDMS), which has a wide range of applications in machine learning, e.g., data sampling and feature selection. Given a set of points in a metric space, the goal of MDMS is to maximize $f(S) = g(S) + \lambda \cdot \text{div}(S)$ subject to a cardinality constraint $|S| \le k$, where $g(S)$ is a monotone submodular function and $\text{div}(S) = \min_{u,v \in S : u \ne v} \text{dist}(u,v)$ is the *max-min diversity* objective. We propose the `GIST` algorithm, which gives a $\frac{1}{2}$-approximation guarantee for MDMS by approximating a series of maximum independent set problems with a bicriteria greedy algorithm. We also prove that it is NP-hard to approximate within a factor of $0.5584$. Finally, we show in our empirical study that `GIST` outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks for a single-shot data sampling task on ImageNet.

paragraphs: Selecting a small dataset or feature subset can involve two goals: retaining useful information and avoiding near-duplicate choices. This paper formalizes a problem that adds monotone submodular utility to a weighted diversity term, subject to a maximum subset size. Submodular utility captures diminishing returns, while diversity is measured by the distance between the closest selected pair.

GIST tackles this combined objective through a sequence of maximum independent set problems, using a bicriteria greedy procedure to approximate them. The algorithm guarantees an objective value at least half the optimum. This is a guarantee for the combined utility-and-diversity objective, rather than separate half-optimal guarantees for each component.

The paper also proves that approximation within a factor of 0.5584 is NP-hard, placing a computational barrier near its achieved guarantee. In a single-shot ImageNet data-sampling evaluation, GIST outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods. Together, the results supply a practical selection algorithm, a worst-case performance guarantee, and evidence of usefulness for the tested sampling task.
summary.tldr: GIST selects useful, well-separated subsets with a one-half approximation guarantee and strong reported ImageNet sampling results.

title: GIST: Greedy Independent Set Thresholding for Max-Min Diversification with Submodular Utility

abstract: Motivated by the recently shown connection between self-attention and (kernel) principal component analysis (PCA), we revisit the fundamentals of PCA. Using the difference-of-convex (DC) framework, we present several novel formulations and provide new theoretical insights. In particular, we show the kernelizability and out-of-sample applicability for a PCA-like family of problems. Moreover, we uncover that simultaneous iteration, which is connected to the classical QR algorithm, is an instance of the difference-of-convex algorithm (DCA), offering an optimization perspective on this longstanding method. Further, we describe new algorithms for PCA and empirically compare them with state-of-the-art methods. Lastly, we introduce a kernelizable dual formulation for a robust variant of PCA that minimizes the $l_1$-deviation of the reconstruction errors.

paragraphs: Motivated by connections between self-attention and principal component analysis, this paper revisits PCA through optimization and duality. It uses the difference-of-convex framework, which expresses an objective through a difference of convex components. This perspective yields several new formulations and theoretical insights into PCA and related problems.

The authors establish that a family of PCA-like problems can be kernelized and applied to previously unseen samples. They also show that simultaneous iteration, a method connected to the classical QR algorithm, is an instance of the difference-of-convex algorithm. This provides an optimization interpretation of an established iterative procedure.

Building on these formulations, the paper introduces new PCA algorithms and compares them empirically with state-of-the-art methods. It also develops a kernelizable dual formulation for a robust PCA variant based on minimizing absolute reconstruction deviations. The contributions connect classical algorithms, kernel methods, and robust reconstruction objectives through a shared mathematical viewpoint, broadening the ways these problems can be formulated and analyzed.
summary.tldr: A difference-of-convex perspective yields new PCA formulations, explains simultaneous iteration, and supports kernelizable methods including a robust reconstruction variant.

title: Rethinking PCA Through Duality

abstract: A cascade over a network refers to the diffusion process where behavior changes occurring in one part of an interconnected population lead to a series of sequential changes throughout the entire population. In recent years, there has been a surge in interest and efforts to understand and model cascade mechanisms since they motivate many significant research topics across different disciplines. The propagation structure of cascades is governed by underlying diffusion networks that are often hidden. Inferring diffusion networks thus enables interventions in cascading process to maximize information propagation and provides insights into the Granger causality of interaction mechanisms among individuals. In this project, we propose a novel double network mixture model for inferring latent diffusion network in presence of strong cascade heterogeneity. The new model represents cascade pathways as a distributional mixture over diffusion networks that capture different cascading patterns at the population level. We develop a data-driven optimization method to infer diffusion networks using only visible temporal cascade records, avoiding the need to model complex and heterogeneous individual states. Both statistical and computational guarantees are established for the proposed method. We apply the proposed model to analyze research topic cascades in social sciences across U.S. universities and uncover the latent research topic diffusion network among top U.S. social science programs.

paragraphs: A cascade occurs when changes spread sequentially through an interconnected population. The connections carrying those changes are often hidden, so researchers must infer them from observable events. This paper addresses that inference problem when cascades differ substantially, making it important to represent multiple population-level patterns of propagation.

The authors propose a double network mixture model that represents cascade pathways through a distributional mixture over diffusion networks. Different networks capture different patterns of spreading. A data-driven optimization method estimates these networks using temporal cascade records alone, avoiding the need to explicitly model the complex and heterogeneous states of individual participants.

The paper establishes both statistical and computational guarantees for the method. It also applies the approach to research-topic cascades across U.S. universities, recovering a latent topic-diffusion network among leading social science programs. The resulting networks provide a representation of how topics propagate and support investigation of Granger-causal interaction patterns. More broadly, the work makes heterogeneous cascades amenable to network inference using their observed timing.
summary.tldr: A mixture model infers hidden diffusion networks from event timings while accommodating different cascade patterns.

title: Diffusion Network Inference for Cross-layer Cascades

abstract: Consider the task of locating an unknown target point using approximate distance queries: in each round, a reconstructor selects a reference point and receives a noisy version of its distance to the target. This problem arises naturally in various contexts—from localization in GPS and sensor networks to privacy-aware data access—making it relevant from the perspective of both the reconstructor (seeking accurate recovery) and the responder (aiming to limit information disclosure, e.g., for privacy or security reasons). We study this reconstruction game through a learning-theoretic lens, focusing on the rate and limits of the best possible reconstruction error. Our first result provides a tight geometric characterization of the optimal error in terms of the Chebyshev radius, a classical concept from geometry. This characterization applies to all compact metric spaces (in fact, to all totally bounded spaces) and yields explicit formulas for natural subsets of the Euclidean metric. Our second result addresses the asymptotic behavior of reconstruction, distinguishing between pseudo-finite spaces, where the optimal error is attained after finitely many queries, and spaces where the approximation curve exhibits a nontrivial decay. We characterize pseudo-finiteness for convex subsets of Euclidean spaces.
