paragraphs: The paper studies a game in which one party tries to locate an unknown point by choosing reference points and receiving approximate distances to the target. This captures both a reconstruction objective and an information-protection objective: the questioner wants accurate recovery, while the responder may want to limit what the answers reveal.

The first result tightly characterizes the best achievable reconstruction error using the Chebyshev radius, a geometric measure associated with enclosing a set. The characterization applies to all compact metric spaces and, more generally, all totally bounded spaces. It also produces explicit formulas for natural subsets of Euclidean space, connecting the abstract error limit to concrete geometric settings.

The second result concerns how reconstruction approaches its optimal accuracy as queries accumulate. In spaces called pseudo-finite, the optimal error can be reached after finitely many queries. Other spaces exhibit a nontrivial approximation curve. The authors characterize pseudo-finiteness for convex Euclidean subsets, distinguishing settings where finitely many queries reach the limit from those with continuing approximation behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper geometrically characterizes optimal reconstruction error from approximate distances and studies when finitely many queries can attain it.

title: Reconstruction and Secrecy under Approximate Distance Queries

abstract: The Boolean Satisfiability Problem (SAT) plays a crucial role in cryptanalysis, enabling tasks like key recovery and distinguisher construction. Conflict-Driven Clause Learning (CDCL) has emerged as the dominant paradigm in modern SAT solving, and machine learning has been increasingly integrated with CDCL-based SAT solvers to tackle complex cryptographic problems. However, the lack of a unified evaluation framework, inconsistent input formats, and varying modeling approaches hinder fair comparison. Besides, cryptographic SAT instances also differ structurally from standard SAT problems, and the absence of standardized datasets further complicates evaluation. To address these issues, we introduce SAT4CryptoBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for assessing machine learning–based solvers in cryptanalysis. SAT4CryptoBench provides diverse SAT datasets in both Arithmetic Normal Form (ANF) and Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF), spanning various algorithms, rounds, and key sizes. Our framework evaluates three levels of machine learning integration: standalone distinguishers for instance classification, heuristic enhancement for guiding solving strategies, and hyperparameter optimization for adapting to specific problem distributions. Experiments demonstrate that ANF-based networks consistently achieve superior performance over CNF-based networks in learning cryptographic features. Nonetheless, current ML techniques struggle to generalize across algorithms and instance sizes, with computational overhead potentially offsetting benefits on simpler cases. Despite this, ML-driven optimization strategies notably improve solver efficiency on cryptographic SAT instances. Besides, we propose BASIN, a bitwise solver taking plaintext-ciphertext bitstrings as inputs. Crucially, its superior performance on high-round problems highlights the importance of input modeling and the advantage of direct input representations for complex cryptographic structures.

summary.tldr: SAT4CryptoBench standardizes evaluation of learned cryptographic SAT solvers and shows that input representation strongly affects their benefits and generalization.

title: Bridging Crypto with ML-based Solvers: the SAT Formulation and Benchmarks

abstract: Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL) policies have achieved Best-of-Both-Worlds (BOBW) results in various settings through hybrid regularizers, whereas analogous results for Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) remain limited due to inherent analytical challenges. To advance the analytical foundations of FTPL, we revisit classical FTRL-FTPL duality for unbounded perturbations and establish BOBW results for FTPL under a broad family of asymmetric unbounded Fréchet-type perturbations, including hybrid perturbations combining Gumbel-type and Fréchet-type tails. These results not only extend the BOBW results of FTPL but also offer new insights into designing alternative FTPL policies competitive with hybrid regularization approaches. Motivated by earlier observations in two-armed bandits, we further investigate the connection between the $1/2$-Tsallis entropy and a Fréchet-type perturbation. Our numerical observations suggest that it corresponds to a symmetric Fréchet-type perturbation, and based on this, we establish the first BOBW guarantee for symmetric unbounded perturbations in the two-armed setting. In contrast, in general multi-armed bandits, we find an instance in which symmetric Fréchet-type perturbations violate the standard condition for BOBW analysis, which is a problem not observed with asymmetric or nonnegative Fréchet-type perturbations. Although this example does not rule out alternative analyses achieving BOBW results, it suggests the limitations of directly applying the relationship observed in two-armed cases to the general case and thus emphasizes the need for further investigation to fully understand the behavior of FTPL in broader settings.

To advance the analytical foundations of FTPL, we revisit classical FTRL-FTPL duality for unbounded perturbations and establish BOBW results for FTPL under a broad family of asymmetric unbounded Fréchet-type perturbations, including hybrid perturbations combining Gumbel-type and Fréchet-type tails. These results not only extend the BOBW results of FTPL but also offer new insights into designing alternative FTPL policies competitive with hybrid regularization approaches. Motivated by earlier observations in two-armed bandits, we further investigate the connection between the $1/2$-Tsallis entropy and a Fréchet-type perturbation. Our numerical observations suggest that it corresponds to a symmetric Fréchet-type perturbation, and based on this, we establish the first BOBW guarantee for symmetric unbounded perturbations in the two-armed setting. In contrast, in general multi-armed bandits, we find an instance in which symmetric Fréchet-type perturbations violate the standard condition for BOBW analysis, which is a problem not observed with asymmetric or nonnegative Fréchet-type perturbations. Although this example does not rule out alternative analyses achieving BOBW results, it suggests the limitations of directly applying the relationship observed in two-armed cases to the general case and thus emphasizes the need for further investigation to fully understand the behavior of FTPL in broader settings.

paragraphs: Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader chooses actions using randomly perturbed scores, while Follow-the-Regularized-Leader uses explicit regularization. Best-of-Both-Worlds guarantees are better established for the latter. This paper revisits the mathematical relationship between the two approaches to expand what can be proved for perturbation-based policies with unbounded randomness.

The authors establish guarantees for a broad family of asymmetric Fréchet-type perturbations, including hybrids with Gumbel-type and Fréchet-type tails. They also investigate a possible connection between one-half Tsallis entropy and symmetric Fréchet-type perturbations. Numerical observations suggest that correspondence, and the paper establishes a Best-of-Both-Worlds guarantee for symmetric unbounded perturbations in the two-armed case.

The extension to more arms is qualified. The authors exhibit an instance where symmetric Fréchet-type perturbations violate a standard condition used in Best-of-Both-Worlds analysis, unlike the asymmetric or nonnegative variants considered. This does not prove such guarantees are impossible through another analysis. It shows why the two-armed relationship cannot simply be carried over using the same analytical condition.
summary.tldr: The paper broadens Best-of-Both-Worlds guarantees for perturbed-leader bandit policies while identifying an obstacle to extending symmetric two-arm results.

title: Revisiting Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader with Unbounded Perturbations in Bandit Problems

abstract: Multi-view 3D reconstruction remains a core challenge in computer vision. Recent methods, such as DUSt3R and its successors, directly regress pointmaps from image pairs without relying on known scene geometry or camera parameters. However, the performance of these models is constrained by the diversity and scale of available training data. In this work, we introduce Puzzles, a data augmentation strategy that synthesizes an unbounded volume of high-quality, posed video-depth data from just a single image or video clip. By simulating diverse camera trajectories and realistic scene geometry through targeted image transformations, Puzzles significantly enhances data variety. Extensive experiments show that integrating Puzzles into existing video‑based 3D reconstruction pipelines consistently boosts performance, all without modifying the underlying network architecture. Notably, models trained on only 10% of the original data, augmented with Puzzles, achieve accuracy comparable to those trained on the full dataset.

Notably, training with only 10% of the original data plus the augmentation achieves accuracy comparable to training on the full dataset. This demonstrates substantial data efficiency in the evaluated settings and highlights synthetic variation as a practical way to strengthen reconstruction training.
summary.tldr: Puzzles synthesizes varied video-depth training data, allowing evaluated 3D reconstruction models to match full-data accuracy using 10% of the original data.

title: Puzzles: Unbounded Video-Depth Augmentation for Scalable End-to-End 3D Reconstruction

abstract: Graphical models have been widely used as parsimonious encoders of assumptions of the underlying causal system and provide a basis for causal inferences. Models encoding stronger constraints tend to require higher expressive power, which are also harder, and sometimes impossible to empirically falsify. In this paper, we introduce two new collections of distributions that include counterfactual quan- tities which are experimentally accessible under counterfactual randomizations. Correspondingly, we define two new classes of graphical models for encoding empirically testable constraints in these distributions. We further present a sound and complete calculus, based on counterfactual calculus, which licenses inferences in these two new models with rules that are within the empirically falsifiable bound- ary. Finally, we formulate a hierarchy over several graphical models based on the constraints they encode and study the fundamental trade-off between the expressive power and empirical falsifiability of different models across the hierarchy.

paragraphs: Causal graphical models encode assumptions about how a system works, allowing researchers to draw conclusions about interventions and alternative outcomes. More expressive models can encode stronger assumptions, but those assumptions may become harder to challenge with experiments. This paper studies that tension for counterfactual inference: reasoning about outcomes under alternative circumstances.

The authors introduce two collections of distributions containing counterfactual quantities that can be accessed experimentally under counterfactual randomizations. They then define two corresponding classes of graphical models. The key design choice is to make the constraints represented by these models empirically testable, connecting their mathematical language to quantities that the specified experiments can expose.

The paper also supplies a sound and complete inference calculus for these models, with rules remaining within that testable boundary. It places the new models in a broader hierarchy organized by their constraints. The resulting framework clarifies how the ability to express causal assumptions trades off against the ability to falsify them empirically.
summary.tldr: Two new graphical model classes support counterfactual reasoning while keeping their encoded constraints experimentally testable.

title: A Hierarchy of Graphical Models for Counterfactual Inferences

abstract: Hypergraphs effectively model higher-order relationships in natural phenomena, capturing complex interactions beyond pairwise connections. We introduce a novel hypergraph message passing framework inspired by interacting particle systems, where hyperedges act as fields inducing shared node dynamics. By incorporating attraction, repulsion, and Allen-Cahn forcing terms, particles of varying classes and features achieve class-dependent equilibrium, enabling separability through the particle-driven message passing. We investigate both first-order and second-order particle system equations for modeling these dynamics, which mitigate over-smoothing and heterophily thus can capture complete interactions. The more stable second-order system permits deeper message passing. Furthermore, we enhance deterministic message passing with stochastic element to account for interaction uncertainties. We prove theoretically that our approach mitigates over-smoothing by maintaining a positive lower bound on the hypergraph Dirichlet energy during propagation and thus to enable hypergraph message passing to go deep. Empirically, our models demonstrate competitive performance on diverse real-world hypergraph node classification tasks, excelling on both homophilic and heterophilic datasets. Source code is available at \href{https://github.com/Xuan-Elfin/HAMP}{the link}.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent relationships involving groups of nodes, allowing learning systems to describe interactions beyond pairs. Passing information repeatedly through these groups can make node representations too similar, a problem called over-smoothing. The paper develops a message-passing framework inspired by interacting particles, with hyperedges acting as fields that influence shared node dynamics.

The dynamics combine attraction, repulsion, and Allen-Cahn forcing terms to produce class-dependent equilibria that help keep representations separable. The authors investigate both first-order and second-order systems, finding the second-order formulation more stable and suitable for deeper propagation. They also introduce stochasticity to represent uncertainty in interactions rather than treating every exchange as deterministic.

The theoretical analysis establishes a positive lower bound on hypergraph Dirichlet energy during propagation, supporting the claim that the method resists over-smoothing. Empirical node-classification results are competitive across real-world datasets, including those connecting similar classes and those connecting different classes. Together, the analysis and experiments connect particle dynamics with deeper hypergraph learning that preserves useful distinctions between nodes.
summary.tldr: Particle-inspired hypergraph dynamics preserve distinctions between node representations and support deeper message passing.

title: How Particle System Theory Enhances Hypergraph Message Passing

abstract: With the development of large language models (LLMs), efficient inference through Key-Value (KV) cache compression has attracted considerable attention, especially for long-context generation. To compress the KV cache, recent methods identify critical KV tokens through static modeling of attention scores. However, these methods often struggle to accurately determine critical tokens as they neglect the *temporal patterns* in attention scores, resulting in a noticeable degradation in LLM performance. To address this challenge, we propose **AttentionPredictor**, which is the **first learning-based method to directly predict attention patterns for KV cache compression and critical token identification**. Specifically, AttentionPredictor learns a lightweight, unified convolution model to dynamically capture spatiotemporal patterns and predict the next-token attention scores. An appealing feature of AttentionPredictor is that it accurately predicts the attention score and shares the unified prediction model, which consumes negligible memory, among all transformer layers. Moreover, we propose a cross-token critical cache prefetching framework that hides the token estimation time overhead to accelerate the decoding stage. By retaining most of the attention information, AttentionPredictor achieves **13$\times$** KV cache compression and **5.6$\times$** speedup in a cache offloading scenario with comparable LLM performance, significantly outperforming the state-of-the-arts. The code is available at https://github.com/MIRALab-USTC/LLM-AttentionPredictor.

paragraphs: Language models keep a key-value cache of information from earlier tokens to support generation. Compressing that cache requires identifying which entries will remain useful. The paper argues that methods based on static attention scores miss how attention changes over time, which can cause them to discard important information and reduce model performance.

AttentionPredictor learns to forecast attention scores for the next token. A lightweight convolutional model captures patterns across tokens and time, and the same prediction model is shared across transformer layers with negligible memory consumption. This turns cache selection into a prediction problem informed by the evolving attention history.

The system also prefetches critical cache entries across tokens, hiding the time spent estimating their importance to accelerate decoding. In a cache offloading scenario, the authors report 13-fold cache compression and a 5.6-fold speedup with comparable language-model performance. These results show the benefit of combining predictive token selection with a retrieval schedule that reduces its overhead; the reported speedup specifically concerns the offloading setting.
summary.tldr: AttentionPredictor forecasts changing attention patterns to compress the KV cache, reporting 13-fold compression and a 5.6-fold speedup in an offloading scenario.

title: AttentionPredictor: Temporal Patterns Matter for KV Cache Compression

abstract: Achieving general agile whole-body control on humanoid robots remains a major challenge due to diverse motion demands and data conflicts. While existing frameworks excel in training single motion-specific policies, they struggle to generalize across highly varied behaviors due to conflicting control requirements and mismatched data distributions. In this work, we propose BumbleBee (BB), an expert-generalist learning framework that combines motion clustering and sim-to-real adaptation to overcome these challenges. BB first leverages an autoencoder-based clustering method to group behaviorally similar motions using motion features and motion descriptions. Expert policies are then trained within each cluster and refined with real-world data through iterative delta action modeling to bridge the sim-to-real gap. Finally, these experts are distilled into a unified generalist controller that preserves agility and robustness across all motion types. Experiments on two simulations and a real humanoid robot demonstrate that BB achieves state-of-the-art general whole-body control, setting a new benchmark for agile, robust, and generalizable humanoid performance in the real world.

paragraphs: A humanoid controller must handle movements with very different demands on the whole body. Combining them in one training process can introduce conflicting control requirements and mismatched data distributions. BumbleBee addresses this difficulty by first organizing and learning specialized behaviors, then combining the resulting expertise into a general controller.

An autoencoder-based clustering method groups behaviorally similar motions using both motion features and descriptions. Each cluster receives an expert policy. Those experts are then refined with real-world data through iterative delta action modeling, which helps address differences between simulated and physical behavior. Finally, the refined experts are distilled into a single generalist controller.

This sequence makes motion grouping and adaptation to the real robot part of the route to general control. Experiments in two simulations and on a physical humanoid report state-of-the-art whole-body control, with agility and robustness across the motion types considered. The results support the framework's strategy of learning compatible behavior groups before consolidation, while using real-world feedback to improve the expertise being transferred.
summary.tldr: BumbleBee clusters motions, adapts specialist policies with real-world data, and distills them into one agile humanoid controller.

title: From Experts to a Generalist: Toward General Whole-Body Control for Humanoid Robots

abstract: Knowledge distillation is a promising approach to transfer capabilities from complex teacher models to smaller, resource-efficient student models that can be deployed easily, particularly in task-aware scenarios. However, existing methods of task-aware distillation typically require substantial quantities of data which may be unavailable or expensive to obtain in many practical scenarios. In this paper, we address this challenge by introducing a novel strategy called **Co**unterfactual-explanation-infused **D**istillation CoD for *few-shot task-aware knowledge distillation by systematically infusing counterfactual explanations*. Counterfactual explanations (CFEs) refer to inputs that can flip the output prediction of the teacher model with minimum perturbation. Our strategy CoD leverages these CFEs to precisely map the teacher's decision boundary with significantly fewer samples. We provide theoretical guarantees for motivating the role of CFEs in distillation, from both statistical and geometric perspectives. We mathematically show that CFEs can improve parameter estimation by providing more informative examples near the teacher’s decision boundary. We also derive geometric insights on how CFEs effectively act as knowledge probes, helping the students mimic the teacher's decision boundaries more effectively than standard data. We perform experiments across various datasets and LLMs to show that CoD outperforms standard distillation approaches in few-shot regimes (as low as 8 - 512 samples). Notably, CoD only uses half of the original samples used by the baselines, paired with their corresponding CFEs and still improves performance.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from a larger teacher model to a smaller student, but task-specific distillation often needs substantial training data. This paper examines how to make that transfer effective when only a few examples are available. Its approach focuses on examples that reveal where the teacher changes its decision.

CoD adds counterfactual explanations: minimally modified inputs that flip the teacher's prediction. These examples probe the teacher's decision boundary, giving the student information about both a prediction and the nearby change that would reverse it. The authors provide statistical and geometric theory motivating this strategy, including how informative boundary examples can improve parameter estimation and help students reproduce the teacher's decision structure.

Experiments across datasets and language models show improvements over standard distillation in settings with 8 to 512 samples. CoD uses half as many original examples as the baselines, paired with corresponding counterfactuals, and still improves performance. The finding concerns the value of carefully constructed training information: counterfactual pairs can make a small collection of original examples more useful for task-aware transfer.
summary.tldr: CoD improves few-shot distillation by pairing examples with minimal changes that flip the teacher's prediction and reveal its decision boundary.

title: Few-Shot Knowledge Distillation of LLMs With Counterfactual Explanations

abstract: Chain-of-Thought reasoning has emerged as a powerful approach for solving complex math- ematical and logical problems. However, it can often veer off track through incorrect or unsubstantiated inferences. Formal mathematical reasoning, which can be checked with a formal verifier, is one approach to addressing this issue. However, currently LLMs are simply not good enough to solve complex problems in a formal way, and even just formalizing an informal problem statement can be challenging. Motivated by this fact, in this work we consider the problem of learning reliable verifiers for sequential reasoning, including natural language Chain-of-Thought reasoning. That is, given a problem statement and step-by-step solution in natural language, the aim of the verifier is to output [Yes] if the reasoning steps in the solution are all valid, and [No] otherwise. In this work we give a formal PAC-learning framework for studying this problem. We propose and analyze several natural verification goals, at different levels of strength, in this framework. We provide sample complexity upper-bounds for learning verifiers satisfying these goals, as well as lower-bound and impossibility results for learning other natural verification objectives without additional assumptions.

paragraphs: Step-by-step language-model reasoning can contain invalid or unsupported inferences. Formal verification offers one route to checking correctness, but producing formal solutions and even formalizing an informal problem remain difficult. This paper instead studies what it means to learn a reliable verifier for sequential reasoning expressed in natural language.

The intended verifier receives a problem and its proposed solution, accepting only when all reasoning steps are valid. The authors place this learning problem in a formal PAC-learning framework, which supports statements about learnability and the amount of data needed. They define several verification objectives with different strengths, allowing reliability requirements to be analyzed separately.

For some objectives, the paper derives upper bounds on sample complexity, establishing sufficient amounts of training data within its framework. For other natural objectives, it proves lower bounds or impossibility results without additional assumptions. The contribution therefore clarifies both achievable verification guarantees and obstacles to stronger ones, providing a theoretical basis for evaluating claims about learned reasoning checkers.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes learning natural-language reasoning verifiers and proves sample-complexity guarantees alongside limits on stronger verification goals.

title: On Learning Verifiers and Implications to Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

abstract: Test-time scaling in agentic tasks often relies on generating long reasoning traces ("think" more) before acting, but this does not allow agents to acquire new information from the environment or adapt behavior over time. In this work, we propose scaling test-time interaction, an untapped dimension for test-time scaling that increases the agent's interaction horizon to enable rich behaviors such as exploration, backtracking, and dynamic re-planning within a single rollout. To demonstrate the promise of this scaling dimension, we situate our study in the domain of web agents. We first show that even prompting-based interaction scaling can improve task success on web benchmarks non-trivially. Building on this, we introduce TTI, a curriculum-based online reinforcement learning (RL) approach that trains agents by adaptively adjusting their interaction lengths during rollout. Using a Gemma 3 12B model, TTI sets a new state-of-the-art among open-source agents trained on public data on WebVoyager and WebArena. Case studies further reveal that TTI enables agents to balance exploration and exploitation adaptively. Our results establish interaction scaling as a powerful, complementary axis to scaling per-action compute, offering new avenues for training robust and adaptive agents.

paragraphs: An agent can spend extra computation reasoning before an action, but that alone does not give it new observations from its environment. This paper studies another resource: allowing more interaction within a single rollout. A longer interaction horizon creates opportunities to explore, revisit earlier decisions, and revise plans as new information arrives.

The study focuses on web agents and first finds that prompting alone can make expanded interaction improve task success. The authors then introduce TTI, an online reinforcement-learning approach with a curriculum that adaptively adjusts interaction lengths during training rollouts. This trains agents to use additional interaction opportunities as part of their behavior.

Using Gemma 3 12B, TTI achieves the best reported results on WebVoyager and WebArena among open-source agents trained on public data. Case studies show agents adaptively balancing exploration with pursuing promising actions. The results support interaction length as a useful complement to computation spent on each action, with the evaluated gains coming from learning how to engage with the environment over a longer sequence.
summary.tldr: TTI trains web agents to use longer, adaptive interactions, improving benchmark success through exploration, backtracking, and replanning.

title: Thinking vs. Doing: Improving Agent Reasoning by Scaling Test-Time Interaction

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) 3D relighting requires novel view synthesis under unseen lighting conditions that differ significantly from the observed images. Existing relighting methods, which assume consistent light source distributions between training and testing, often degrade in OOD scenarios. We introduce **MetaGS** to tackle this challenge from two perspectives. First, we propose a meta-learning approach to train 3D Gaussian splatting, which explicitly promotes learning generalizable Gaussian geometries and appearance attributes across diverse lighting conditions, even with biased training data. Second, we embed fundamental physical priors from the *Blinn-Phong* reflection model into Gaussian splatting, which enhances the decoupling of shading components and leads to more accurate 3D scene reconstruction. Results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of MetaGS in challenging OOD relighting tasks, supporting efficient point-light relighting and generalizing well to unseen environment lighting maps.

paragraphs: MetaGS tackles rendering a 3D scene from new viewpoints under lighting that differs substantially from the observed images. Relighting methods can degrade when they assume training and testing lights follow similar distributions. The paper addresses this mismatch by combining a learning strategy aimed at generalization with a physically informed model of reflection.

The learning component applies meta-learning to 3D Gaussian splatting. It explicitly encourages geometry and appearance attributes that remain useful across diverse lighting conditions, including when the training data are biased. The modeling component incorporates physical priors from the Blinn-Phong reflection model. These priors help separate shading components, supporting more accurate reconstruction of the underlying scene.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate effectiveness under challenging lighting shifts. The method supports efficient point-light relighting and generalizes well to previously unseen environment lighting maps in the reported evaluations. The two contributions address complementary parts of the problem: learning attributes that transfer across lighting conditions and structuring the scene representation so that shading components can be more accurately distinguished.
summary.tldr: MetaGS combines meta-learning and reflection-model priors to improve 3D scene relighting under unfamiliar lighting conditions.

title: MetaGS: A Meta-Learned Gaussian-Phong Model for Out-of-Distribution 3D Scene Relighting

abstract: The problem of learning multiple consecutive tasks, known as lifelong learning, is of great importance to the creation of intelligent, general-purpose, and flexible machines. In this paper, we develop a method for online multi-task learning in the lifelong learning setting. The proposed Efficient Lifelong Learning Algorithm (ELLA) maintains a sparsely shared basis for all task models, transfers knowledge from the basis to learn each new task, and refines the basis over time to maximize performance across all tasks. We show that ELLA has strong connections to both online dictionary learning for sparse coding and state-of-the-art batch multi-task learning methods, and provide robust theoretical performance guarantees. We show empirically that ELLA yields nearly identical performance to batch multi-task learning while learning tasks sequentially in three orders of magnitude (over 1,000x) less time.

The proposed Efficient Lifelong Learning Algorithm (ELLA) maintains a sparsely shared basis for all task models, transfers knowledge from the basis to learn each new task, and refines the basis over time to maximize performance across all tasks. We show empirically that ELLA yields nearly identical performance to batch multi-task learning while learning tasks sequentially in three orders of magnitude (over 1,000x) less time.

paragraphs: Lifelong learning involves learning a sequence of tasks while using experience from earlier ones. This paper introduces ELLA, an online multi-task learning method designed for that setting. Its central challenge is to share useful information across tasks while updating the shared representation as additional tasks arrive.

ELLA maintains a common basis from which individual task models are built, with sparse sharing determining how tasks use that basis. A new task draws on the current basis, and learning then refines the basis with performance across all tasks in mind. This makes the shared representation both a source of transferred knowledge and an object that continues to improve.

The authors connect the method to online dictionary learning for sparse coding and to batch multi-task learning, and provide theoretical performance guarantees. In their experiments, sequential learning achieves nearly the same performance as batch multi-task learning while taking over 1,000 times less time. This is an empirical result supporting the efficiency of the proposed lifelong-learning approach.
summary.tldr: ELLA incrementally refines a sparsely shared task basis, achieving near-batch performance with over 1,000-fold less learning time in the reported experiments.

title: ELLA: An Efficient Lifelong Learning Algorithm

abstract: We propose a sampling scheme suitable for reducing a data set prior to selecting a hypothesis with minimum empirical risk. The sampling only considers a subset of the ultimate (unknown) hypothesis set, but can nonetheless guarantee that the final excess risk will compare favorably with utilizing the entire original data set. We demonstrate the practical benefits of our approach on a large dataset which we subsample and subsequently fit with boosted trees.

paragraphs: The paper considers reducing a dataset before choosing a predictive model by empirical risk minimization. Empirical risk minimization selects the hypothesis with the smallest measured training loss. Subsampling can reduce the amount of data involved in that later selection, but the sample must still support a useful final learning decision.

The proposed scheme has an unusual feature: it considers only a subset of the hypotheses that may ultimately be available to the learner. The complete eventual hypothesis set is unknown at sampling time. Despite this mismatch, the authors provide a guarantee that the final excess risk compares favorably with using the entire original dataset.

This result connects an early data reduction decision to the quality of a later learning procedure with a broader hypothesis set. The authors also demonstrate practical benefits by subsampling a large dataset and then fitting boosted trees. The contribution therefore includes both a risk guarantee for subsequent learning and an application showing the usefulness of the sampling scheme.
summary.tldr: A subsampling scheme provides favorable excess-risk guarantees even when it sees only part of the eventual hypothesis set.

title: Loss-Proportional Subsampling for Subsequent ERM

abstract: Infinite hidden Markov models (iHMMs) are nonparametric Bayesian extensions of hidden Markov models (HMMs) with an infinite number of states. Though flexible in describing sequential data, the generative formulation of iHMMs could limit their discriminative ability in sequential prediction tasks. Our paper introduces max-margin infinite HMMs (M2iHMMs), new infinite HMMs that explore the max-margin principle for discriminative learning. By using the theory of Gibbs classifiers and data augmentation, we develop efficient beam sampling algorithms without making restricting mean-field assumptions or truncated approximation. For single variate classification, M2iHMMs reduce to a new formulation of DP mixtures of max-margin machines. Empirical results on synthetic and real data sets show that our methods obtain superior performance than other competitors in both single variate classification and sequential prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Infinite hidden Markov models extend ordinary hidden Markov models with an unbounded state space. This makes them flexible descriptions of sequences, but their generative formulation can limit performance when the goal is discriminative prediction. The paper introduces max-margin infinite HMMs to bring a prediction-oriented learning principle into that flexible Bayesian framework.

Their inference approach avoids restrictive mean-field assumptions and truncated approximations. For single-variate classification, the model reduces to a new form of Dirichlet process mixture of max-margin machines, connecting the sequential model to a related classification construction.

The contribution includes both the new model and an inference method that works without the particular simplifying approximations identified in the abstract.
summary.tldr: Max-margin infinite HMMs combine Bayesian state-space flexibility with discriminative learning and efficient inference without truncation or mean-field assumptions.

title: Max-Margin Infinite Hidden Markov Models

abstract: Q-learning, the most popular of reinforcement learning algorithms, has always included an extension to eligibility traces to enable more rapid learning and improved asymptotic performance on non-Markov problems. The lambda parameter smoothly shifts on-policy algorithms such as TD(lambda) and Sarsa(lambda) from a pure bootstrapping form (lambda=0) to a pure Monte Carlo form (lambda=1). In off-policy algorithms, including Q(lambda), GQ(lambda), and off-policy LSTD(lambda), the lambda parameter is intended to play the same role, but does not; on every exploratory action these algorithms bootstrap regardless of the value of lambda, and as a result they fail to approximate Monte Carlo learning when lambda=1. It may seem that this is inevitable for any online off-policy algorithm; if updates are made on each step on which the target policy is followed, then how could just the right updates be ‘un-made’ upon deviation from the target policy? In this paper, we introduce a new version of Q(lambda) that does exactly that, without significantly increased algorithmic complexity. En route to our new Q(lambda), we introduce a new derivation technique based on the forward-view/backward-view analysis familiar from TD(lambda) but extended to apply at every time step rather than only at the end of episodes. We apply this technique to derive first a new off-policy version of TD(lambda), called PTD(lambda), and then our new Q(lambda), called PQ(lambda).

paragraphs: The paper addresses a mismatch between what the lambda parameter is intended to do and what existing off-policy learning algorithms actually do. In on-policy methods, lambda moves learning from bootstrapping, which uses current value estimates, toward Monte Carlo learning, which uses experienced returns. Existing off-policy methods interrupt this progression by bootstrapping whenever an exploratory action occurs, even when lambda equals one.

The authors introduce PQ(lambda), a version of Q(lambda) designed to restore the Monte Carlo endpoint. Its central challenge is handling updates already made before an action departs from the target policy. The method can effectively undo the appropriate earlier updates without substantially increasing algorithmic complexity.

They first derive an off-policy prediction method, PTD(lambda), and then PQ(lambda). This supplies a way to reason about online updates while preserving the intended relationship between bootstrapping and Monte Carlo learning.
summary.tldr: PQ(lambda) restores the Monte Carlo endpoint of off-policy Q(lambda) through a derivation that accounts for updates at every time step.

title: A new Q(lambda) with interim forward view and Monte Carlo equivalence

abstract: We study the graph clustering problem where each observation (edge or no-edge between a pair of nodes) may have a different level of confidence/uncertainty. We propose a clustering algorithm that is based on optimizing an appropriate weighted objective, where larger weights are given to observations with lower uncertainty. Our approach leads to a convex optimization problem that is efficiently solvable. We analyze our approach under a natural generative model, and establish theoretical guarantees for recovering the underlying clusters. Our main result is a general theorem that applies to any given weight and distribution for the uncertainty. By optimizing over the weights, we derive a provably optimal weighting scheme, which matches the information theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors and leads to strong performance bounds in several specific settings. By optimizing over the uncertainty distribution, we show that non-uniform uncertainties can actually help. In particular, if the graph is built by spending a limited amount of resource to take measurement on each node pair, then it is beneficial to allocate the resource in a non-uniform fashion to obtain accurate measurements on a few pairs of nodes, rather than obtaining inaccurate measurements on many pairs. We provide simulation results that validate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Graph clustering often relies on observations of whether pairs of nodes are connected, but those observations may have unequal reliability. This paper gives more weight to lower-uncertainty observations and formulates clustering as an efficiently solvable convex optimization problem. Both observed edges and observed absences can carry different confidence levels.

Under a generative model, the authors establish recovery guarantees through a theorem covering arbitrary choices of weights and uncertainty distributions. Optimizing the weights produces a provably optimal scheme that matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. In the studied resource-allocation setting, concentrating measurement resources to obtain accurate observations for a few node pairs is preferable to spreading them across many inaccurate observations. Simulations validate the theoretical findings. The contribution therefore informs both how to cluster an existing uncertain graph and how to allocate resources when collecting its measurements.
summary.tldr: Confidence-weighted convex graph clustering achieves strong recovery guarantees and shows that concentrating measurement accuracy can improve clustering.

title: Weighted Graph Clustering with Non-Uniform Uncertainties

abstract: We propose an algorithm-independent framework to equip existing optimization methods with primal-dual certificates. Such certificates and corresponding rate of convergence guarantees are important for practitioners to diagnose progress, in particular in machine learning applications. We obtain new primal-dual convergence rates, e.g., for the Lasso as well as many L1, Elastic Net, group Lasso and TV-regularized problems. The theory applies to any norm-regularized generalized linear model. Our approach provides efficiently computable duality gaps which are globally defined, without modifying the original problems in the region of interest.

We obtain new primal-dual convergence rates, e.g., for the Lasso as well as many L1, Elastic Net, group Lasso and TV-regularized problems. The theory applies to any norm-regularized generalized linear model. Our approach provides efficiently computable duality gaps which are globally defined, without modifying the original problems in the region of interest.

paragraphs: An optimization method produces successive candidate solutions, but assessing their progress requires a meaningful measure of remaining error. This paper proposes an algorithm-independent framework for adding primal-dual certificates to existing methods. These certificates provide a way to diagnose optimization progress, with particular relevance to machine learning problems.

The framework supplies efficiently computable duality gaps and corresponding convergence-rate guarantees. The authors obtain new primal-dual rates for Lasso and many problems involving L1, Elastic Net, group Lasso, or total-variation regularization. More generally, the theory covers generalized linear models regularized by any norm, giving the approach a broad class of applications.

A stated feature is that the duality gaps are defined globally while the original optimization problem remains unchanged in the region of interest. This connects practical progress measurement with guarantees about how those measurements improve. Because the framework is algorithm-independent, its role is to equip optimization methods with certificates rather than requiring one specific solver for every covered problem.
summary.tldr: An algorithm-independent framework gives norm-regularized learning problems computable primal-dual certificates and convergence rates.

title: Primal-Dual Rates and Certificates

abstract: Many machine learning problems involve Monte Carlo gradient estimators. As a prominent example, we focus on Monte Carlo variational inference (MCVI) in this paper. The performance of MCVI crucially depends on the variance of its stochastic gradients. We propose variance reduction by means of Quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) sampling. QMC replaces N i.i.d. samples from a uniform probability distribution by a deterministic sequence of samples of length N. This sequence covers the underlying random variable space more evenly than i.i.d. draws, reducing the variance of the gradient estimator. With our novel approach, both the score function and the reparameterization gradient estimators lead to much faster convergence. We also propose a new algorithm for Monte Carlo objectives, where we operate with a constant learning rate and increase the number of QMC samples per iteration. We prove that this way, our algorithm can converge asymptotically at a faster rate than SGD . We furthermore provide theoretical guarantees on qmc for Monte Carlo objectives that go beyond MCVI , and support our findings by several experiments on large-scale data sets from various domains.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo variational inference relies on gradients estimated from samples, and the variability of those estimates strongly affects optimization. The paper proposes using Quasi-Monte Carlo sampling to reduce that variability. Its central idea is to replace independent uniform draws with a deterministic sequence that covers the underlying space more evenly.

More even coverage improves the gradient estimates used during learning. The authors report substantially faster convergence for both score-function and reparameterization estimators, two ways of constructing gradients for these objectives. The contribution therefore applies to multiple gradient-estimation approaches within variational inference, rather than depending on just one of them.

The paper also introduces an algorithm that keeps the learning rate constant while increasing the number of QMC samples per iteration. It proves that this approach can attain a faster asymptotic convergence rate than SGD. Additional theoretical guarantees cover Monte Carlo objectives beyond variational inference, and experiments on large datasets from several domains support the findings. The approach ties optimization progress to increasingly accurate sampling.
summary.tldr: Quasi-Monte Carlo sampling reduces gradient variance and can accelerate variational inference and other Monte Carlo optimization problems.

title: Quasi-Monte Carlo Variational Inference

abstract: Estimators computed from adaptively collected data do not behave like their non-adaptive brethren.Rather, the sequential dependence of the collection policy can lead to severe distributional biases that persist even in the infinite data limit. We develop a general method – $\mathbf{W}$-decorrelation – for transforming the bias of adaptive linear regression estimators into variance. The method uses only coarse-grained information about the data collection policy and does not need access to propensity scores or exact knowledge of the policy.We bound the finite-sample bias and variance of the $\mathbf{W}$-estimator and develop asymptotically correct confidence intervals based on a novel martingale central limit theorem. We then demonstrate the empirical benefits of the generic $\mathbf{W}$-decorrelation procedure in two different adaptive data settings: the multi-armed bandit and the autoregressive time series.

paragraphs: When data collection responds to earlier observations, ordinary regression intuition can become unreliable. The collection policy creates sequential dependence, and the resulting estimation biases can persist even with arbitrarily large amounts of data. This paper studies how to obtain reliable inference for linear models in that adaptive setting.

The proposed method, W-decorrelation, transforms the bias of an adaptive regression estimator into variance. This makes the tradeoff explicit: reducing systematic distortion can come at the cost of greater variability. The procedure requires only broad information about the collection policy, without needing exact policy knowledge or propensity scores describing its selection probabilities.

The authors bound the estimator’s bias and variance for finite samples and establish asymptotically correct confidence intervals through a new martingale central limit theorem. Experiments in multi-armed bandits and autoregressive time series demonstrate empirical benefits. Together, these results address both the accuracy of adaptive estimates and the reliability of the uncertainty statements attached to them.
summary.tldr: W-decorrelation trades adaptive regression bias for variance to support more reliable estimation and asymptotically correct confidence intervals.

title: Accurate Inference for Adaptive Linear Models

abstract: In machine learning, learning often corresponds to changing the parameters of a parameterized function. A learning rule is an algorithm or mathematical expression that specifies precisely how the parameters should be changed. When creating a machine learning system, we must make two decisions: what representation should be used (i.e., what parameterized function should be used) and what learning rule should be used to search through the resulting set of representable functions. In this paper we focus on gradient-like learning rules, wherein these two decisions are coupled in a subtle (and often unintentional) way. Using most learning rules, these two decisions are coupled in a subtle (and often unintentional) way. That is, using the same learning rule with two different representations that can represent the same sets of functions can result in two different outcomes. After arguing that this coupling is undesirable, particularly when using neural networks, we present a method for partially decoupling these two decisions for a broad class of gradient-like learning rules that span unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, and supervised learning.

paragraphs: Building a learning system involves choosing both a parameterized representation and a rule for updating its parameters. This paper examines how those choices interact in gradient-like learning. Two representations can describe exactly the same collection of functions, yet applying the same learning rule to each can produce different outcomes.

The issue is that the representation influences more than which functions are available: it also affects how the learning rule searches among them. The authors argue that this often unintended coupling is undesirable, particularly for neural networks. Equivalent expressive capacity therefore does not, by itself, make two representations interchangeable during learning.

The proposed method partially separates the learning rule from the choice of representation. It applies to a broad family of gradient-like rules spanning supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning. The contribution is a general way to reduce this dependence across several learning settings. Its stated scope is partial decoupling, so the result does not imply complete independence from every representation choice.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes a way to partially separate gradient-like learning behavior from how functions are parameterized.

title: Decoupling Gradient-Like Learning Rules from Representations

abstract: Many real-world decision problems are characterized by multiple conflicting objectives which must be balanced based on their relative importance. In the dynamic weights setting the relative importance changes over time and specialized algorithms that deal with such change, such as a tabular Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithm by Natarajan and Tadepalli (2005), are required. However, this earlier work is not feasible for RL settings that necessitate the use of function approximators. We generalize across weight changes and high-dimensional inputs by proposing a multi-objective Q-network whose outputs are conditioned on the relative importance of objectives and we introduce Diverse Experience Replay (DER) to counter the inherent non-stationarity of the Dynamic Weights setting. We perform an extensive experimental evaluation and compare our methods to adapted algorithms from Deep Multi-Task/Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning and show that our proposed network in combination with DER dominates these adapted algorithms across weight change scenarios and problem domains.

paragraphs: Many decision problems involve several objectives whose relative importance changes over time. An agent must therefore adapt its behavior as priorities shift. Earlier tabular reinforcement-learning work addressed this setting, but it does not suit problems that require function approximation to handle their inputs.

The paper proposes a multi-objective Q-network whose outputs depend on the current relative importance of the objectives. This allows the network to generalize across changing weights as well as high-dimensional inputs. The authors also introduce Diverse Experience Replay, or DER, to counter the non-stationarity that arises when the importance of objectives changes during learning.

An extensive experimental evaluation compares the methods with adapted deep multi-task and multi-objective reinforcement-learning algorithms. The proposed network together with DER dominates those adapted methods across the evaluated weight-change scenarios and problem domains. The findings support treating changing priorities as an explicit input to value prediction while also modifying experience replay to address the resulting changes in the learning problem.
summary.tldr: A weight-conditioned Q-network and Diverse Experience Replay improve multi-objective reinforcement learning when priorities change over time.

title: Dynamic Weights in Multi-Objective Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Fine-tuning large pretrained models is an effective transfer mechanism in NLP. However, in the presence of many downstream tasks, fine-tuning is parameter inefficient: an entire new model is required for every task. As an alternative, we propose transfer with adapter modules. Adapter modules yield a compact and extensible model; they add only a few trainable parameters per task, and new tasks can be added without revisiting previous ones. The parameters of the original network remain fixed, yielding a high degree of parameter sharing. To demonstrate adapter’s effectiveness, we transfer the recently proposed BERT Transformer model to $26$ diverse text classification tasks, including the GLUE benchmark. Adapters attain near state-of-the-art performance, whilst adding only a few parameters per task. On GLUE, we attain within $0.8%$ of the performance of full fine-tuning, adding only $3.6%$ parameters per task. By contrast, fine-tuning trains $100%$ of the parameters per task.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a large pretrained language model works well for transfer learning, but serving many tasks means maintaining a separate full model for each one. This paper proposes adapter modules as a more compact approach. Each task receives a small set of trainable additions while the original network’s parameters remain fixed.

The design allows extensive parameter sharing across tasks and supports adding new tasks without revisiting previous ones. Its practical appeal comes from concentrating task-specific learning in a small part of the overall system. The shared pretrained network supplies a common foundation, while the adapters provide the parameters that change for each task.

The authors evaluate this approach by transferring BERT to 26 text classification tasks, including GLUE. Adapters achieve near state-of-the-art performance. On GLUE, they come within 0.8% of full fine-tuning performance while adding 3.6% parameters per task, compared with training all parameters for each fully fine-tuned model. These results demonstrate a favorable empirical tradeoff between task performance and the amount of task-specific parameterization.
summary.tldr: Small task-specific adapters keep BERT’s original parameters fixed while achieving performance close to full fine-tuning with far fewer added parameters.

title: Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP

abstract: This paper introduces an efficient second-order method for solving the elastic net problem. Its key innovation is a computationally efficient technique for injecting curvature information in the optimization process which admits a strong theoretical performance guarantee. In particular, we show improved run time over popular first-order methods and quantify the speed-up in terms of statistical measures of the data matrix. The improved time complexity is the result of an extensive exploitation of the problem structure and a careful combination of second-order information, variance reduction techniques, and momentum acceleration. Beside theoretical speed-up, experimental results demonstrate great practical performance benefits of curvature information, especially for ill-conditioned data sets.

Its key innovation is a computationally efficient technique for injecting curvature information in the optimization process which admits a strong theoretical performance guarantee. In particular, we show improved run time over popular first-order methods and quantify the speed-up in terms of statistical measures of the data matrix. The improved time complexity is the result of an extensive exploitation of the problem structure and a careful combination of second-order information, variance reduction techniques, and momentum acceleration. Beside theoretical speed-up, experimental results demonstrate great practical performance benefits of curvature information, especially for ill-conditioned data sets.

paragraphs: The paper develops a faster method for solving the elastic net optimization problem. Its central idea is to incorporate curvature, which describes how the objective's slope changes across directions. The challenge addressed is to obtain the optimization benefits of this second-order information through a computationally efficient procedure.

The algorithm combines curvature information with variance reduction and momentum acceleration, making extensive use of the elastic net problem's structure. The authors prove an improved runtime relative to popular first-order methods and express the speedup using statistical measures of the data matrix. This ties the theoretical benefit to properties of the input data rather than presenting acceleration as an unexplained implementation effect.

Experiments show substantial practical benefits from using curvature, especially for ill-conditioned datasets. In such cases, optimization must handle directions with markedly different behavior, making information beyond the current gradient particularly relevant. The paper's contribution is the combination of an efficient second-order construction, a quantified theoretical improvement, and experimental evidence that the resulting acceleration is useful in practice.
summary.tldr: An efficient curvature-aware elastic net solver combines second-order information, variance reduction, and momentum to achieve theoretical and practical speedups.

title: Curvature-Exploiting Acceleration of Elastic Net Computations

abstract: Interest has been rising lately towards methods representing data in non-Euclidean spaces, e.g. hyperbolic or spherical that provide specific inductive biases useful for certain real-world data properties, e.g. scale-free, hierarchical or cyclical. However, the popular graph neural networks are currently limited in modeling data only via Euclidean geometry and associated vector space operations. Here, we bridge this gap by proposing mathematically grounded generalizations of graph convolutional networks (GCN) to (products of) constant curvature spaces. We do this by i) introducing a unified formalism permitting a differentiable interpolation between all geometries of constant curvature irrespective of their sign, ii) leveraging gyro-barycentric coordinates that generalize the classic Euclidean concept of the center of mass. Our class of models smoothly recover their Euclidean counterparts when the curvature goes to zero from either side. Empirically, we outperform Euclidean GCNs in the tasks of node classification and distortion minimization for symbolic data exhibiting non-Euclidean behavior, according to their discrete curvature.

We do this by i) introducing a unified formalism permitting a differentiable interpolation between all geometries of constant curvature irrespective of their sign, ii) leveraging gyro-barycentric coordinates that generalize the classic Euclidean concept of the center of mass. Empirically, we outperform Euclidean GCNs in the tasks of node classification and distortion minimization for symbolic data exhibiting non-Euclidean behavior, according to their discrete curvature.

Hyperbolic and spherical spaces offer useful biases for structures such as hierarchies and cycles. This paper extends graph convolutional networks beyond ordinary Euclidean geometry, allowing their representations and operations to live in constant curvature spaces and combinations of those spaces.

The construction has two main ingredients. A unified mathematical description allows differentiable movement between negative, zero, and positive curvature. Gyro-barycentric coordinates supply a generalization of the familiar center of mass, supporting the aggregation operations needed by graph networks. As curvature approaches zero from either direction, the resulting models smoothly recover their Euclidean counterparts.

Experiments show improvements over Euclidean graph convolutional networks on node classification and distortion minimization for symbolic data whose discrete curvature indicates non-Euclidean behavior. These findings support matching representation geometry to the structure of the data in the evaluated settings. The contribution also makes these geometries part of a connected model family, rather than treating each geometry as an unrelated architecture.
summary.tldr: The paper generalizes graph convolutional networks across constant curvature geometries and reports gains on data exhibiting non-Euclidean structure.

title: Constant Curvature Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: It is still common to use Q-learning and temporal difference (TD) learning{—}even though they have divergence issues and sound Gradient TD alternatives exist{—}because divergence seems rare and they typically perform well. However, recent work with large neural network learning systems reveals that instability is more common than previously thought. Practitioners face a difficult dilemma: choose an easy to use and performant TD method, or a more complex algorithm that is more sound but harder to tune and all but unexplored with non-linear function approximation or control. In this paper, we introduce a new method called TD with Regularized Corrections (TDRC), that attempts to balance ease of use, soundness, and performance. It behaves as well as TD, when TD performs well, but is sound in cases where TD diverges. We empirically investigate TDRC across a range of problems, for both prediction and control, and for both linear and non-linear function approximation, and show, potentially for the first time, that Gradient TD methods could be a better alternative to TD and Q-learning.

Its purpose is to reduce the practical cost of choosing a more principled learning method.

The empirical investigation covers prediction and control, using both linear and nonlinear function approximation. The results suggest that Gradient TD methods could be preferable to conventional TD and Q-learning. That conclusion is deliberately qualified: the evidence supports their potential as practical alternatives across the studied problems, rather than establishing universal superiority for every reinforcement-learning task.
summary.tldr: TDRC seeks to combine TD’s practical performance with sound corrections, and experiments suggest Gradient TD methods could be competitive alternatives.

title: Gradient Temporal-Difference Learning with Regularized Corrections

abstract: Neural networks and tree ensembles are state-of-the-art learners, each with its unique statistical and computational advantages. We aim to combine these advantages by introducing a new layer for neural networks, composed of an ensemble of differentiable decision trees (a.k.a. soft trees). While differentiable trees demonstrate promising results in the literature, they are typically slow in training and inference as they do not support conditional computation. We mitigate this issue by introducing a new sparse activation function for sample routing, and implement true conditional computation by developing specialized forward and backward propagation algorithms that exploit sparsity. Our efficient algorithms pave the way for jointly training over deep and wide tree ensembles using first-order methods (e.g., SGD). Experiments on 23 classification datasets indicate over 10x speed-ups compared to the differentiable trees used in the literature and over 20x reduction in the number of parameters compared to gradient boosted trees, while maintaining competitive performance. Moreover, experiments on CIFAR, MNIST, and Fashion MNIST indicate that replacing dense layers in CNNs with our tree layer reduces the test loss by 7-53% and the number of parameters by 8x. We provide an open-source TensorFlow implementation with a Keras API.

Such trees can participate in gradient-based training, but existing versions are often slow because they do not support conditional computation. The authors aim to preserve differentiability while allowing computation to depend on the routes activated by each input.

A new sparse activation function controls sample routing, and specialized forward and backward algorithms exploit that sparsity. Together, these components implement conditional computation during both prediction and training. They make joint training of deep and wide tree ensembles feasible with first-order optimization methods such as stochastic gradient descent.

Across 23 classification datasets, experiments report speedups exceeding tenfold over earlier differentiable trees and more than twentyfold fewer parameters than gradient-boosted trees, with competitive performance. Replacing dense CNN layers on CIFAR, MNIST, and Fashion MNIST reduces test loss by 7–53% and parameter count eightfold. The authors also provide a TensorFlow implementation with a Keras interface, making the proposed layer available as a practical model component.
summary.tldr: Sparse routing and specialized propagation make differentiable tree ensembles conditionally computed neural layers with substantial reported speed and parameter savings.

title: The Tree Ensemble Layer: Differentiability meets Conditional Computation

abstract: While the impact of variational inference (VI) on posterior inference in a fixed generative model is well-characterized, its role in regularizing a learned generative model when used in variational autoencoders (VAEs) is poorly understood. We study the regularizing effects of variational distributions on learning in generative models from two perspectives. First, we analyze the role that the choice of variational family plays in imparting uniqueness to the learned model by restricting the set of optimal generative models. Second, we study the regularization effect of the variational family on the local geometry of the decoding model. This analysis uncovers the regularizer implicit in the $\beta$-VAE objective, and leads to an approximation consisting of a deterministic autoencoding objective plus analytic regularizers that depend on the Hessian or Jacobian of the decoding model, unifying VAEs with recent heuristics proposed for training regularized autoencoders. We empirically verify these findings, observing that the proposed deterministic objective exhibits similar behavior to the $\beta$-VAE in terms of objective value and sample quality.

paragraphs: The paper studies how variational inference shapes the generative model learned by a variational autoencoder. Its focus is the regularization caused by the chosen family of approximate posterior distributions. This asks how an inference choice influences learning itself, beyond its role in approximating a posterior for an already fixed model.

The authors analyze two effects. First, the variational family restricts the set of optimal generative models, helping impart uniqueness to the learned model. Second, it regularizes the decoder's local geometry. This second analysis reveals a regularizer implicit in the beta-VAE objective and leads to an approximate deterministic autoencoding objective with explicit regularizers depending on the decoder's Hessian or Jacobian.

The approximation connects beta-VAEs with heuristics for training regularized autoencoders by expressing related effects through decoder derivatives. Empirical tests find that the deterministic objective behaves similarly to the beta-VAE in objective value and sample quality. The result supports this interpretation of implicit regularization, while the stated relationship remains an approximation rather than an exact equivalence in every setting.
summary.tldr: The paper explains how variational families regularize beta-VAEs and derives a deterministic approximation with decoder-dependent regularizers and similar empirical behavior.

title: On Implicit Regularization in $β$-VAEs

abstract: We propose inertial versions of block coordinate descent methods for solving non-convex non-smooth composite optimization problems. Our methods possess three main advantages compared to current state-of-the-art accelerated first-order methods: (1) they allow using two different extrapolation points to evaluate the gradients and to add the inertial force (we will empirically show that it is more efficient than using a single extrapolation point), (2) they allow to randomly select the block of variables to update, and (3) they do not require a restarting step. We prove the subsequential convergence of the generated sequence under mild assumptions, prove the global convergence under some additional assumptions, and provide convergence rates. We deploy the proposed methods to solve non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) and show that they compete favorably with the state-of-the-art NMF algorithms. Additional experiments on non-negative approximate canonical polyadic decomposition, also known as nonnegative tensor factorization, are also provided.

We prove the subsequential convergence of the generated sequence under mild assumptions, prove the global convergence under some additional assumptions, and provide convergence rates. paragraphs: The paper develops block coordinate optimization methods for composite objectives that can be both non-convex and non-smooth. These methods update groups of variables and incorporate inertia, using information from earlier motion to influence subsequent steps. The aim is to combine flexible block updates with accelerated optimization behavior.

A distinctive feature is the use of two extrapolation points: one for evaluating gradients and another for adding the inertial contribution. The authors empirically find this more efficient than using one point. Their methods also allow random selection of the variable block to update and do not require a restart step.

The theoretical guarantees distinguish between levels of convergence. Subsequential convergence holds under mild assumptions, while convergence of the full sequence requires additional assumptions; the paper also provides rates. These are convergence claims, not a claim of finding a global optimum in every non-convex problem. Experiments on non-negative matrix factorization show favorable competition with existing methods, and further experiments address non-negative tensor factorization.
summary.tldr: Inertial block proximal methods use separate extrapolation points and flexible block selection, with conditional convergence guarantees and favorable factorization experiments.

title: Inertial Block Proximal Methods for Non-Convex Non-Smooth Optimization

abstract: Invariance (defined in a general sense) has been one of the most effective priors for representation learning. Direct factorization of parametric models is feasible only for a small range of invariances, while regularization approaches, despite improved generality, lead to nonconvex optimization. In this work, we develop a \emph{convex} representation learning algorithm for a variety of generalized invariances that can be modeled as semi-norms. Novel Euclidean embeddings are introduced for kernel representers in a semi-inner-product space, and approximation bounds are established. This allows invariant representations to be learned efficiently and effectively as confirmed in our experiments, along with accurate predictions.

paragraphs: Representation learning often benefits from invariance: a representation should remain insensitive to changes that the learning problem treats as irrelevant. Building such behavior directly into a parametric model supports only a limited range of invariances. More general regularization approaches are available, but the abstract identifies nonconvex optimization as a difficulty with those approaches.

This paper develops a convex learning algorithm for generalized invariances that can be expressed as semi-norms. Its construction introduces Euclidean embeddings for kernel representers in a semi-inner-product space. These embeddings provide the mathematical bridge used by the algorithm, and the authors establish bounds on their approximation.

The reported experiments show efficient learning of invariant representations together with accurate predictions. The approach matters because it combines a range of expressible invariances with a convex optimization formulation, rather than limiting the contribution to one particular invariance. Its stated scope is the class of generalized invariances modeled by semi-norms, with approximation bounds supporting the representation construction.
summary.tldr: A convex algorithm learns representations for generalized invariances expressible as semi-norms, using new embeddings with approximation bounds.

title: Convex Representation Learning for Generalized Invariance in Semi-Inner-Product Space

abstract: Plug-and-play (PnP) is a non-convex framework that combines ADMM or other proximal algorithms with advanced denoiser priors. Recently, PnP has achieved great empirical success, especially with the integration of deep learning-based denoisers. However, a key problem of PnP based approaches is that they require manual parameter tweaking. It is necessary to obtain high-quality results across the high discrepancy in terms of imaging conditions and varying scene content. In this work, we present a tuning-free PnP proximal algorithm, which can automatically determine the internal parameters including the penalty parameter, the denoising strength and the terminal time. A key part of our approach is to develop a policy network for automatic search of parameters, which can be effectively learned via mixed model-free and model-based deep reinforcement learning. We demonstrate, through numerical and visual experiments, that the learned policy can customize different parameters for different states, and often more efficient and effective than existing handcrafted criteria. Moreover, we discuss the practical considerations of the plugged denoisers, which together with our learned policy yield state-of-the-art results. This is prevalent on both linear and nonlinear exemplary inverse imaging problems, and in particular, we show promising results on Compressed Sensing MRI and phase retrieval.
