paragraphs: Plug-and-play imaging methods combine an optimization procedure with a denoiser that supplies prior information about images. Although effective in practice, they often require manual parameter adjustment across imaging conditions and scene content. This paper develops a method that automatically chooses internal parameters, including the penalty parameter, denoising strength, and stopping time.

The central component is a policy network that searches for parameter choices. It is trained using a mixture of model-free and model-based deep reinforcement learning. The learned policy can choose different parameters for different states of the reconstruction process, making parameter selection responsive to the current problem-solving situation.

Numerical and visual experiments show that these choices are often more efficient and effective than existing handcrafted criteria. The authors also examine practical denoiser considerations; together with the policy, these yield state-of-the-art results on the evaluated linear and nonlinear inverse imaging problems. Compressed sensing MRI and phase retrieval provide promising examples. The findings support replacing repeated manual tuning with a learned policy in the demonstrated reconstruction settings.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement-learned policy automatically selects plug-and-play reconstruction parameters and stopping times, improving results on the evaluated imaging problems.

title: Tuning-free Plug-and-Play Proximal Algorithm for Inverse Imaging Problems

abstract: Dropout is a widely-used regularization technique, often required to obtain state-of-the-art for a number of architectures. This work demonstrates that dropout introduces two distinct but entangled regularization effects: an explicit effect (also studied in prior work) which occurs since dropout modifies the expected training objective, and, perhaps surprisingly, an additional implicit effect from the stochasticity in the dropout training update. This implicit regularization effect is analogous to the effect of stochasticity in small mini-batch stochastic gradient descent. We disentangle these two effects through controlled experiments. We then derive analytic simplifications which characterize each effect in terms of the derivatives of the model and the loss, for deep neural networks. We demonstrate these simplified, analytic regularizers accurately capture the important aspects of dropout, showing they faithfully replace dropout in practice.

paragraphs: Dropout is widely used to regularize neural networks, but this paper argues that its influence has two distinct components. One is explicit: dropout changes the training objective after averaging over its randomness. The other is implicit: randomness in the training updates changes the learning process itself.

The authors connect this implicit component to the regularizing effect of stochasticity in small-minibatch stochastic gradient descent. They use controlled experiments to disentangle the two dropout effects, which are normally intertwined during training. This distinction matters because examining only the average objective leaves out an additional source of regularization.

The paper then derives simplified analytic expressions for both effects in deep neural networks, using derivatives of the model and the loss. In practical evaluations, these analytic regularizers capture the important aspects of dropout and can faithfully replace it. The findings provide a more detailed explanation of dropout's behavior: both the objective being optimized and the randomness of the optimization updates contribute to the regularization observed in the studied networks.
summary.tldr: Dropout regularizes through both its expected objective and stochastic updates, and analytic regularizers can reproduce these effects in practice.

title: The Implicit and Explicit Regularization Effects of Dropout

abstract: In general, graph representation learning methods assume that the train and test data come from the same distribution. In this work we consider an underexplored area of an otherwise rapidly developing field of graph representation learning: The task of out-of-distribution (OOD) graph classification, where train and test data have different distributions, with test data unavailable during training. Our work shows it is possible to use a causal model to learn approximately invariant representations that better extrapolate between train and test data. Finally, we conclude with synthetic and real-world dataset experiments showcasing the benefits of representations that are invariant to train/test distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Graph classification methods commonly assume that training and test graphs follow the same distribution. This paper examines what happens when that assumption does not hold and test data are unavailable during training. Its focus is learning graph representations that support extrapolation across distributions, with size invariance providing the organizing theme of the work.

The authors use a causal model to learn representations that are approximately invariant. The goal is to represent graphs in a way that remains useful when moving from the training distribution to a different test distribution. Because the target data cannot be inspected during training, the approach must derive this capacity from the available training information and the causal modeling framework.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate benefits from these representations under train-test distribution shifts. The stated result is that causal modeling can enable better extrapolation through approximate invariance. This makes the contribution relevant to graph classification beyond matched-distribution evaluation, while preserving the distinction between improved transfer in the studied settings and exact invariance to every possible shift.
summary.tldr: A causal modeling approach learns approximately invariant graph representations that improve classification across distribution shifts.

title: Size-Invariant Graph Representations for Graph Classification Extrapolations

abstract: This work introduces Bilinear Classes, a new structural framework, which permit generalization in reinforcement learning in a wide variety of settings through the use of function approximation. The framework incorporates nearly all existing models in which a polynomial sample complexity is achievable, and, notably, also includes new models, such as the Linear Q*/V* model in which both the optimal Q-function and the optimal V-function are linear in some known feature space. Our main result provides an RL algorithm which has polynomial sample complexity for Bilinear Classes; notably, this sample complexity is stated in terms of a reduction to the generalization error of an underlying supervised learning sub-problem. These bounds nearly match the best known sample complexity bounds for existing models. Furthermore, this framework also extends to the infinite dimensional (RKHS) setting: for the the Linear Q*/V* model, linear MDPs, and linear mixture MDPs, we provide sample complexities that have no explicit dependence on the explicit feature dimension (which could be infinite), but instead depends only on information theoretic quantities.

paragraphs: Bilinear Classes provide a shared framework for studying when reinforcement learning can generalize through function approximation. Instead of treating each tractable model separately, the paper identifies a structural class encompassing nearly all existing models with polynomial sample complexity. It also includes new cases, notably one where both optimal action values and optimal state values are linear in known features.

The main result supplies an algorithm with polynomial sample complexity for this class. Its guarantee is expressed through the generalization error of an underlying supervised learning problem. This connection matters because it relates the amount of interaction needed for reinforcement learning to the statistical difficulty of a learning subproblem. For existing models, the resulting bounds nearly match the best previously known guarantees.

The framework also reaches infinite-dimensional kernel feature spaces. For the specified linear value-function and transition models, the bounds depend on information-theoretic quantities rather than explicitly on feature dimension. This allows the analysis to remain meaningful even when the feature representation itself is infinite-dimensional.
summary.tldr: Bilinear Classes unify many provably learnable reinforcement learning models and connect their sample requirements to supervised generalization.

title: Bilinear Classes: A Structural Framework for Provable Generalization in RL

abstract: We propose ADOM – an accelerated method for smooth and strongly convex decentralized optimization over time-varying networks. ADOM uses a dual oracle, i.e., we assume access to the gradient of the Fenchel conjugate of the individual loss functions. Up to a constant factor, which depends on the network structure only, its communication complexity is the same as that of accelerated Nesterov gradient method. To the best of our knowledge, only the algorithm of Rogozin et al. (2019) has a convergence rate with similar properties. However, their algorithm converges under the very restrictive assumption that the number of network changes can not be greater than a tiny percentage of the number of iterations. This assumption is hard to satisfy in practice, as the network topology changes usually can not be controlled. In contrast, ADOM merely requires the network to stay connected throughout time.

ADOM uses a dual oracle, i.e., we assume access to the gradient of the Fenchel conjugate of the individual loss functions. Up to a constant factor, which depends on the network structure only, its communication complexity is the same as that of accelerated Nesterov gradient method. To the best of our knowledge, only the algorithm of Rogozin et al. (2019) has a convergence rate with similar properties. However, their algorithm converges under the very restrictive assumption that the number of network changes can not be greater than a tiny percentage of the number of iterations. This assumption is hard to satisfy in practice, as the network topology changes usually can not be controlled. In contrast, ADOM merely requires the network to stay connected throughout time.

paragraphs: Decentralized optimization distributes a learning problem across a network whose participants communicate to reach a solution. When connections change during optimization, maintaining fast convergence becomes harder. ADOM addresses this setting for smooth, strongly convex objectives, with an accelerated method designed to accommodate a changing network.

The method assumes access to a dual oracle: the gradient of the Fenchel conjugate of each participant's loss function. Under its assumptions, ADOM's communication complexity matches that of accelerated Nesterov gradient descent up to a constant factor determined only by network structure. This comparison concerns the communication needed to optimize, rather than claiming identical costs for every part of the computation.

The network condition is central to the contribution. A previous method with similar convergence properties allowed changes during only a very small fraction of iterations. ADOM instead requires the network to remain connected throughout time. It therefore supports continuing changes in who communicates with whom, provided those changes preserve connectivity, while retaining an accelerated communication guarantee.
summary.tldr: ADOM provides accelerated decentralized optimization on changing networks that remain connected, assuming access to the required dual gradients.

title: ADOM: Accelerated Decentralized Optimization Method for Time-Varying Networks

abstract: Q-learning, which seeks to learn the optimal Q-function of a Markov decision process (MDP) in a model-free fashion, lies at the heart of reinforcement learning. Focusing on the synchronous setting (such that independent samples for all state-action pairs are queried via a generative model in each iteration), substantial progress has been made recently towards understanding the sample efficiency of Q-learning. To yield an entrywise $\varepsilon$-accurate estimate of the optimal Q-function, state-of-the-art theory requires at least an order of $\frac{|S||A|}{(1-\gamma)^5\varepsilon^{2}}$ samples in the infinite-horizon $\gamma$-discounted setting. In this work, we sharpen the sample complexity of synchronous Q-learning to the order of $\frac{|S||A|}{(1-\gamma)^4\varepsilon^2}$ (up to some logarithmic factor) for any $0<\varepsilon <1$, leading to an order-wise improvement in $\frac{1}{1-\gamma}$. Analogous results are derived for finite-horizon MDPs as well. Notably, our sample complexity analysis unveils the effectiveness of vanilla Q-learning, which matches that of speedy Q-learning without requiring extra computation and storage. Our result is obtained by identifying novel error decompositions and recursion relations, which might shed light on how to study other variants of Q-learning.

paragraphs: Q-learning estimates the value of taking each action in each state without learning an explicit environment model. This paper sharpens its sample-efficiency theory in the synchronous setting. Here, a generative model provides independent samples for every state-action pair at each iteration, an assumption that defines the analyzed sampling process.

For infinite-horizon discounted problems, the new bound reduces dependence on the effective horizon, represented by one divided by one minus the discount factor, from the fifth power to the fourth. The bound retains dependence on the number of state-action pairs and the inverse square of the desired error tolerance, up to logarithmic factors. The authors also obtain analogous finite-horizon results.

The improvement comes from new error decompositions and recursion relationships in the analysis. It shows that vanilla Q-learning matches the sample complexity of speedy Q-learning without its extra computation and storage. The finding strengthens what can be guaranteed for the standard algorithm under synchronous sampling, and the authors suggest that the analytical tools may help study other Q-learning variants.
summary.tldr: A sharper analysis improves synchronous Q-learning's horizon dependence and shows vanilla Q-learning matches speedy Q-learning's sample complexity.

title: Tightening the Dependence on Horizon in the Sample Complexity of Q-Learning

abstract: Current graph representation (GR) algorithms require huge demand of human experts in hyperparameter tuning, which significantly limits their practical applications, leading to an urge for automated graph representation without human intervention. Although automated machine learning (AutoML) serves as a good candidate for automatic hyperparameter tuning, little literature has been reported on automated graph presentation learning and the only existing work employs a black-box strategy, lacking insights into explaining the relative importance of different hyperparameters. To address this issue, we study explainable automated graph representation with hyperparameter importance in this paper. We propose an explainable AutoML approach for graph representation (e-AutoGR) which utilizes explainable graph features during performance estimation and learns decorrelated importance weights for different hyperparameters in affecting the model performance through a non-linear decorrelated weighting regression. These learned importance weights can in turn help to provide more insights in hyperparameter search procedure. We theoretically prove the soundness of the decorrelated weighting algorithm. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed e-AutoGR model against state-of-the-art methods in terms of both model performance and hyperparameter importance explainability.

It then learns importance weights through a nonlinear regression procedure designed to decorrelate the weighting of hyperparameters. Experiments on real-world datasets report improvements over leading methods in both model performance and the explainability of hyperparameter importance. The contribution therefore joins automated tuning with a structured account of which choices influence its results, rather than treating search quality as the only objective.
summary.tldr: e-AutoGR automates graph representation tuning while learning interpretable importance weights for the hyperparameters that affect performance.

title: Explainable Automated Graph Representation Learning with Hyperparameter Importance

abstract: Recent empirical evidence suggests that the Weston-Watkins support vector machine is among the best performing multiclass extensions of the binary SVM. Current state-of-the-art solvers repeatedly solve a particular subproblem approximately using an iterative strategy. In this work, we propose an algorithm that solves the subproblem exactly using a novel reparametrization of the Weston-Watkins dual problem. For linear WW-SVMs, our solver shows significant speed-up over the state-of-the-art solver when the number of classes is large. Our exact subproblem solver also allows us to prove linear convergence of the overall solver.

paragraphs: The Weston-Watkins support vector machine extends binary SVM classification to problems with multiple classes. The paper is motivated by empirical evidence that this formulation performs well among multiclass SVM variants. Its focus is the computation needed to train the model, particularly a subproblem that existing solvers repeatedly address using an approximate iterative procedure.

The authors introduce a new way to express the dual optimization problem. This reparametrization makes it possible to solve the recurring subproblem exactly. The contribution therefore changes a component used throughout the overall training algorithm: each call to that component can obtain an exact subproblem solution rather than relying on successive approximations.

For linear Weston-Watkins SVMs, the resulting solver shows a substantial speed advantage over the state-of-the-art solver when many classes are present. Exact subproblem solutions also enable a proof that the overall solver converges at a geometric rate. The paper thus connects a targeted optimization improvement with both an observed training-speed benefit and a stronger convergence guarantee.
summary.tldr: An exact solver for a recurring Weston-Watkins SVM subproblem speeds linear multiclass training and enables a geometric convergence proof.

title: An exact solver for the Weston-Watkins SVM subproblem

abstract: Meta-learning has proven to be a powerful paradigm for transferring the knowledge from previous tasks to facilitate the learning of a novel task. Current dominant algorithms train a well-generalized model initialization which is adapted to each task via the support set. The crux lies in optimizing the generalization capability of the initialization, which is measured by the performance of the adapted model on the query set of each task. Unfortunately, this generalization measure, evidenced by empirical results, pushes the initialization to overfit the meta-training tasks, which significantly impairs the generalization and adaptation to novel tasks. To address this issue, we actively augment a meta-training task with “more data” when evaluating the generalization. Concretely, we propose two task augmentation methods, including MetaMix and Channel Shuffle. MetaMix linearly combines features and labels of samples from both the support and query sets. For each class of samples, Channel Shuffle randomly replaces a subset of their channels with the corresponding ones from a different class. Theoretical studies show how task augmentation improves the generalization of meta-learning. Moreover, both MetaMix and Channel Shuffle outperform state-of-the-art results by a large margin across many datasets and are compatible with existing meta-learning algorithms.

This paper presents empirical evidence that optimizing this measure can still overfit the meta-training tasks, weakening adaptation to new tasks despite the intended focus on generalization.

The authors augment tasks when evaluating generalization. MetaMix linearly combines features and labels from support and query samples. Channel Shuffle replaces a randomly selected subset of channels for samples of one class with corresponding channels from another class. Both methods expand the information used during task-level training through transformations of the available examples.

The paper provides theoretical analysis of how task augmentation improves meta-learning generalization. Experiments report large improvements over state-of-the-art results across many datasets, and both methods can be used with existing meta-learning algorithms. The findings indicate that how a task is presented during generalization evaluation can matter substantially, beyond the choice of initialization-learning algorithm itself.
summary.tldr: MetaMix and Channel Shuffle augment meta-training tasks to improve adaptation and generalization to new tasks.

title: Improving Generalization in Meta-learning via Task Augmentation

abstract: Neural Ordinary Differential Equations model dynamical systems with ODEs learned by neural networks. However, ODEs are fundamentally inadequate to model systems with long-range dependencies or discontinuities, which are common in engineering and biological systems. Broader classes of differential equations (DE) have been proposed as remedies, including delay differential equations and integro-differential equations. Furthermore, Neural ODE suffers from numerical instability when modelling stiff ODEs and ODEs with piecewise forcing functions. In this work, we propose Neural Laplace, a unifying framework for learning diverse classes of DEs including all the aforementioned ones. Instead of modelling the dynamics in the time domain, we model it in the Laplace domain, where the history-dependencies and discontinuities in time can be represented as summations of complex exponentials. To make learning more efficient, we use the geometrical stereographic map of a Riemann sphere to induce more smoothness in the Laplace domain. In the experiments, Neural Laplace shows superior performance in modelling and extrapolating the trajectories of diverse classes of DEs, including the ones with complex history dependency and abrupt changes.

paragraphs: Neural differential-equation models learn how a system evolves, but ordinary differential equations are inadequate for the long-range dependencies and discontinuities highlighted in this paper. Neural ODE approaches also encounter numerical instability with stiff dynamics and piecewise forcing. Neural Laplace seeks a unified framework for these cases and for broader equation classes involving delays or accumulated history.

The method learns in the Laplace domain rather than directly describing changes over time. In that representation, history dependence and time-domain discontinuities can be expressed through sums of complex exponentials. The authors also use a stereographic mapping associated with the Riemann sphere to encourage greater smoothness in the Laplace representation and make learning more efficient.

Experiments show superior modeling and extrapolation of trajectories across diverse differential-equation classes, including systems with complicated history dependence and abrupt changes. The contribution is a shared representation for learning several kinds of dynamics. Its reported results cover both fitting trajectories and extending predictions beyond the observed portion of those trajectories.
summary.tldr: Neural Laplace learns dynamics in the Laplace domain to model diverse differential equations, including systems with memory and abrupt changes.

title: Neural Laplace: Learning diverse classes of differential equations in the Laplace domain

abstract: In this paper, we explore applications of deep learning in statistical physics. We choose the Boltzmann equation as a typical example, where neural networks serve as a closure to its moment system. We present two types of neural networks to embed the convexity of entropy and to preserve the minimum entropy principle and intrinsic mathematical structures of the moment system of the Boltzmann equation. We derive an error bound for the generalization gap of convex neural networks which are trained in Sobolev norm and use the results to construct data sampling methods for neural network training. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the neural entropy closure is significantly faster than classical optimizers while maintaining sufficient accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies how neural networks can accelerate a calculation in statistical physics while retaining its mathematical structure. The example is the moment system associated with the Boltzmann equation, where a closure supplies information needed to complete the system. The authors use neural networks for this closure and make entropy-related structure a central design requirement.

They present two network types that embed entropy convexity and preserve the minimum entropy principle and intrinsic properties of the moment system. This connects network design to the mathematical requirements of the physical model. The paper also derives a generalization-gap bound for convex networks trained in a Sobolev norm, then uses that analysis to construct sampling methods for training data.

Numerical experiments show that the neural entropy closure is significantly faster than classical optimizers while retaining sufficient accuracy. The result supports structured neural approximations for this specific computational task. Its contribution combines architectural constraints, a theoretical treatment of generalization, and data sampling informed by that theory, rather than relying on prediction accuracy as the sole design consideration.
summary.tldr: Entropy-convex neural closures preserve Boltzmann moment-system structure and run faster than classical optimizers in the reported numerical experiments.

title: Structure Preserving Neural Networks: A Case Study in the Entropy Closure of the Boltzmann Equation

abstract: Generative models of biological sequences are a powerful tool for learning from complex sequence data, predicting the effects of mutations, and designing novel biomolecules with desired properties. To evaluate generative models it is important to accurately measure differences between high-dimensional distributions. In this paper we propose the “KSD-B”, a novel divergence measure for distributions over biological sequences that is based on the kernelized Stein discrepancy (KSD). The KSD-B can be evaluated even when the normalizing constant of the model is unknown; it allows for variable length sequences and can take into account biological notions of sequence distance. Unlike previous KSDs over discrete spaces the KSD-B (a) is theoretically guaranteed to detect convergence and non-convergence of distributions over sequence space and (b) can be efficiently estimated in practice. We demonstrate the advantages of the KSD-B on problems with synthetic and real data, and apply it to measure the fit of state-of-the-art machine learning models. Overall, the KSD-B enables rigorous evaluation of generative biological sequence models, allowing the accuracy of models, sampling procedures, and library designs to be checked reliably.

paragraphs: Evaluating a biological sequence generator requires comparing distributions over many possible sequences. A useful comparison must accommodate features such as varying sequence lengths and biologically meaningful differences between sequences. This paper introduces KSD-B, a discrepancy measure designed to support those comparisons and assess how well a generative model fits sequence data.

KSD-B builds on the kernelized Stein discrepancy. One practical benefit is that it remains computable when a model's normalizing constant is unknown, so evaluation does not require that quantity. It also supports variable-length sequences and can incorporate biological notions of sequence distance. These features connect the statistical comparison to the structure of the objects being modeled.

The authors establish guarantees that KSD-B detects both convergence and non-convergence of distributions over sequence space, while remaining efficiently estimable. They demonstrate its advantages using synthetic and real data and evaluate the fit of existing machine learning models. The contribution supports checking model accuracy, sampling procedures, and sequence-library designs through a discrepancy with both theoretical and practical foundations.
summary.tldr: KSD-B provides an efficiently estimable, theoretically grounded way to evaluate biological sequence distributions, including variable-length sequences and unnormalized models.

title: A Kernelized Stein Discrepancy for Biological Sequences

abstract: To characterize the functions spaces explored by multi-layer neural networks (NNs), we introduce Neural Hilbert Ladders (NHLs), a collection of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSes) that are defined iteratively and adaptive to training. First, we prove a correspondence between functions expressed by L-layer NNs and those belonging to L-level NHLs. Second, we prove generalization guarantees for learning the NHL based on a new complexity measure. Third, corresponding to the training of multi-layer NNs in the infinite-width mean-field limit, we derive an evolution of the NHL characterized by the dynamics of multiple random fields. Finally, we examine linear and shallow NNs from the new perspective and complement the theory with numerical results.

paragraphs: This paper develops a mathematical description of the function spaces explored by multilayer neural networks. Its proposed object, a Neural Hilbert Ladder, is a sequence of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces defined recursively. The spaces adapt during training, allowing the description to account for changes in the network's learned representation.

The authors prove a correspondence between functions represented by a network with L layers and functions belonging to a ladder with L levels. They also introduce a complexity measure and use it to establish generalization guarantees for learning these ladders. Together, these results connect what the network can represent with a framework for analyzing learning beyond the training data.

The paper further derives how the ladder evolves when network training is considered in the infinite-width mean-field limit. That evolution is described through multiple random fields, placing the training dynamics inside the same mathematical framework. Analyses of linear and shallow networks, accompanied by numerical results, illustrate the perspective in simpler cases. The contribution unifies representation, generalization, and limiting training dynamics within one construction.
summary.tldr: Neural Hilbert Ladders describe multilayer networks through adaptive function spaces, linking representation, generalization, and infinite-width training dynamics.

title: Multi-Layer Neural Networks as Trainable Ladders of Hilbert Spaces

abstract: Stochastically Extended Adversarial (SEA) model is introduced by Sachs et al. (2022) as an interpolation between stochastic and adversarial online convex optimization. Under the smoothness condition, they demonstrate that the expected regret of optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) depends on the cumulative stochastic variance $\sigma_{1:T}^2$ and the cumulative adversarial variation $\Sigma_{1:T}^2$ for convex functions. They also provide a slightly weaker bound based on the maximal stochastic variance $\sigma_{\max}^2$ and the maximal adversarial variation $\Sigma_{\max}^2$ for strongly convex functions. Inspired by their work, we investigate the theoretical guarantees of optimistic online mirror descent (OMD) for the SEA model. For convex and smooth functions, we obtain the same $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\sigma_{1:T}^2}+\sqrt{\Sigma_{1:T}^2})$ regret bound, without the convexity requirement of individual functions. For strongly convex and smooth functions, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(\min\{\log (\sigma_{1:T}^2+\Sigma_{1:T}^2), (\sigma_{\max}^2 + \Sigma_{\max}^2) \log T\})$ bound, better than their $\mathcal{O}((\sigma_{\max}^2 + \Sigma_{\max}^2) \log T)$ result. For exp-concave and smooth functions, we achieve a new $\mathcal{O}(d\log(\sigma_{1:T}^2+\Sigma_{1:T}^2))$ bound. Owing to the OMD framework, we further establish dynamic regret for convex and smooth functions, which is more favorable in non-stationary online scenarios.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization can involve both random variation and deliberate changes in the loss sequence. The Stochastically Extended Adversarial model interpolates between those settings. This paper analyzes optimistic online mirror descent within that model, seeking regret guarantees that reflect each source of difficulty rather than only the time horizon.

For smooth convex objectives, the method matches a bound based on the square roots of cumulative stochastic variance and adversarial variation, without requiring every individual function to be convex. For strongly convex objectives, the analysis improves earlier guarantees by taking the better of cumulative-variation and maximum-variation expressions. It also establishes a new bound for smooth exp-concave functions.

The mirror-descent framework further supports dynamic regret analysis, relevant when the appropriate comparator changes over time. The contribution is theoretical: it broadens and sharpens environment-sensitive guarantees across several objective classes. These rates depend on smoothness and the relevant convexity conditions, rather than providing the same advantage for arbitrary online losses.
summary.tldr: Optimistic mirror descent obtains sharper variation-sensitive regret guarantees across stochastic, adversarial, and changing online environments.

title: Optimistic Online Mirror Descent for Bridging Stochastic and Adversarial Online Convex Optimization

abstract: In this paper, we present a new method for few-sample supervised feature selection (FS). Our method first learns the manifold of the feature space of each class using kernels capturing multi-feature associations. Then, based on Riemannian geometry, a composite kernel is computed, extracting the differences between the learned feature associations. Finally, a FS score based on spectral analysis is proposed. Considering multi-feature associations makes our method multivariate by design. This in turn allows for the extraction of the hidden manifold underlying the features and avoids overfitting, facilitating few-sample FS. We showcase the efficacy of our method on illustrative examples and several benchmarks, where our method demonstrates higher accuracy in selecting the informative features compared to competing methods. In addition, we show that our FS leads to improved classification and better generalization when applied to test data.

Considering multi-feature associations makes our method multivariate by design. paragraphs: Selecting useful features from only a small number of labeled examples is difficult because the available data must reveal which measurements carry class information. This paper develops a supervised feature selection method that considers associations among multiple features. Its starting point is the structure of those associations within each class.

The method first uses kernels to learn a feature manifold for each class, capturing how features relate to one another. It then applies Riemannian geometry to construct a composite kernel that extracts differences between the learned associations. Finally, spectral analysis produces a feature selection score. This sequence turns class-dependent relationships among features into a basis for choosing informative inputs.

The authors attribute the method's suitability for few-sample learning to its multivariate design, which reveals underlying feature structure and avoids overfitting. Illustrative examples and benchmarks show more accurate identification of informative features than competing methods. The selected features also improve classification and generalization on test data, connecting the selection procedure to the performance of the eventual predictive model.
summary.tldr: A geometry-based feature selection method uses class-specific associations among features to improve selection and classification with few training examples.

title: Few-Sample Feature Selection via Feature Manifold Learning

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have continuously achieved new milestones in object detection. However, the considerable computation and memory burden compromise their efficiency and generalization of deployment on resource-constraint devices. Besides, efficient transformer-based detectors designed by existing works can hardly achieve a realistic speedup, especially on multi-core processors (e.g., GPUs). The main issue is that the current literature solely concentrates on building algorithms with minimal computation, oblivious that the practical latency can also be affected by the memory access cost and the degree of parallelism. Therefore, we propose SpeedDETR, a novel speed-aware transformer for end-to-end object detectors, achieving high-speed inference on multiple devices. Specifically, we design a latency prediction model which can directly and accurately estimate the network latency by analyzing network properties, hardware memory access pattern, and degree of parallelism. Following the effective local-to-global visual modeling process and the guidance of the latency prediction model, we build our hardware-oriented architecture design and develop a new family of SpeedDETR. Experiments on the MS COCO dataset show SpeedDETR outperforms current DETR-based methods on Tesla V100. Even acceptable speed inference can be achieved on edge GPUs.

paragraphs: Reducing a detector’s computation does not necessarily produce a matching reduction in runtime. The paper argues that transformer-based object detectors also depend on memory access costs and the degree of parallelism available on the hardware. Designs focused only on computation can therefore miss practical speed improvements, especially on multicore processors such as GPUs.

SpeedDETR uses a latency prediction model to guide architecture design. The predictor analyzes network properties, hardware memory access patterns, and parallelism to estimate runtime directly. Combined with a local-to-global visual modeling process, this guidance produces a family of hardware-oriented transformer detectors. The design objective is connected to actual inference latency rather than computation counts alone.

Experiments on MS COCO report that SpeedDETR outperforms current DETR-based methods on Tesla V100 hardware. The authors also report acceptable inference speed on edge GPUs and high-speed inference across multiple devices. These findings support accounting for hardware behavior during model design, with the reported evidence tied to the evaluated detectors and devices.
summary.tldr: SpeedDETR designs transformer detectors around predicted hardware latency, accounting for memory access and parallelism as well as computation.

title: SpeedDETR: Speed-aware Transformers for End-to-end Object Detection

abstract: Many compression techniques have been proposed to reduce the communication overhead of Federated Learning training procedures. However, these are typically designed for compressing model updates, which are expected to decay throughout training. As a result, such methods are inapplicable to downlink (i.e., from the parameter server to clients) compression in the cross-device setting, where heterogeneous clients may appear only once during training and thus must download the model parameters. Accordingly, we propose DoCoFL – a new framework for downlink compression in the cross-device setting. Importantly, DoCoFL can be seamlessly combined with many uplink compression schemes, rendering it suitable for bi-directional compression. Through extensive evaluation, we show that DoCoFL offers significant bi-directional bandwidth reduction while achieving competitive accuracy to that of a baseline without any compression.

However, these are typically designed for compressing model updates, which are expected to decay throughout training. As a result, such methods are inapplicable to downlink (i.e., from the parameter server to clients) compression in the cross-device setting, where heterogeneous clients may appear only once during training and thus must download the model parameters. Accordingly, we propose DoCoFL – a new framework for downlink compression in the cross-device setting. Importantly, DoCoFL can be seamlessly combined with many uplink compression schemes, rendering it suitable for bi-directional compression. Through extensive evaluation, we show that DoCoFL offers significant bi-directional bandwidth reduction while achieving competitive accuracy to that of a baseline without any compression.

paragraphs: Federated learning requires communication in both directions: clients receive model parameters from a server and send model updates back. Many compression methods focus on updates, whose size in value is expected to shrink during training. The paper explains why techniques built around that behavior do not directly address sending full model parameters to participating devices.

This distinction matters in cross-device learning, where clients are heterogeneous and may participate only once. Such clients still need to download the model, so reducing the cost of outgoing updates leaves a separate communication burden. DoCoFL is a framework designed specifically to compress this server-to-client transfer. It can also be combined with many existing methods for compressing client-to-server updates.

The authors evaluate the combined communication savings and report substantial bandwidth reductions in both directions, with accuracy competitive with an uncompressed baseline. The finding is empirical rather than a claim of identical accuracy in every setting. DoCoFL’s contribution is to make downlink compression a compatible part of a broader federated communication strategy.
summary.tldr: DoCoFL compresses server-to-device model downloads and combines with uplink compression to reduce federated learning bandwidth while retaining competitive accuracy.

title: DoCoFL: Downlink Compression for Cross-Device Federated Learning

abstract: Several recent studies have elucidated why knowledge distillation (KD) improves model performance. However, few have researched the other advantages of KD in addition to its improving model performance. In this study, we have attempted to show that KD enhances the interpretability as well as the accuracy of models. We measured the number of concept detectors identified in network dissection for a quantitative comparison of model interpretability. We attributed the improvement in interpretability to the class-similarity information transferred from the teacher to student models. First, we confirmed the transfer of class-similarity information from the teacher to student model via logit distillation. Then, we analyzed how class-similarity information affects model interpretability in terms of its presence or absence and degree of similarity information. We conducted various quantitative and qualitative experiments and examined the results on different datasets, different KD methods, and according to different measures of interpretability. Our research showed that KD models by large models could be used more reliably in various fields. The code is available at https://github.com/Rok07/KD_XAI.git.
originalAbstract: Several recent studies have elucidated why knowledge distillation (KD) improves model performance. However, few have researched the other advantages of KD in addition to its improving model performance. In this study, we have attempted to show that KD enhances the interpretability as well as the accuracy of models. We measured the number of concept detectors identified in network dissection for a quantitative comparison of model interpretability. We attributed the improvement in interpretability to the class-similarity information transferred from the teacher to student models. First, we confirmed the transfer of class-similarity information from the teacher to student model via logit distillation. Then, we analyzed how class-similarity information affects model interpretability in terms of its presence or absence and degree of similarity information. We conducted various quantitative and qualitative experiments and examined the results on different datasets, different KD methods, and according to different measures of interpretability. Our research showed that KD models by large models could be used more reliably in various fields. The code is available at https://github.com/Rok07/KD_XAI.git.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using information from a teacher model. This paper investigates whether its benefits extend beyond predictive accuracy to interpretability. The authors quantify one aspect of interpretability through network dissection, counting internal concept detectors identified in the model.

Their proposed explanation centers on class-similarity information transferred from teacher to student. They first confirm that logit distillation conveys this information, then examine how interpretability changes with its presence, absence, and degree. This connects the observed interpretability benefit to what the teacher communicates about relationships among classes.

The study includes quantitative and qualitative experiments across datasets, distillation methods, and interpretability measures. Its results support the claim that distillation can improve both accuracy and interpretability in the evaluated models. The practical implication is that a teacher’s guidance may shape how a student represents concepts, as well as how accurately it predicts. The evidence grounds interpretability in the measures examined, including identifiable concept detectors within the network.
summary.tldr: The study links improved student-model interpretability under knowledge distillation to class-similarity information transferred by the teacher.

title: On the Impact of Knowledge Distillation for Model Interpretability

abstract: The class-wise training losses often diverge as a result of the various levels of intra-class and inter-class appearance variation, and we find that the diverging class-wise training losses cause the uncalibrated prediction with its reliability. To resolve the issue, we propose a new calibration method to synchronize the class-wise training losses. We design a new training loss to alleviate the variance of class-wise training losses by using multiple class-wise scaling factors. Since our framework can compensate the training losses of overfitted classes with those of under-fitted classes, the integrated training loss is preserved, preventing the performance drop even after the model calibration. Furthermore, our method can be easily employed in the post-hoc calibration methods, allowing us to use the pre-trained model as an initial model and reduce the additional computation for model calibration. We validate the proposed framework by employing it in the various post-hoc calibration methods, which generally improves calibration performance while preserving accuracy, and discover through the investigation that our approach performs well with unbalanced datasets and untuned hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Calibration concerns how well a model’s confidence reflects the reliability of its predictions. This paper links unreliable confidence to differences in training loss across classes. Those differences can arise because visual variation within and between classes makes some classes easier to fit than others, leaving uneven patterns of overfitting and underfitting.

The proposed method uses separate scaling factors for each class to reduce variation among their training losses. It balances the losses of overfitted classes against those of underfitted classes while preserving the integrated training loss. The framework can be incorporated into post-hoc calibration methods, starting from a pretrained model to reduce the additional computation needed.

Across several post-hoc methods, the approach generally improves calibration while preserving classification accuracy. The authors also report good performance with unbalanced datasets and untuned hyperparameters. The stated findings support treating differences between class-level fitting behavior as a useful calibration signal, with the loss-balancing construction intended to improve confidence reliability while maintaining the model’s predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Balancing class-specific training losses generally improves post-hoc confidence calibration while preserving accuracy in the reported evaluations.

title: Scaling of Class-wise Training Losses for Post-hoc Calibration

abstract: Transformers for graph data are increasingly widely studied and successful in numerous learning tasks. Graph inductive biases are crucial for Graph Transformers, and previous works incorporate them using message-passing modules and/or positional encodings. However, Graph Transformers that use message-passing inherit known issues of message-passing, and differ significantly from Transformers used in other domains, thus making transfer of research advances more difficult. On the other hand, Graph Transformers without message-passing often perform poorly on smaller datasets, where inductive biases are more crucial. To bridge this gap, we propose the Graph Inductive bias Transformer (GRIT) — a new Graph Transformer that incorporates graph inductive biases without using message passing. GRIT is based on several architectural changes that are each theoretically and empirically justified, including: learned relative positional encodings initialized with random walk probabilities, a flexible attention mechanism that updates node and node-pair representations, and injection of degree information in each layer. We prove that GRIT is expressive — it can express shortest path distances and various graph propagation matrices. GRIT achieves state-of-the-art empirical performance across a variety of graph datasets, thus showing the power that Graph Transformers without message-passing can deliver.

paragraphs: Graph Transformers need architectural guidance that reflects how nodes are connected. Previous approaches often supply this through message passing, but doing so brings known message-passing issues and makes the architecture less like Transformers in other domains. Models without message passing, meanwhile, can struggle on smaller datasets where structural guidance matters more.

The proposed Graph Inductive bias Transformer, or GRIT, incorporates that guidance through several changes. It learns relative positional encodings initialized from random-walk probabilities, updates both node and node-pair representations through attention, and adds node degree information at every layer. Together, these choices make graph structure available inside the Transformer without a message-passing module.

The authors justify the architectural components theoretically and empirically. They prove that GRIT can represent shortest-path distances and various graph propagation matrices, and report state-of-the-art results across several graph datasets. The findings show that removing message passing need not mean giving up useful graph structure. GRIT’s design provides an alternative route to both expressive graph representations and strong measured performance.
summary.tldr: GRIT embeds graph structure into Transformer attention and positional representations without message passing, achieving strong theoretical expressiveness and empirical results.

title: Graph Inductive Biases in Transformers without Message Passing

abstract: Machine learning models are often personalized with categorical attributes that define groups. In this work, we show that personalization with group attributes can inadvertently reduce performance at a group level – i.e., groups may receive unnecessarily inaccurate predictions by sharing their personal characteristics. We present formal conditions to ensure the fair use of group attributes in a prediction task, and describe how they can be checked by training one additional model. We characterize how fair use conditions be violated due to standard practices in model development, and study the prevalence of fair use violations in clinical prediction tasks. Our results show that personalization often fails to produce a tailored performance gain for every group who reports personal data, and underscore the need to evaluate fair use when personalizing models with characteristics that are protected, sensitive, self-reported, or costly to acquire.
originalAbstract: Machine learning models are often personalized with categorical attributes that define groups. In this work, we show that personalization with group attributes can inadvertently reduce performance at a group level – i.e., groups may receive unnecessarily inaccurate predictions by sharing their personal characteristics. We present formal conditions to ensure the fair use of group attributes in a prediction task, and describe how they can be checked by training one additional model. We characterize how fair use conditions be violated due to standard practices in model development, and study the prevalence of fair use violations in clinical prediction tasks. Our results show that personalization often fails to produce a tailored performance gain for every group who reports personal data, and underscore the need to evaluate fair use when personalizing models with characteristics that are protected, sensitive, self-reported, or costly to acquire.

paragraphs: Personalizing predictions with categorical group attributes can seem like a way to make a model more useful to each group. This paper shows that providing such information can instead lead to unnecessarily inaccurate predictions for some groups. The concern is whether each participating group actually benefits from the use of its characteristics.

The authors formalize conditions for fair use of group attributes and describe a way to check them by training one additional model. They also characterize how ordinary model-development practices can violate these conditions. This turns the broad expectation that personalization should help into requirements that can be evaluated in a prediction task.

Studies of clinical prediction tasks find that personalization often fails to provide a tailored performance improvement for every group reporting personal data. The result does not say that personalization always harms performance; it shows why its benefits need group-level scrutiny. The authors emphasize checking fair use when attributes are protected, sensitive, self-reported, or costly to obtain.
summary.tldr: Personalization can harm some groups, and formal fair-use checks assess whether sharing group attributes actually improves their predictions.

title: When Personalization Harms Performance: Reconsidering the Use of Group Attributes in Prediction

abstract: Recent studies have experimentally shown that we can achieve in non-Euclidean metric space effective and efficient graph embedding, which aims to obtain the vertices’ representations reflecting the graph’s structure in the metric space. Specifically, graph embedding in hyperbolic space has experimentally succeeded in embedding graphs with hierarchical-tree structure, e.g., data in natural languages, social networks, and knowledge bases. However, recent theoretical analyses have shown a much higher upper bound on non-Euclidean graph embedding’s generalization error than Euclidean one’s, where a high generalization error indicates that the incompleteness and noise in the data can significantly damage learning performance. It implies that the existing bound cannot guarantee the success of graph embedding in non-Euclidean metric space in a practical training data size, which can prevent non-Euclidean graph embedding’s application in real problems. This paper provides a novel upper bound of graph embedding’s generalization error by evaluating the local Rademacher complexity of the model as a function set of the distances of representation couples. Our bound clarifies that the performance of graph embedding in non-Euclidean metric space, including hyperbolic space, is better than the existing upper bounds suggest. Specifically, our new upper bound is polynomial in the metric space’s geometric radius $R$ and can be $O(\frac{1}{S})$ at the fastest, where $S$ is the training data size. Our bound is significantly tighter and faster than the existing one, which can be exponential to $R$ and $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{S}})$ at the fastest. Specific calculations on example cases show that graph embedding in non-Euclidean metric space can outperform that in Euclidean space with much smaller training data than the existing bound has suggested.

paragraphs: Graph embedding represents vertices through locations whose distances reflect graph structure. Experiments have shown advantages for non-Euclidean spaces, particularly hyperbolic representations of hierarchical graphs. Yet earlier generalization bounds were so large that they offered weak guarantees at practical data sizes, leaving a gap between empirical success and theoretical support.

This paper derives a new bound using local Rademacher complexity, treating the model as a collection of distance functions between representation pairs. The resulting dependence on the space's geometric radius R is polynomial, whereas earlier bounds could depend exponentially on R. Its fastest training-data dependence is O(1/S), compared with the earlier fastest O(1/√S).

These are improved upper bounds on generalization error, showing that previous analyses could substantially overstate the error permitted by theory. Calculations for example cases further indicate that non-Euclidean embeddings can outperform Euclidean ones with much less training data than older bounds suggested. The result strengthens theoretical support for these geometries without asserting that they win for every graph.
summary.tldr: Tighter generalization bounds give stronger theoretical support for non-Euclidean graph embeddings at practical training-data sizes.

title: Tight and fast generalization error bound of graph embedding in metric space

abstract: Personalized federated learning (FL) aims to collaboratively train a personalized model for each client. Previous methods do not adaptively determine who to collaborate at a fine-grained level, making them difficult to handle diverse data heterogeneity levels and those cases where malicious clients exist. To address this issue, our core idea is to learn a collaboration graph, which models the benefits from each pairwise collaboration and allocates appropriate collaboration strengths. Based on this, we propose a novel personalized FL algorithm, pFedGraph, which consists of two key modules: (1) inferring the collaboration graph based on pairwise model similarity and dataset size at server to promote fine-grained collaboration and (2) optimizing local model with the assistance of aggregated model at client to promote personalization. The advantage of pFedGraph is flexibly adaptive to diverse data heterogeneity levels and model poisoning attacks, as the proposed collaboration graph always pushes each client to collaborate more with similar and beneficial clients. Extensive experiments show that pFedGraph consistently outperforms the other $14$ baseline methods across various heterogeneity levels and multiple cases where malicious clients exist. Code will be available at https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/pFedGraph.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning aims to give each client a useful individual model while benefiting from collaboration. Deciding who should collaborate matters when clients have different data or when some clients are malicious. This paper proposes learning a collaboration graph that represents the benefit and strength of each pairwise relationship.

The resulting algorithm, pFedGraph, divides the work between server and clients. The server infers the graph using pairwise model similarity and dataset size. Each client then optimizes its local model with help from an aggregated model. The graph steers clients toward stronger collaboration with similar, beneficial partners while the local optimization supports personalization.

Experiments compare pFedGraph with 14 baseline methods across different levels of data heterogeneity and multiple settings containing malicious clients. The authors report consistent improvements in these evaluations. The approach makes collaboration itself adaptive, helping explain its reported ability to handle both variation among clients and model-poisoning attacks without treating every potential partner as equally useful.
summary.tldr: pFedGraph learns which clients should collaborate and how strongly to improve personalized federated learning under heterogeneous and malicious-client settings.

title: Personalized Federated Learning with Inferred Collaboration Graphs

abstract: By jointly learning multiple tasks, multi-task learning (MTL) can leverage the shared knowledge across tasks, resulting in improved data efficiency and generalization performance. However, a major challenge in MTL lies in the presence of conflicting gradients, which can hinder the fair optimization of some tasks and subsequently impede MTL’s ability to achieve better overall performance. Inspired by fair resource allocation in communication networks, we formulate the optimization of MTL as a utility maximization problem, where the loss decreases across tasks are maximized under different fairness measurements. To address the problem, we propose FairGrad, a novel optimization objective. FairGrad not only enables flexible emphasis on certain tasks but also achieves a theoretical convergence guarantee. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method can achieve state-of-the-art performance among gradient manipulation methods on a suite of multi-task benchmarks in supervised learning and reinforcement learning. Furthermore, we incorporate the idea of $\alpha$-fairness into the loss functions of various MTL methods. Extensive empirical studies demonstrate that their performance can be significantly enhanced. Code is available at https://github.com/OptMN-Lab/fairgrad.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning shares knowledge across tasks, but their training signals can conflict. A step that benefits one task may interfere with progress on another, making it difficult to distribute improvement fairly. This paper treats that conflict as a resource-allocation problem inspired by communication networks.

The authors formulate training as utility maximization over decreases in task losses. Different fairness measurements specify how those improvements should be distributed. Their proposed objective, FairGrad, supports flexible emphasis on particular tasks and comes with a theoretical convergence guarantee. Fairness here concerns the allocation of optimization progress across tasks.

Across supervised-learning and reinforcement-learning benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance among gradient-manipulation methods. They also incorporate α-fairness into the loss functions of other multi-task methods and find significant empirical improvements. The results suggest that an explicit choice about how to share progress can be useful both as a new optimization objective and as a modification to existing approaches.
summary.tldr: FairGrad allocates loss improvements across tasks using fairness-based utility maximization, with a convergence guarantee and strong benchmark performance.

title: Fair Resource Allocation in Multi-Task Learning

abstract: In the realm of reinforcement learning (RL), accounting for risk is crucial for making decisions under uncertainty, particularly in applications where safety and reliability are paramount. In this paper, we introduce a general framework on Risk-Sensitive Distributional Reinforcement Learning (RS-DisRL), with static Lipschitz Risk Measures (LRM) and general function approximation. Our framework covers a broad class of risk-sensitive RL, and facilitates analysis of the impact of estimation functions on the effectiveness of RSRL strategies and evaluation of their sample complexity. We design two innovative meta-algorithms: RS-DisRL-M, a model-based strategy for model-based function approximation, and RS-DisRL-V, a model-free approach for general value function approximation. With our novel estimation techniques via Least Squares Regression (LSR) and Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) in distributional RL with augmented Markov Decision Process (MDP), we derive the first $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{K})$ dependency of the regret upper bound for RSRL with static LRM, marking a pioneering contribution towards statistically efficient algorithms in this domain.

paragraphs: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning considers how uncertainty in outcomes should affect decisions. This paper develops a distributional reinforcement-learning framework that supports general function approximation and a class of static Lipschitz risk measures. The scope of the theory is tied to that risk-measure class, allowing the authors to analyze learning efficiency under an explicit mathematical setting.

The framework includes two meta-algorithms. RS-DisRL-M uses a model-based approach with model-based function approximation, while RS-DisRL-V uses a model-free approach with general value-function approximation. New estimation methods based on least squares regression and maximum likelihood operate in distributional reinforcement learning with an augmented Markov decision process.

The authors derive a regret upper bound with square-root dependence on K, up to logarithmic factors, for the stated risk-sensitive setting. They also provide a framework for examining how estimation functions affect strategy effectiveness and sample complexity. The result is a theoretical contribution toward statistically efficient risk-sensitive learning, covering both model-based and model-free approaches under the specified assumptions on risk measures.
summary.tldr: A distributional RL framework provides model-based and model-free risk-sensitive algorithms with a square-root regret dependence under static Lipschitz risk measures.

title: Provable Risk-Sensitive Distributional Reinforcement Learning with General Function Approximation

abstract: We present a novel approach for differentially private data synthesis of protected tabular datasets, a relevant task in highly sensitive domains such as healthcare and government. Current state-of-the-art methods predominantly use marginal-based approaches, where a dataset is generated from private estimates of the marginals. In this paper, we introduce PrivPGD, a new generation method for marginal-based private data synthesis, leveraging tools from optimal transport and particle gradient descent. Our algorithm outperforms existing methods on a large range of datasets while being highly scalable and offering the flexibility to incorporate additional domain-specific constraints.

paragraphs: Releasing useful versions of sensitive tabular datasets requires a way to preserve information while protecting the underlying records. This paper studies differentially private data synthesis, with healthcare and government as motivating domains. Its focus is the generation of synthetic data from private estimates of marginal distributions, which summarize selected aspects of the original data.

PrivPGD introduces a new generation method within this marginal-based approach. It uses tools from optimal transport and particle gradient descent to construct the synthetic dataset. The contribution therefore concerns how private statistical estimates are turned into data that can be released, a central step in making those estimates useful.

The authors report that PrivPGD outperforms existing methods across a large range of datasets while remaining highly scalable. They also emphasize its ability to incorporate additional constraints specific to an application domain. These findings matter together: a generation method needs to produce useful data, handle substantial workloads, and accommodate requirements beyond the statistical summaries alone. PrivPGD is presented as addressing all three within private data synthesis.
summary.tldr: PrivPGD uses optimal transport and particle gradient descent for scalable private tabular-data synthesis with support for domain-specific constraints.

title: Privacy-Preserving Data Release Leveraging Optimal Transport and Particle Gradient Descent

abstract: We investigate the computational limits of the memory retrieval dynamics of modern Hopfield models from the fine-grained complexity analysis. Our key contribution is the characterization of a phase transition behavior in the efficiency of all possible modern Hopfield models based on the norm of patterns. Specifically, we establish an upper bound criterion for the norm of input query patterns and memory patterns. Only below this criterion, sub-quadratic (efficient) variants of the modern Hopfield model exist, assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH). To showcase our theory, we provide a formal example of efficient constructions of modern Hopfield models using low-rank approximation when the efficient criterion holds. This includes a derivation of a lower bound on the computational time, scaling linearly with $\max$$\{$ # of stored memory patterns, length of input query sequence$\}$. In addition, we prove its memory retrieval error bound and exponential memory capacity.

paragraphs: Modern Hopfield models retrieve stored patterns in response to input queries. This paper asks when that retrieval can be made computationally efficient, studying the question through fine-grained complexity analysis. Its central finding is a transition in computational feasibility governed by the norms of the query patterns and stored memory patterns.

The authors establish a norm criterion delimiting the regime where subquadratic variants can exist, assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis. This is a conditional computational boundary, not an unconditional impossibility claim. Within the efficient regime, they give a formal construction using low-rank approximation to demonstrate that the theoretical opportunity can be realized.

The analysis also derives a runtime lower bound that scales linearly with the larger of the number of stored patterns and the input query-sequence length. For the construction, the authors prove a retrieval-error bound and exponential memory capacity. Together, these results relate computational cost to pattern magnitude while also addressing retrieval quality and storage capacity, giving a more complete picture than speed analysis alone.
summary.tldr: A conditional complexity analysis identifies a pattern-norm boundary for efficient Hopfield retrieval and provides a low-rank construction within the efficient regime.

title: On Computational Limits of Modern Hopfield Models: A Fine-Grained Complexity Analysis

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViT), when paired with large-scale pretraining, have shown remarkable performance across various computer vision tasks, primarily due to their weak inductive bias. However, while such weak inductive bias aids in pretraining scalability, this may hinder the effective adaptation of ViTs for visuo-motor control tasks as a result of the absence of control-centric inductive biases. Such absent inductive biases include spatial locality and translation equivariance bias which convolutions naturally offer. To this end, we introduce Convolution Injector (CoIn), an add-on module that injects convolutions which are rich in locality and equivariance biases into a pretrained ViT for effective adaptation in visuo-motor control. We evaluate CoIn with three distinct types of pretrained ViTs (CLIP, MVP, VC-1) across 12 varied control tasks within three separate domains (Adroit, MetaWorld, DMC), and demonstrate that CoIn consistently enhances control task performance across all experimented environments and models, validating the effectiveness of providing pretrained ViTs with control-centric biases.

paragraphs: A vision model that recognizes images well may still need help turning visual observations into effective actions. This paper examines that adaptation problem for pretrained Vision Transformers. Their relatively weak built-in assumptions support large-scale pretraining, but the authors argue that missing assumptions about spatial structure may make adaptation to visual control harder.

The proposed Convolution Injector, or CoIn, adds convolutions to a pretrained transformer. Convolutions provide spatial locality: they emphasize relationships among nearby image features. They also provide translation equivariance, meaning that shifting an input produces a corresponding shift in its features. CoIn brings these control-relevant properties into the adaptation process while using the pretrained visual model.

The evaluation covers CLIP, MVP, and VC-1 across 12 control tasks in Adroit, MetaWorld, and DMC. CoIn improves performance in every tested environment and model combination. These results support the value of adding control-oriented spatial assumptions when adapting pretrained transformers, with the reported consistency applying to the combinations evaluated in the study.
summary.tldr: CoIn adds convolutional spatial biases to pretrained Vision Transformers and improves performance across all tested visual control settings.

title: Adapting Pretrained ViTs with Convolution Injector for Visuo-Motor Control

abstract: In this paper, we study hybrid neural representations for spherical data, a domain of increasing relevance in scientific research. In particular, our work focuses on weather and climate data as well as cosmic microwave background (CMB) data. Although previous studies have delved into coordinate-based neural representations for spherical signals, they often fail to capture the intricate details of highly nonlinear signals. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach named Hybrid Neural Representations for Spherical data (HNeR-S). Our main idea is to use spherical feature-grids to obtain positional features which are combined with a multi-layer perceptron to predict the target signal. We consider feature-grids with equirectangular and hierarchical equal area isolatitude pixelization structures that align with weather data and CMB data, respectively. We extensively verify the effectiveness of our HNeR-S for regression, super-resolution, temporal interpolation, and compression tasks.

abstract: We study the optimal transport (OT) problem for measures supported on a graph metric space. Recently, Le et al. (2022) leverage the graph structure and propose a variant of OT, namely Sobolev transport (ST), which yields a closed-form expression for a fast computation. However, ST is essentially coupled with the $L^p$ geometric structure within its definition which makes it nontrivial to utilize ST for other prior structures. In contrast, the classic OT has the flexibility to adapt to various geometric structures by modifying the underlying cost function. An important instance is the Orlicz-Wasserstein (OW) which moves beyond the $L^p$ structure by leveraging the Orlicz geometric structure. Comparing to the usage of standard $p$-order Wasserstein, OW remarkably helps to advance certain machine learning approaches. Nevertheless, OW brings up a new challenge on its computation due to its two-level optimization formulation. In this work, we leverage a specific class of convex functions for Orlicz structure to propose the generalized Sobolev transport (GST). GST encompasses the ST as its special case, and can be utilized for prior structures beyond the $L^p$ geometry. In connection with the OW, we show that one only needs to simply solve a univariate optimization problem to compute the GST, unlike the complex two-level optimization problem in OW. We empirically illustrate that GST is several-order faster than the OW. Moreover, we provide preliminary evidences on the advantages of GST for document classification and for several tasks in topological data analysis.

Orlicz-Wasserstein transport supports more flexible geometric structure, at the computational cost of a nested, two-level optimization problem.

This construction includes ordinary Sobolev transport as a special case while accommodating prior structures beyond Lp geometry. It therefore expands the kinds of geometric information available within this graph-based transport framework.

A central computational result is that evaluating the generalized measure requires only optimization over a single variable. This is substantially simpler than the two-level formulation used by Orlicz-Wasserstein transport. Experiments report speedups of several orders of magnitude over that alternative. The authors also present preliminary evidence of benefits for document classification and topological data analysis, suggesting potential application value alongside the computational gain.
summary.tldr: Generalized Sobolev transport supports richer graph geometries while requiring only a single-variable optimization for computation.

title: Generalized Sobolev Transport for Probability Measures on a Graph

abstract: Heuristics are widely used for dealing with complex search and optimization problems. However, manual design of heuristics can be often very labour extensive and requires rich working experience and knowledge. This paper proposes Evolution of Heuristic (EoH), a novel evolutionary paradigm that leverages both Large Language Models (LLMs) and Evolutionary Computation (EC) methods for Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD). EoH represents the ideas of heuristics in natural language, termed thoughts. They are then translated into executable codes by LLMs. The evolution of both thoughts and codes in an evolutionary search framework makes it very effective and efficient for generating high-performance heuristics. Experiments on three widely studied combinatorial optimization benchmark problems demonstrate that EoH outperforms commonly used handcrafted heuristics and other recent AHD methods including FunSearch. Particularly, the heuristic produced by EoH with a low computational budget (in terms of the number of queries to LLMs) significantly outperforms widely-used human hand-crafted baseline algorithms for the online bin packing problem.
