paragraphs: Heuristics provide practical ways to tackle difficult search and optimization problems, but designing them manually can require substantial expertise and labor. Evolution of Heuristics, or EoH, combines language models with evolutionary computation to automate that design process. Its central move is to represent an algorithm’s idea as well as its executable implementation.

EoH expresses heuristic ideas in natural language, calling them thoughts, and uses a language model to translate those thoughts into code. An evolutionary search then develops both the thoughts and the code. This gives the search two connected representations to work with: a description of the strategy and a program that carries it out.

Experiments on three combinatorial optimization benchmarks show EoH outperforming commonly used handcrafted heuristics and recent automatic-design approaches, including FunSearch. For online bin packing, the authors report that a heuristic produced with relatively few language-model queries significantly exceeds widely used human-designed baselines. These findings support the usefulness of evolving verbal ideas alongside implementations, with query efficiency forming an explicit part of the reported advantage.
summary.tldr: EoH evolves natural-language heuristic ideas and executable code together to automate effective algorithm design.

title: Evolution of Heuristics: Towards Efficient Automatic Algorithm Design Using Large Language Model

abstract: This paper addresses the growing need for efficient large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices, driven by increasing cloud costs and latency concerns. We focus on designing top-quality LLMs with fewer than a billion parameters, a practical choice for mobile deployment. Contrary to prevailing belief emphasizing the pivotal role of data and parameter quantity in determining model quality, our investigation underscores the significance of model architecture for sub-billion scale LLMs. Leveraging deep and thin architectures, coupled with embedding sharing and grouped-query attention mechanisms, we establish a strong baseline network denoted as MobileLLM, which attains a remarkable 2.7%/4.3% accuracy boost over preceding 125M/350M state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we propose an immediate block-wise weight-sharing approach with no increase in model size and only marginal latency overhead. The resultant models, denoted as MobileLLM-LS, demonstrate a further accuracy enhancement of 0.7%/0.8% than MobileLLM 125M/350M. Moreover, MobileLLM model family shows significant improvements compared to previous sub-billion models on chat benchmarks, and demonstrates close correctness to LLaMA-v2 7B in API calling tasks, highlighting the capability of small models for common on-device use cases.

The paper emphasizes architecture as a significant determinant of quality at this scale. Its question is how to use a small parameter budget effectively enough to support practical language-model tasks.

The baseline combines deep, thin networks with shared embeddings and grouped-query attention. A further variant, MobileLLM-LS, introduces immediate block-wise weight sharing without increasing model size and with only marginal latency overhead. summary.tldr: MobileLLM shows that carefully designed architectures and weight sharing can improve sub-billion-parameter models for on-device tasks.

title: MobileLLM: Optimizing Sub-billion Parameter Language Models for On-Device Use Cases

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation of multivariate time series aims to train a model to adapt its classification ability from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain, where there are differences in the distribution between domains. Existing methods extract domain-invariant features directly via a shared feature extractor, neglecting the exploration of the underlying causal patterns, which undermines their reliability, especially in complex multivariate dynamic systems. To address this problem, we propose CauDiTS, an innovative framework for unsupervised domain adaptation of multivariate time series. CauDiTS adopts an adaptive rationale disentangler to disentangle domain-common causal rationales and domain-specific correlations from variable interrelationships. The stability of causal rationales across domains is vital for filtering domainspecific perturbations and facilitating the extraction of domain-invariant representations. Moreover, we promote the cross-domain consistency of intra-class causal rationales employing the learning strategies of causal prototype consistency and domain-intervention causality invariance. CauDiTS is evaluated on four benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: CauDiTS tackles classification when labeled multivariate time series come from one domain but the model must operate in another domain without labels. Differences between the domains can make learned relationships unreliable. The paper argues that directly extracting shared features overlooks underlying causal patterns, especially when several variables interact within a complex dynamic system.

Its adaptive rationale disentangler separates relationships into domain-common causal rationales and domain-specific correlations. The intended benefit is to retain stable reasons for a classification while filtering changes specific to a domain. Stability across domains is central to this approach: it supplies the basis for learning representations that can transfer despite distribution differences.

The framework also encourages examples from the same class to have consistent causal rationales across domains. It does this through causal prototype consistency and domain-intervention causality invariance. Evaluations on four benchmark datasets report better performance than state-of-the-art methods. These findings support the framework’s usefulness for the tested adaptation tasks, where the challenge is transferring classification ability without obtaining labels in the target domain.
summary.tldr: CauDiTS improves time-series domain adaptation by separating shared causal rationales from domain-specific correlations.

title: CauDiTS: Causal Disentangled Domain Adaptation of Multivariate Time Series

abstract: Learning to defer with multiple experts is a framework where the learner can choose to defer the prediction to several experts. While this problem has received significant attention in classification contexts, it presents unique challenges in regression due to the infinite and continuous nature of the label space. In this work, we introduce a novel framework of regression with deferral, which involves deferring the prediction to multiple experts. We present a comprehensive analysis for both the single-stage scenario, where there is simultaneous learning of predictor and deferral functions, and the two-stage scenario, which involves a pre-trained predictor with a learned deferral function. We introduce new surrogate loss functions for both scenarios and prove that they are supported by $H$-consistency bounds. These bounds provide consistency guarantees that are stronger than Bayes consistency, as they are non-asymptotic and hypothesis set-specific. Our framework is versatile, applying to multiple experts, accommodating any bounded regression losses, addressing both instance-dependent and label-dependent costs, and supporting both single-stage and two-stage methods. Our single-stage formulation subsumes as a special case the recent regression with abstention (Cheng et al., 2023) framework, where only a single expert is considered, specifically for the squared loss and a label-independent cost. Minimizing our proposed loss functions directly leads to novel algorithms for regression with deferral. We report the results of extensive experiments showing the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: A regression system may benefit from handing a prediction to an expert instead of always answering itself. Choosing among several experts is complicated by regression’s continuous range of possible outputs. This paper develops a framework that learns when to predict and when to defer, while accounting for the costs of those decisions.

The authors analyze two training arrangements. In the single-stage case, the predictor and deferral function are learned together. In the two-stage case, a deferral function is learned for an existing pretrained predictor. Both receive new surrogate losses supported by H-consistency bounds, which provide non-asymptotic guarantees tied to the chosen hypothesis set.

The framework accommodates multiple experts, any bounded regression loss, and costs depending on either the instance or its label. Its single-stage formulation also includes a prior single-expert abstention setting as a special case. Minimizing the proposed objectives produces new deferral algorithms, and extensive experiments demonstrate their effectiveness. The contribution combines flexible decision costs with theoretical support for learning the predictor’s delegation behavior.
summary.tldr: A regression framework learns when to defer to multiple experts, with surrogate objectives backed by hypothesis-specific consistency guarantees.

title: Regression with Multi-Expert Deferral

abstract: The implicit bias of gradient-based training algorithms has been considered mostly beneficial as it leads to trained networks that often generalize well. However, Frei et al. (2023) show that such implicit bias can harm adversarial robustness. Specifically, they show that if the data consists of clusters with small inter-cluster correlation, a shallow (two-layer) ReLU network trained by gradient flow generalizes well, but it is not robust to adversarial attacks of small radius. Moreover, this phenomenon occurs despite the existence of a much more robust classifier that can be explicitly constructed from a shallow network. In this paper, we extend recent analyses of neuron alignment to show that a shallow network with a polynomial ReLU activation (pReLU) trained by gradient flow not only generalizes well but is also robust to adversarial attacks. Our results highlight the importance of the interplay between data structure and architecture design in the implicit bias and robustness of trained networks.

paragraphs: Training algorithms favor some solutions over others even without an explicit instruction to do so. This implicit bias can help networks generalize, but good predictions on ordinary examples do not automatically imply resistance to adversarial perturbations. The paper investigates whether the same training tendency can support both properties when the network architecture changes.

The starting point is an earlier result for clustered data with weak correlations between clusters. In that setting, a shallow ReLU network trained by gradient flow generalizes well but remains vulnerable to small adversarial attacks, even though a more robust shallow classifier exists. This separates what the architecture can represent from what its training procedure actually selects.

The authors extend analyses of neuron alignment to shallow networks using polynomial ReLU activations. They show that these networks, when trained by gradient flow in the analyzed setting, can both generalize and resist adversarial attacks. The finding makes the interaction between data structure and activation design central: implicit bias can support robustness, but its effects depend on the architecture and problem being studied.
summary.tldr: For the analyzed setting, polynomial ReLU activations allow gradient-flow training of shallow networks to support both generalization and adversarial robustness.

title: Can Implicit Bias Imply Adversarial Robustness?

abstract: We consider the problem of quantifying the amount of influence one agent can exert on another in the setting of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). As a step towards a unified approach to express agents’ interdependencies, we introduce the total and state influence measurement functions. Both of these are valid for all common MARL systems, such as the discounted reward setting. Additionally, we propose novel quantities, called the total impact measurement (TIM) and state impact measurement (SIM), that characterize one agent’s influence on another by the maximum impact it can have on the other agents’ expected returns and represent instances of impact measurement functions in the average reward setting. Furthermore, we provide approximation algorithms for TIM and SIM with simultaneously learning approximations of agents’ expected returns, error bounds, stability analyses under changes of the policies, and convergence guarantees. The approximation algorithm relies only on observing other agents’ actions and is, other than that, fully decentralized. Through empirical studies, we validate our approach’s effectiveness in identifying intricate influence structures in complex interactions. Our work appears to be the first study of determining influence structures in the multi-agent average reward setting with convergence guarantees.

This paper asks how to quantify that influence rather than simply observe that interactions exist. It introduces total and state influence measurement functions intended to express dependencies across common multi-agent settings, including discounted rewards.

These quantities describe influence through the maximum effect one agent can have on another agent's expected return. Empirical studies show that it can identify intricate influence structures in complex interactions. The contribution combines a way to define influence with a way to estimate it and theoretical support for those estimates in the average-reward setting.
summary.tldr: The paper defines and estimates agents' influence on one another's returns, with decentralized algorithms and convergence guarantees for the average-reward setting.

title: Detecting Influence Structures in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study the in-context learning dynamics of large language models (LLMs) using three instrumental learning tasks adapted from cognitive psychology. We find that LLMs update their beliefs in an asymmetric manner and learn more from better-than-expected outcomes than from worse-than-expected ones. Furthermore, we show that this effect reverses when learning about counterfactual feedback and disappears when no agency is implied. We corroborate these findings by investigating idealized in-context learning agents derived through meta-reinforcement learning, where we observe similar patterns. Taken together, our results contribute to our understanding of how in-context learning works by highlighting that the framing of a problem significantly influences how learning occurs, a phenomenon also observed in human cognition.

paragraphs: This paper studies how language models change their beliefs as they receive feedback within a context. The authors use three instrumental learning tasks adapted from cognitive psychology. Their focus is whether outcomes that are better or worse than expected have equal influence on the model's subsequent learning and behavior.

In the studied tasks, the models learn more from better-than-expected outcomes than from worse-than-expected outcomes. However, the direction of this asymmetry reverses for counterfactual feedback, which concerns outcomes of alternatives to the action taken. The asymmetry also disappears when the task framing does not imply that the learner has agency.

The authors find similar patterns in idealized in-context learning agents obtained through meta-reinforcement learning. Together, these observations suggest that feedback processing depends substantially on how the learning problem is framed. The result is more specific than a general tendency toward optimism: the same kind of positive or negative surprise can have different influence depending on agency and the meaning of the feedback.
summary.tldr: Language models update beliefs asymmetrically, with the direction and presence of that asymmetry depending on feedback and agency.

title: In-Context Learning Agents Are Asymmetric Belief Updaters

abstract: Recent diffusion models have manifested extraordinary capabilities in generating high-quality, diverse, and innovative images guided by textual prompts. Nevertheless, these state-of-the-art models may encounter the challenge of concept bleeding when generating images with multiple entities or attributes in the prompt, leading to the unanticipated merging or overlapping of distinct objects in the synthesized result. The current work exploits auxiliary networks to produce mask-constrained regions for entities, necessitating the training of an object detection network. In this paper, we investigate the bleeding reason and find that the cross-attention map associated with a specific entity or attribute tends to extend beyond its intended focus, encompassing the background or other unrelated objects and thereby acting as the primary source of concept bleeding. Motivated by this, we propose Entity Localization and Anchoring (ELA) to drive the entity to concentrate on the expected region accurately during inference, eliminating the necessity for training. Specifically, we initially identify the region corresponding to each entity and subsequently employ a tailored loss function to anchor entities within their designated positioning areas. Extensive experiments demonstrate its superior capability in precisely generating multiple objects as specified in the textual prompts.

paragraphs: Text-guided diffusion models can struggle when a prompt describes several objects or attributes. Distinct concepts may merge or overlap in the generated image, a problem called concept bleeding. This paper investigates that failure and identifies cross-attention spreading outside the intended object region as its primary source, including attention extending into backgrounds or unrelated objects.

The proposed Entity Localization and Anchoring method, or ELA, acts during inference. It first identifies the image region associated with each entity, then uses a tailored loss to keep that entity focused within its designated area. This connects a spatial diagnosis of the problem with a spatial correction applied while generating the image.

ELA requires no training, whereas the prior approach described in the abstract relies on training an auxiliary object detector to produce constrained regions. Extensive experiments show stronger ability to generate multiple objects as requested in text. The findings support inference-time attention control as a way to ease concept bleeding and improve correspondence between prompts and images.
summary.tldr: ELA reduces concept bleeding by locating entities and anchoring their attention to intended image regions during inference.

title: Easing Concept Bleeding in Diffusion via Entity Localization and Anchoring

abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning optimizes large, pre-trained foundation models by updating a subset of parameters; in this class, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is particularly effective. Inspired by an effort to investigate the different roles of LoRA matrices during fine-tuning, this paper characterizes and leverages unexpected asymmetry in the importance of low-rank adapter matrices. Specifically, when updating the parameter matrices of a neural network by adding a product $BA$, we observe that the $B$ and $A$ matrices have distinct functions: $A$ extracts features from the input, while $B$ uses these features to create the desired output. Based on this observation, we demonstrate that fine-tuning $B$ is inherently more effective than fine-tuning $A$, and that a random untrained $A$ should perform nearly as well as a fine-tuned one. Using an information-theoretic lens, we also bound the generalization of low-rank adapters, showing that the parameter savings of exclusively training $B$ improves the bound. We support our conclusions with experiments on RoBERTa, BART-Large, LLaMA-2, and ViTs. The code and data is available at https://github.com/Jiacheng-Zhu-AIML/AsymmetryLoRA

Based on this observation, we demonstrate that fine-tuning $B$ is inherently more effective than fine-tuning $A$, and that a random untrained $A$ should perform nearly as well as a fine-tuned one. We support our conclusions with experiments on RoBERTa, BART-Large, LLaMA-2, and ViTs. The code and data is available at https://github.com/Jiacheng-Zhu-AIML/AsymmetryLoRA

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, changes a pretrained network by adding a weight update expressed as the product of two smaller matrices, B and A. This paper investigates whether those matrices contribute equally during fine-tuning. Its central observation is that their roles differ: A extracts input features, while B converts those features into the desired output.

The authors use this distinction to argue that training B is inherently more effective than training A. They further show that leaving A randomly initialized and untrained should perform nearly as well as learning it. This suggests a more economical adaptation strategy: concentrate trainable parameters in the part of the adapter that determines how extracted features affect the output.

An information-theoretic analysis gives a generalization bound that improves when only B is trained, because fewer parameters are learned. Experiments involving RoBERTa, BART-Large, LLaMA-2, and vision transformers support the conclusions. The improved bound and empirical evidence together motivate selective adapter training, without making the bound itself a guarantee of better performance on every task.
summary.tldr: LoRA’s two matrices play unequal roles, and training only the output-facing matrix can preserve performance while improving a generalization bound.

title: Asymmetry in Low-Rank Adapters of Foundation Models

abstract: Despite the great progress of 3D vision, data privacy and security issues in 3D deep learning are not explored systematically. In the domain of 2D images, many availability attacks have been proposed to prevent data from being illicitly learned by unauthorized deep models. However, unlike images represented on a fixed dimensional grid, point clouds are characterized as unordered and unstructured sets, posing a significant challenge in designing an effective availability attack for 3D deep learning. In this paper, we theoretically show that extending 2D availability attacks directly to 3D point clouds under distance regularization is susceptible to the degeneracy, rendering the generated poisons weaker or even ineffective. This is because in bi-level optimization, introducing regularization term can result in update directions out of control. To address this issue, we propose a novel Feature Collision Error-Minimization (FC-EM) method, which creates additional shortcuts in the feature space, inducing different update directions to prevent the degeneracy of bi-level optimization. Moreover, we provide a theoretical analysis that demonstrates the effectiveness of the FC-EM attack. Extensive experiments on typical point cloud datasets, 3D intracranial aneurysm medical dataset, and 3D face dataset verify the superiority and practicality of our approach.

Applying ideas developed for images to 3D point clouds is difficult because point clouds are unordered, unstructured sets rather than fixed grids. This paper examines why a direct transfer of image-based attacks can produce weak or ineffective poisoned point-cloud data.

The theoretical analysis identifies a degeneracy when these attacks use distance regularization in bi-level optimization. Adding the regularization term can make update directions uncontrolled. The proposed Feature Collision Error-Minimization method, FC-EM, introduces additional shortcuts in feature space, inducing different update directions to prevent this degeneracy. Its design therefore responds to a specific optimization failure identified by the analysis.

The authors provide a theoretical argument for FC-EM’s effectiveness and evaluate it on standard point-cloud datasets, a 3D intracranial aneurysm dataset, and a 3D face dataset. The experiments support its superiority and practicality in the tested settings. The contribution combines an explanation of why direct 2D-to-3D transfer can fail with a feature-space method intended to repair that failure.
summary.tldr: FC-EM addresses an optimization degeneracy that weakens image-derived availability attacks when applied to 3D point clouds.

title: Toward Availability Attacks in 3D Point Clouds

abstract: Long-range graph tasks — those dependent on interactions between ‘distant’ nodes — are an open problem in graph neural network research. Real-world benchmark tasks, especially the Long Range Graph Benchmark, have become popular for validating the long-range capability of proposed architectures. However, this is an empirical approach that lacks both robustness and theoretical underpinning; a more principled characterization of the long-range problem is required. To bridge this gap, we formalize long-range interactions in graph tasks, introduce a range measure for operators on graphs, and validate it with synthetic experiments. We then leverage our measure to examine commonly used tasks and architectures, and discuss to what extent they are, in fact, long-range. We believe our work advances efforts to define and address the long-range problem on graphs, and that our range measure will aid evaluation of new datasets and architectures.

paragraphs: Graph learning tasks can depend on interactions between distant nodes, but establishing how much long-range interaction a task requires is difficult. Researchers commonly use performance on designated benchmarks as evidence of long-range capability. This paper argues that such empirical evidence needs a more robust theoretical characterization of what range means.

The authors formalize long-range interactions and introduce a range measure for operators on graphs. They validate the measure through synthetic experiments, then apply it to commonly used tasks and architectures. This provides a way to investigate the extent to which those tasks and models actually involve long-range interactions.

The contribution centers on measurement and evaluation. A formal notion of range can help connect claims about a model's capabilities to the interactions a task demands. The authors position their measure as a tool for assessing new datasets and architectures and for clarifying the long-range problem itself, supporting more principled interpretation of benchmark results.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes graph interaction range and introduces a measure for examining long-range claims about tasks and architectures.

title: On Measuring Long-Range Interactions in Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Pre-trained foundation models (FMs) have shown exceptional performance in univariate time series forecasting tasks. However, several practical challenges persist, including managing intricate dependencies among features and quantifying uncertainty in predictions. This study aims to tackle these critical limitations by introducing adapters—feature-space transformations that facilitate the effective use of pre-trained univariate time series FMs for multivariate tasks. Adapters operate by projecting multivariate inputs into a suitable latent space and applying the FM independently to each dimension. Inspired by the literature on representation learning and partially stochastic Bayesian neural networks, we present a range of adapters and optimization/inference strategies. Experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the efficacy of adapters, demonstrating substantial enhancements in forecasting accuracy and uncertainty quantification compared to baseline methods. Our framework, AdaPTS, positions adapters as a modular, scalable, and effective solution for leveraging time series FMs in multivariate contexts, thereby promoting their wider adoption in real-world applications. We release the code at https://github.com/abenechehab/AdaPTS.

paragraphs: A model trained to forecast one time series does not directly address all the challenges of forecasting several related variables. Relationships between variables can matter, and useful predictions should also describe uncertainty. AdaPTS addresses these issues by adapting pretrained univariate forecasting models to multivariate prediction through transformations of the input feature space.

Its adapters project multiple input variables into a latent representation, where the existing foundation model runs independently on each dimension. This places the work of representing relationships between features in the adapter, while retaining the forecasting capabilities of the pretrained model. The authors develop several adapter designs and training and inference strategies, drawing on representation learning and Bayesian neural networks with partially stochastic components.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show substantial improvements in both forecasting accuracy and uncertainty quantification relative to the tested baselines. The contribution is a modular way to reuse univariate forecasting models for a broader class of problems. Its reported benefits concern both what the model predicts and how well it expresses uncertainty about those predictions.
summary.tldr: AdaPTS uses feature-space adapters to turn pretrained univariate forecasting models into effective probabilistic multivariate forecasters.

title: AdaPTS: Adapting Univariate Foundation Models to Probabilistic Multivariate Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Geometry is a ubiquitous tool in computer graphics, design, and engineering. However, the lack of large shape datasets limits the application of state-of-the-art supervised learning methods and motivates the exploration of alternative learning strategies. To this end, we introduce geometry-informed neural networks (GINNs) – a framework for training shape-generative neural fields without data by leveraging user-specified design requirements in the form of objectives and constraints. By adding diversity as an explicit constraint, GINNs avoid mode-collapse and can generate multiple diverse solutions, often required in geometry tasks. Experimentally, we apply GINNs to several problems spanning physics, geometry, and engineering design, showing control over geometrical and topological properties, such as surface smoothness or the number of holes. These results demonstrate the potential of training shape-generative models without data, paving the way for new generative design approaches without large datasets.

paragraphs: Learning to generate shapes typically depends on examples, but large shape datasets are not always available for design and engineering problems. Geometry-informed neural networks, or GINNs, instead train shape-generative neural fields from user-specified objectives and constraints. The design requirements supply the training signal without requiring a dataset of example shapes.

The framework also treats diversity as an explicit constraint. This addresses mode collapse, where a generator repeatedly produces the same or very similar solutions. In design tasks, several distinct shapes may satisfy the requirements, so producing a range of possibilities is itself useful. GINNs incorporate that requirement directly alongside the other objectives and constraints.

Experiments span physics, geometry, and engineering design. They demonstrate control over properties including surface smoothness and the number of holes, covering both geometric appearance and topology. The stated results support the potential of generating diverse, controlled shapes without large datasets. The approach shifts the source of guidance toward specified design requirements, making those requirements central to what the generator learns to produce.
summary.tldr: GINNs generate diverse shapes by training on design objectives and constraints without requiring example shape datasets.

title: Geometry-Informed Neural Networks

abstract: Neural scaling laws offer valuable insights for designing robust sequence processing architectures. While these laws have been extensively characterized in other modalities, their behavior in speech remains comparatively underexplored. In this work, we introduce OWLS, an open-access, reproducible suite of multilingual speech recognition and translation models spanning 0.25B to 18B parameters, with the 18B version being the largest speech model, to the best of our knowledge. OWLS leverages up to 360K hours of public speech data across 150 languages, enabling a systematic investigation into how data, model, and compute scaling each influence performance in multilingual speech tasks. We use OWLS to derive neural scaling laws, showing how final performance can be reliably predicted when scaling. Scaling to larger models can improve ASR performance across the board, in both low and high resource languages, improving the accessibility of speech technologies. Finally, we show how OWLS can be used to power new research directions by discovering emergent abilities in large-scale speech models. Model checkpoints will be released on https://huggingface.co/collections/espnet/owls-scaling-laws-for-speech-recognition-and-translation-67ab7f991c194065f057ce8d for future studies.

paragraphs: Scaling laws describe how model performance changes as resources increase, helping guide choices about model size, training data, and computation. Their behavior in speech has received less attention than in other modalities. OWLS provides a reproducible, open-access suite for investigating these relationships in multilingual speech recognition and translation.

The suite spans models with 0.25 billion to 18 billion parameters and uses up to 360,000 hours of public speech data across 150 languages. This range lets the authors systematically examine the effects of scaling data, model size, and compute. They derive scaling laws that reliably predict final performance as these resources increase.

The authors find that larger models can improve automatic speech recognition for both low-resource and high-resource languages. They also report emergent abilities in large speech models, illustrating the suite's usefulness for further research. The contribution combines a broad experimental platform with predictive relationships for scaling, offering evidence that increased model scale can benefit multilingual speech technologies across different levels of language data availability.
summary.tldr: OWLS studies multilingual speech scaling with models up to 18 billion parameters, deriving predictive laws and finding benefits across language resource levels.

title: OWLS: Scaling Laws for Multilingual Speech Recognition and Translation Models

abstract: Bilevel optimization is a powerful tool for many machine learning problems, such as hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning. Estimating hypergradients (also known as implicit gradients) is crucial for developing gradient-based methods for bilevel optimization. In this work, we propose a computationally efficient technique for incorporating curvature information into the approximation of hypergradients and present a novel algorithmic framework based on the resulting enhanced hypergradient computation. We provide convergence rate guarantees for the proposed framework in both deterministic and stochastic scenarios, particularly showing improved computational complexity over popular gradient-based methods in the deterministic setting. This improvement in complexity arises from a careful exploitation of the hypergradient structure and the inexact Newton method. In addition to the theoretical speedup, numerical experiments demonstrate the significant practical performance benefits of incorporating curvature information.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves an optimization problem whose outcome depends on another optimization problem. It appears in applications such as choosing hyperparameters and meta-learning. Gradient-based approaches need hypergradients, which describe how the outer objective changes through the inner problem. Computing useful approximations to these quantities is therefore central to making such approaches efficient.

This paper proposes an efficient way to incorporate curvature information into hypergradient approximation. Curvature describes how gradients change, providing information beyond a local direction of improvement. The authors build an algorithmic framework around the enhanced approximation, carefully exploiting hypergradient structure together with an inexact Newton method to reduce the computational effort required.

The framework comes with convergence-rate guarantees in both deterministic and stochastic settings. The stated improvement in computational complexity over popular gradient-based methods applies specifically to the deterministic setting. Numerical experiments also demonstrate substantial practical benefits from including curvature. Together, these results support using additional local information when it can be incorporated economically into the hypergradient computation.
summary.tldr: An efficient curvature-aware hypergradient approximation improves deterministic bilevel optimization complexity and delivers practical benefits in numerical experiments.

title: Efficient Curvature-Aware Hypergradient Approximation for Bilevel Optimization

abstract: Despite recent advancements of fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) to facilitate agent tasks, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methodologies for agent remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce three key strategies for PEFT in agent tasks: 1) Inspired by the increasingly dominant Reason+Action paradigm, we first decompose the capabilities necessary for the agent tasks into three distinct roles: reasoner, executor, and summarizer. The reasoner is responsible for comprehending the user’s query and determining the next role based on the execution trajectory. The executor is tasked with identifying the appropriate functions and parameters to invoke. The summarizer conveys the distilled information from conversations back to the user. 2) We then propose the Mixture-of-Roles (MoR) framework, which comprises three specialized Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) groups, each designated to fulfill a distinct role. By focusing on their respective specialized capabilities and engaging in collaborative interactions, these LoRAs collectively accomplish the agent task. 3) To effectively fine-tune the framework, we develop a multi-role data generation pipeline based on publicly available datasets, incorporating role-specific content completion and reliability verification. We conduct extensive experiments and thorough ablation studies on various LLMs and agent benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method. This project is publicly available at https://mor-agent.github.io

paragraphs: An LLM agent must understand a request, choose actions, invoke functions correctly, and communicate the result. MoRAgent organizes these capabilities into three roles to study parameter-efficient agent tuning. The approach treats role specialization as a way to structure adaptation, with distinct components learning different parts of the overall workflow.

The reasoner interprets the user's query and selects the next role using the execution history. The executor chooses functions and their arguments. The summarizer turns information from the interaction into a response for the user. The Mixture-of-Roles framework assigns a specialized Low-Rank Adaptation group to each role, and the groups collaborate to complete agent tasks.

To train this framework, the authors build a data-generation pipeline from publicly available datasets. It fills in role-specific content and verifies reliability, aligning the training material with the division of responsibilities. Experiments and ablation studies across multiple language models and agent benchmarks demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution combines a structured adaptation architecture with a corresponding way to generate training data.
summary.tldr: MoRAgent uses specialized LoRA groups for reasoning, execution, and summarization, supported by a role-specific training-data pipeline.

title: MoRAgent: Parameter Efficient Agent Tuning with Mixture-of-Roles

abstract: Large Video Models (LVMs) built upon Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in video understanding but often suffer from misalignment with human intuition and video hallucination issues. To address these challenges, we introduce VistaDPO, a novel framework for Video Hierarchical Spatial-Temporal Direct Preference Optimization. VistaDPO enhances text-video preference alignment across three hierarchical levels: i) Instance Level, aligning overall video content with responses; ii) Temporal Level, aligning video temporal semantics with event descriptions; and iii) Perceptive Level, aligning spatial objects with language tokens. Given the lack of datasets for fine-grained video-language preference alignment, we construct VistaDPO-7k, a dataset of 7.2K QA pairs annotated with chosen and rejected responses, along with spatial-temporal grounding information such as timestamps, keyframes, and bounding boxes. Extensive experiments on benchmarks such as Video Hallucination, Video QA, and Captioning performance tasks demonstrate that VistaDPO significantly improves the performance of existing LVMs, effectively mitigating video-language misalignment and hallucination.

paragraphs: Large video models can produce descriptions that conflict with the video or with human judgments about its content. VistaDPO addresses these alignment and hallucination problems through preference optimization at several levels. The method treats agreement with a video as more than a single judgment about whether an entire response sounds appropriate.

At the instance level, it aligns responses with overall video content. At the temporal level, it connects event descriptions to the video’s temporal meaning. At the perceptive level, it aligns language tokens with spatial objects. To support these distinctions, the authors create VistaDPO-7k: 7.2K question-answer pairs with preferred and rejected responses, accompanied by timestamps, keyframes, and bounding boxes.

Experiments on video hallucination, question answering, and captioning benchmarks report significant improvements to existing large video models. These results support using detailed spatial and temporal grounding within preference training to reduce video-language mismatches. The contribution includes both a hierarchical training framework and the annotated data needed to express preferences at those finer levels.
summary.tldr: VistaDPO combines video-level, temporal, and object-level preference alignment to improve video understanding and reduce hallucinations.

title: $\mathcalVista\mathcalDPO$: Video Hierarchical Spatial-Temporal Direct Preference Optimization for Large Video Models

abstract: Visual deep reinforcement learning (RL) enables robots to acquire skills from visual input for unstructured tasks. However, current algorithms suffer from low sample efficiency, limiting their practical applicability. In this work, we present MENTOR, a method that improves both the architecture and optimization of RL agents. Specifically, MENTOR replaces the standard multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with a mixture-of-experts (MoE) backbone and introduces a task-oriented perturbation mechanism. MENTOR outperforms state-of-the-art methods across three simulation benchmarks and achieves an average of 83% success rate on three challenging real-world robotic manipulation tasks, significantly surpassing the 32% success rate of the strongest existing model-free visual RL algorithm. These results underscore the importance of sample efficiency in advancing visual RL for real-world robotics. Experimental videos are available at https://suninghuang19.github.io/mentor_page/.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement learning lets robots acquire skills from images, but learning can require too much experience to be practical. MENTOR addresses this sample-efficiency problem by changing both the agent’s network architecture and its optimization. The aim is to make visual learning more effective for robotic tasks in unstructured settings.

Architecturally, MENTOR replaces a standard multilayer perceptron with a mixture-of-experts backbone, organizing the network around multiple expert components. It also introduces a task-oriented perturbation mechanism as part of the learning approach. These two changes address how the agent represents its decision process and how that process is optimized during training.

MENTOR outperforms state-of-the-art methods on three simulation benchmarks. Across three challenging real-world manipulation tasks, it reaches an average success rate of 83%, compared with 32% for the strongest existing model-free visual reinforcement-learning algorithm in the comparison. The results provide evidence that the combined architecture and optimization approach can improve practical robotic performance, alongside the paper’s broader focus on making better use of learning experience.
summary.tldr: MENTOR combines a mixture-of-experts backbone with task-oriented perturbation to improve visual reinforcement learning and real-world robotic manipulation.

title: MENTOR: Mixture-of-Experts Network with Task-Oriented Perturbation for Visual Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The remarkable generalization performance of contrastive vision-language models like CLIP is often attributed to the diversity of their training distributions. However, key questions remain unanswered: Can CLIP generalize to an entirely unseen domain when trained on a diverse mixture of domains (domain generalization)? Can it generalize to unseen classes within partially seen domains (compositional generalization)? What factors affect such generalization? To answer these questions, we trained CLIP models on systematically constructed training distributions with controlled domain diversity and object class exposure. Our experiments show that domain diversity is essential for both domain and compositional generalization, yet compositional generalization can be surprisingly weaker than domain generalization when the training distribution contains a suboptimal subset of the test domain. Through data-centric and mechanistic analyses, we find that successful generalization requires the learning of sufficiently shared representations in intermediate layers and circuits.

Can it generalize to unseen classes within partially seen domains (compositional generalization)? What factors affect such generalization? To answer these questions, we trained CLIP models on systematically constructed training distributions with controlled domain diversity and object class exposure. Our experiments show that domain diversity is essential for both domain and compositional generalization, yet compositional generalization can be surprisingly weaker than domain generalization when the training distribution contains a suboptimal subset of the test domain. Through data-centric and mechanistic analyses, we find that successful generalization requires the learning of sufficiently shared representations in intermediate layers and circuits.

paragraphs: CLIP’s ability to generalize is often credited to diverse training data, but diversity alone leaves important questions unresolved. This paper distinguishes transfer to an entirely unseen domain from recognizing unseen classes within a domain that was only partly represented during training. These correspond to domain and compositional generalization.

The authors train CLIP models on deliberately constructed data distributions that control domain diversity and exposure to object classes. In these experiments, domain diversity is essential for both forms of generalization. Yet partial familiarity with a test domain can be associated with surprisingly weaker compositional generalization than transfer to an entirely unseen domain when the observed subset is suboptimal.

Data-focused and mechanistic analyses connect successful generalization to sufficiently shared representations in intermediate layers and circuits. This provides an internal explanation alongside the training-data findings. The study indicates that assessing generalization requires attention to which combinations of domains and classes the model sees, as well as whether its internal representations capture information shared across them.
summary.tldr: Controlled CLIP experiments link generalization to domain diversity and shared internal representations, while showing that partial domain exposure can be problematic.

title: When and How Does CLIP Enable Domain and Compositional Generalization?

abstract: Text classification is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Short text classification has recently captured much attention due to its increased amount from various sources with limited labels and its inherent challenges for its sparsity in words and semantics. Recent studies have adopted self-supervised contrastive learning across different representations to improve performance. However, most of the current models face several challenges. Firstly, the augmentation step might not be able to generate positive and negative samples that are semantically similar and dissimilar to the anchor respectively. Secondly, the text data could be enhanced with external auxiliary information that might introduce noise to the sparse text data. In addition, they are limited in capturing higher-order information such as group-wise interactions. In this work, we propose a novel document simplicial complex construction based on text data for a higher-order message-passing mechanism. We enhance the short text classification performance by contrasting the structural representation with the sequential representation generated by the transformer mechanism for improved outcomes and mitigated issues. The proposed framework, Contrastive Learning with Simplicial Convolutional Networks (C-SCN), leverages the expressive power of graph neural networks, models higher-order information beyond pair-wise relations and enriches features through contrastive learning. Experimental results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the capability of C-SCN to outperform existing models in analysing sequential and complex short-text data.

Short text classification has recently captured much attention due to its increased amount from various sources with limited labels and its inherent challenges for its sparsity in words and semantics. Recent studies have adopted self-supervised contrastive learning across different representations to improve performance. However, most of the current models face several challenges. Firstly, the augmentation step might not be able to generate positive and negative samples that are semantically similar and dissimilar to the anchor respectively. Secondly, the text data could be enhanced with external auxiliary information that might introduce noise to the sparse text data. In addition, they are limited in capturing higher-order information such as group-wise interactions. In this work, we propose a novel document simplicial complex construction based on text data for a higher-order message-passing mechanism. We enhance the short text classification performance by contrasting the structural representation with the sequential representation generated by the transformer mechanism for improved outcomes and mitigated issues. The proposed framework, Contrastive Learning with Simplicial Convolutional Networks (C-SCN), leverages the expressive power of graph neural networks, models higher-order information beyond pair-wise relations and enriches features through contrastive learning. Experimental results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the capability of C-SCN to outperform existing models in analysing sequential and complex short-text data.

paragraphs: Short texts provide few words and limited semantic context, making classification difficult when labels are scarce. Contrastive learning can enrich their representations, but text augmentation may create unsuitable comparison examples. External information can also introduce noise, while ordinary pairwise relationships miss interactions involving groups of elements.

C-SCN constructs a document simplicial complex directly from text to support higher-order message passing. This representation allows the model to capture group-wise relationships beyond pairs. The framework contrasts that structural representation with a sequential representation produced through a transformer mechanism, combining information about relational structure with information about the text sequence.

The two representations give contrastive learning complementary descriptions of the same text, enriching features while addressing the identified representation problems. Experiments on four benchmark datasets show that C-SCN outperforms the existing models evaluated by the authors. The findings support using higher-order structure alongside sequential modeling for short-text classification, where sparse wording makes the quality of the learned representation particularly consequential.
summary.tldr: C-SCN improves short-text classification by contrasting transformer sequence features with structural features that capture group-wise interactions.

title: Contrastive Learning with Simplicial Convolutional Networks for Short-Text Classification

abstract: The complexity of code reviews has driven efforts to automate review comments, but prior approaches oversimplify this task by treating it as snippet-level code-to-text generation and relying on text similarity metrics like BLEU for evaluation. These methods overlook repository context, real-world merge request evaluation, and defect detection, limiting their practicality. To address these issues, we explore the full automation pipeline within the online recommendation service of a company with nearly 400 million daily active users, analyzing industry-grade C++ codebases comprising hundreds of thousands of lines of code. We identify four key challenges: 1) capturing relevant context, 2) improving key bug inclusion (KBI), 3) reducing false alarm rates (FAR), and 4) integrating human workflows. To tackle these, we propose 1) code slicing algorithms for context extraction, 2) a multi-role LLM framework for KBI, 3) a filtering mechanism for FAR reduction, and 4) a novel prompt design for better human interaction. Our approach, validated on real-world merge requests from historical fault reports, achieves a 2$\times$ improvement over standard LLMs and a 10$\times$ gain over previous baselines. While the presented results focus on C++, the underlying framework design leverages language-agnostic principles (e.g., AST-based analysis), suggesting potential for broader applicability.

Code slicing extracts relevant context, a multi-role language-model framework improves inclusion of key bugs, a filtering mechanism reduces false alarms, and a prompt design supports interaction with human reviewers. These components connect technical defect detection with the practical conditions under which review comments are consumed.

The presented results concern C++. The framework also uses language-agnostic principles, including abstract-syntax-tree-based analysis, which the authors identify as a reason it could apply more broadly. That broader applicability remains a stated possibility.
summary.tldr: A repository-aware review pipeline combines context extraction, multi-role models, filtering, and human interaction to improve industrial C++ defect review.

title: Towards Practical Defect-Focused Automated Code Review

abstract: Communication between multiple language model (LM) agents has been shown to scale up the reasoning ability of LMs. While natural language has been the dominant medium for inter-LM communication, it is not obvious this should be the standard: not only does natural language communication incur high inference costs that scale quickly with the number of both agents and messages, but also the decoding process abstracts away too much rich information that could be otherwise accessed from the internal activations. In this work, we propose a simple technique whereby LMs communicate via activations; concretely, we pause an LM $B$’s computation at an intermediate layer, combine its current activation with another LM $A$’s intermediate activation via some function $f$, then pass $f$’s output into the next layer of $B$ and continue the forward pass till decoding is complete. This approach scales up LMs on new tasks with zero additional parameters and data, and saves a substantial amount of compute over natural language communication. We test our method with various functional forms $f$ on two experimental setups—multi-player coordination games and reasoning benchmarks—and find that it achieves up to $27$% improvement over natural language communication across datasets with $<$$1/4$ the compute, illustrating the superiority and robustness of activations as an alternative "language" for communication between LMs.

paragraphs: Language model agents usually communicate by generating text for one another to read. This adds inference costs as agents and messages multiply, and converting internal representations into words can discard useful information. The paper investigates whether agents can communicate more efficiently by sharing intermediate activations directly.

The proposed operation is simple: pause one model at an intermediate layer, combine its activation with an intermediate activation from another model, and feed the combined result into the receiving model’s next layer. Computation then continues through decoding. The authors test several choices of the combining function. Their approach requires no additional parameters or data to apply this communication mechanism on new tasks.

Experiments cover multiplayer coordination games and reasoning benchmarks. The authors report improvements of up to 27% over natural-language communication across datasets, using less than one-quarter of the compute. These results support internal activations as a useful communication medium in the tested setups: agents can exchange information without paying the full cost of expressing and processing every message as text.
summary.tldr: Sharing intermediate activations lets language model agents communicate with no added parameters or data and improves performance and compute efficiency in tested tasks.

title: Communicating Activations Between Language Model Agents

abstract: We study the policy evaluation problem in an online multi-reward multi-policy discounted setting, where multiple reward functions must be evaluated simultaneously for different policies. We adopt an $(\epsilon,\delta)$-PAC perspective to achieve $\epsilon$-accurate estimates with high confidence over finite or convex sets of rewards, a setting that has not been systematically studied in the literature. Building on prior work on Multi-Reward Best Policy Identification, we adapt the MR-NaS exploration scheme to jointly minimize sample complexity for evaluating different policies across different reward sets. Our approach leverages an instance-specific lower bound revealing how the sample complexity scales with a measure of value deviation, guiding the design of an efficient exploration policy. Although computing this bound entails a hard non-convex optimization, we propose an efficient convex approximation that holds for both finite and convex reward sets. Experiments in tabular domains demonstrate the effectiveness of this adaptive exploration scheme. Code repository: https://github.com/rssalessio/multi-reward-multi-policy-eval.

paragraphs: Evaluating a policy means estimating how well it performs, but this paper considers many policies and many reward functions at once. In an online discounted setting, the learner must decide which experience to collect so that all the required evaluations are accurate. The target is a specified error tolerance with high confidence, covering finite or convex reward sets.

The authors adapt the MR-NaS exploration scheme to coordinate data collection across these evaluation requirements. Their design draws on an instance-specific lower bound that connects the required sample count to a measure of value deviation. This gives exploration a problem-dependent target instead of treating every policy and reward combination as equally demanding.

Directly computing the bound requires solving a difficult non-convex optimization problem. The paper supplies an efficient convex approximation applicable to both supported types of reward sets. Experiments in tabular domains demonstrate the effectiveness of the adaptive scheme. Together, the analysis and approximation connect a theoretical description of evaluation difficulty to a usable strategy for collecting data.
summary.tldr: Adaptive exploration coordinates data collection to evaluate multiple policies across reward sets accurately and with high confidence.

title: Adaptive Exploration for Multi-Reward Multi-Policy Evaluation

abstract: We introduce the tokenized linear bandit (TLB) and multi-armed bandit (TMAB), variants of linear and stochastic multi-armed bandit problems inspired by LLM decoding and alignment. In these problems, at each round $t \in [T]$, a user submits a query (context), and the decision maker (DM) sequentially selects a token irrevocably from a token set. Once the sequence is complete, the DM observes a random utility from the user, whose expectation is presented by a sequence function mapping the chosen token sequence to a nonnegative real value that depends on the query. In both problems, we first show that learning is impossible without any structure on the sequence function. We introduce a natural assumption, diminishing distance with more commons (DDMC), and propose algorithms with regret $\tilde{O}(L\sqrt{T})$ and $\tilde{O}(L\sqrt{T^{2/3}})$ for TLB and TMAB, respectively. As a side product, we obtain an (almost) optimality of the greedy decoding for LLM decoding algorithm under DDMC, which justifies the unresaonable effectiveness of greedy decoding in several tasks. This also has an immediate application to decoding-time LLM alignment, when the misaligned utility can be represented as the frozen LLM’s utility and a linearly realizable latent function. We finally validate our algorithm’s performance empirically as well as verify our assumptions using synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: The paper models language-model decoding and alignment as tokenized bandit problems. For each user query, a decision maker builds a sequence one irreversible token choice at a time. Feedback arrives only after the sequence is complete, as a random user utility whose expected value depends on both the sequence and the query.

The authors first show that learning is impossible when the sequence utility has no structure. They introduce an assumption called diminishing distance with more commons, or DDMC, and derive regret bounds for tokenized linear and multi-armed bandit algorithms under that assumption. DDMC also yields an almost-optimality result for greedy decoding, providing a conditional explanation for why simple token-by-token choices can work well.

The framework additionally applies to decoding-time alignment when the misaligned utility can be expressed through a frozen model's utility and a linearly realizable latent function. Synthetic and real-world experiments evaluate algorithm performance and examine the assumptions. The central contribution is to connect sequential token decisions with learnable reward structure, while making explicit the conditions behind the guarantees.
summary.tldr: Tokenized bandit models provide learning guarantees and an almost-optimality result for greedy decoding under the DDMC structural assumption.

title: Tokenized Bandit for LLM Decoding and Alignment

abstract: The recent rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) highlights the critical need for benchmarking their fairness. Conventional fairness metrics, which focus on discrete accuracy-based evaluations (i.e., prediction correctness), fail to capture the implicit impact of model uncertainty (e.g., higher model confidence about one group over another despite similar accuracy). To address this limitation, we propose an uncertainty-aware fairness metric, UCerf, to enable a fine-grained evaluation of model fairness that is more reflective of the internal bias in model decisions. Furthermore, observing data size, diversity, and clarity issues in current datasets, we introduce a new gender-occupation fairness evaluation dataset with 31,756 samples for co-reference resolution, offering a more diverse and suitable benchmark for modern LLMs. Combining our metric and dataset, we provide insightful comparisons of eight open-source LLMs. For example, Mistral-8B exhibits suboptimal fairness due to high confidence in incorrect predictions, a detail overlooked by Equalized Odds but captured by UCerF. Overall, this work provides a holistic framework for LLM evaluation by jointly assessing fairness and uncertainty, enabling the development of more transparent and accountable AI systems.

paragraphs: This paper examines fairness differences that correctness-based evaluation can miss. Two groups may receive similarly accurate predictions even when a language model is systematically more confident about one group. The authors argue that assessing uncertainty alongside accuracy provides a finer-grained view of bias in model decisions.

They introduce UCerf, an uncertainty-aware fairness metric, and a dataset focused on gender and occupation in co-reference resolution. The dataset contains 31,756 examples and is designed to address shortcomings in the size, diversity, and clarity of existing evaluation data. Together, the metric and dataset support comparisons that account for how certain a model is about its answers.

The evaluation covers eight open-source language models. One reported example is Mistral-8B, whose high confidence in incorrect predictions produces a fairness concern detected by UCerf but overlooked by Equalized Odds. This illustrates the paper’s central contribution: uncertainty can reveal disparities that are hidden when evaluation records only whether each answer is correct.
summary.tldr: UCerf combines uncertainty with fairness evaluation to expose disparities that correctness-based metrics can overlook.

title: Is Your Model Fairly Certain? Uncertainty-Aware Fairness Evaluation for LLMs

abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) to align with user preferences is challenging due to the high cost of quality human annotations in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and the generalizability limitations of AI Feedback. To address these challenges, we propose RLTHF, a human-AI hybrid framework that combines LLM-based initial alignment with selective human annotations to achieve full-human annotation alignment with minimal effort. RLTHF identifies hard-to-annotate samples mislabeled by LLMs using a reward model’s reward distribution and iteratively enhances alignment by integrating strategic human corrections while leveraging LLM’s correctly labeled samples. Evaluations on HH-RLHF and TL;DR datasets show that RLTHF reaches full-human annotation-level alignment with only 6-7% of the human annotation effort. Furthermore, models trained on RLTHF’s curated datasets for downstream tasks outperform those trained on fully human-annotated datasets, underscoring the effectiveness of RLTHF.

paragraphs: RLTHF aims to reduce the human effort required to align language models with user preferences. Human annotations are expensive, while AI-generated feedback has generalization limitations. The framework combines an initial round of language-model-based alignment with selective human corrections, concentrating annotation effort on examples where automated judgments go wrong.

The method uses a reward model’s reward distribution to identify difficult examples mislabeled by language models. It then iteratively incorporates targeted human corrections while continuing to use samples the language model labeled correctly. This makes the selection of examples for human review a central part of the alignment process.

On HH-RLHF and TL;DR, the authors report reaching alignment comparable to full human annotation with only 6–7% of the human annotation effort. Models trained on the curated datasets also outperform models trained on fully human-annotated datasets in the reported downstream evaluations. These findings suggest that strategically correcting automated feedback can make a small human annotation budget especially useful.
summary.tldr: RLTHF targets human corrections at difficult AI-labeled examples, matching full-human alignment with 6–7% of the annotation effort in reported evaluations.

title: RLTHF: Targeted Human Feedback for LLM Alignment

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have expanded their capabilities beyond language generation to interact with external tools, enabling automation and real-world applications. However, tool hallucinations—where models either select inappropriate tools or misuse them—pose significant challenges, leading to erroneous task execution, increased computational costs, and reduced system reliability. To systematically address this issue, we define and categorize tool hallucinations into two main types: tool selection hallucination and tool usage hallucination. To evaluate and mitigate these issues, we introduce RelyToolBench, which integrates specialized test cases and novel metrics to assess hallucination-aware task success and efficiency. Finally, we propose Relign, a reliability alignment framework that expands the tool-use action space to include indecisive actions, allowing LLMs to defer tool use, seek clarification, or adjust tool selection dynamically. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that Relign significantly reduces tool hallucinations, improves task reliability, and enhances the efficiency of LLM tool interactions. The code and data will be publicly available.

paragraphs: Language models can fail when interacting with tools by choosing an inappropriate tool or using a tool incorrectly. The paper distinguishes these as tool selection hallucinations and tool usage hallucinations. Both can produce incorrect task execution, consume extra computation, and make tool-based systems less reliable.

To measure these problems, the authors introduce RelyToolBench, with specialized test cases and metrics covering hallucination-aware task success and efficiency. They also propose Relign, a reliability alignment framework that expands the actions available to the model. Alongside tool use, the model can defer action, request clarification, or revise its tool selection as the situation develops.

This broader action space gives the model explicit ways to respond when immediate tool use is inappropriate or uncertain. Extensive experiments report significant reductions in tool hallucinations, improvements in task reliability, and more efficient tool interactions. The contribution combines a clearer evaluation framework with a training approach that makes hesitation and reconsideration part of the model's available behavior.
summary.tldr: Relign reduces tool hallucinations by teaching models to defer, clarify, or reconsider tool choices, evaluated through RelyToolBench.

title: Reducing Tool Hallucination via Reliability Alignment

abstract: This position paper critiques the reliance on rigid racial taxonomies in machine learning, exposing their U.S.-centric nature and lack of global applicability—particularly in Europe, where race categories are not commonly used. These classifications oversimplify racial identity, erasing the experiences of mixed-race individuals and reinforcing outdated essentialist views that contradict the social construction of race. We suggest research agendas in machine learning that move beyond categorical variables to better address discrimination and social inequality.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges the use of fixed racial categories in machine learning. Its central concern is that such categories embed assumptions about identity that do not travel reliably across societies. The authors describe prevailing taxonomies as centered on the United States and question their global applicability, highlighting Europe as a setting where race categories are not commonly used.

The critique also concerns what categorical representations leave out. Rigid groupings can oversimplify identity and erase mixed-race experiences. The authors argue that they can reinforce essentialist ideas about race that conflict with understanding race as socially constructed. The choice of categories therefore carries substantive assumptions about the people being represented.

The paper calls for research agendas that move beyond categorical variables when addressing discrimination and social inequality. Its contribution is a challenge to the framing of these problems, asking researchers to reconsider how racial identity is represented in the first place. The proposed direction keeps discrimination and inequality as research concerns while questioning whether fixed taxonomies adequately express them.
summary.tldr: The paper critiques rigid, U.S.-centered racial categories in machine learning and calls for approaches beyond categorical variables to study discrimination.

title: Position: The Categorization of Race in ML is a Flawed Premise

abstract: Complex tables with multi-level headers, merged cells and heterogeneous layouts pose persistent challenges for large language models (LLMs) in both understanding and reasoning. Existing approaches typically rely on table linearization or normalized grid modeling. However, these representations struggle to explicitly capture hierarchical structures and cross-dimensional dependencies, which can lead to misalignment between structural semantics and textual representations for non-standard tables. To address this issue, we propose an Orthogonal Hierarchical Decomposition (OHD) framework that constructs structure-preserving input representations of complex tables for LLMs. OHD introduces an Orthogonal Tree Induction (OTI) method based on spatial–semantic co-constraints, which decomposes irregular tables into a column tree and a row tree to capture vertical and horizontal hierarchical dependencies, respectively. Building on this representation, we design a dual-pathway association protocol to symmetrically reconstruct the semantic lineage of each cell, and incorporate an LLM as a semantic arbitrator to align multi-level semantic information. We evaluate OHD framework on two complex table question answering benchmarks, AITQA and HiTab. Experimental results show that OHD consistently outperforms existing representation paradigms across multiple evaluation metrics.

paragraphs: The meaning of a table cell can depend on several nested headers, merged cells, and relationships in both row and column directions. Flattening such a table into text or forcing it into a normalized grid can obscure those relationships. Orthogonal Hierarchical Decomposition builds an input representation intended to preserve them for language-model reasoning.

Its Orthogonal Tree Induction method uses spatial and semantic constraints to produce two trees: one for column hierarchies and one for row hierarchies. A dual-pathway association protocol then reconstructs each cell’s semantic lineage through both directions. An LLM acts as a semantic arbitrator to align information across levels, helping connect a cell’s content to the nested categories that give it meaning.

The framework is evaluated on the AITQA and HiTab complex-table question-answering benchmarks, where it consistently outperforms existing representation approaches across multiple metrics. These results support explicitly representing a table’s hierarchy before asking a model to reason over it. The central contribution is a structured account of how a cell inherits meaning from both dimensions of an irregular table.
summary.tldr: OHD represents complex tables through complementary row and column trees to preserve the hierarchical meaning needed for question answering.

title: Orthogonal Hierarchical Decomposition for Structure-Aware Table Understanding with Large Language Models

abstract: We consider minimizing an objective function subject to constraints defined by the intersection of lower-level sets of convex functions. We study two cases: (i) strongly convex and Lipschitz-smooth objective function and (ii) convex but possibly nonsmooth objective function. To deal with the constraints that are not easy to project on, we use a randomized feasibility algorithm with Polyak steps and a random number of sampled constraints per iteration, while taking (sub)gradient steps to minimize the objective function. For case (i), we prove linear convergence in expectation of the objective function values to any prescribed tolerance using an adaptive stepsize. For case (ii), we develop a fully problem parameter-free and adaptive stepsize scheme that yields an $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ worst-case rate in expectation. The infeasibility of the iterates decreases geometrically with the number of feasibility updates almost surely, while for the averaged iterates, we establish an expected lower bound on the function values relative to the optimal value that depends on the distribution for the random number of sampled constraints. For certain choices of sample-size growth, optimal rates are achieved. Finally, simulations on a Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Programming (QCQP) problem, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and logistic regression with group fairness constraints demonstrate the computational efficiency of our algorithm compared to other state-of-the-art methods.
