paragraphs: Constrained optimization can become expensive when projecting onto the full feasible region is difficult. This paper studies feasible regions defined by intersecting lower-level sets of convex functions. Its algorithm combines objective-reducing gradient or subgradient steps with randomized feasibility updates, sampling a random number of constraints per iteration and using Polyak steps.

The guarantees depend on the objective. For strongly convex objectives with Lipschitz-smooth gradients, an adaptive step size gives linear convergence in expectation to any prescribed tolerance. For convex objectives that may be nonsmooth, a fully parameter-free adaptive scheme achieves an expected worst-case rate proportional to one over the square root of the iteration count.

Constraint violation decreases geometrically with the number of feasibility updates almost surely. The analysis also connects bounds for averaged iterates to the distribution governing how many constraints are sampled, with optimal rates under certain sample-size growth choices. Simulations involving quadratic constraints, support vector machines, and fairness-constrained logistic regression demonstrate computational efficiency relative to existing methods.
summary.tldr: Adaptive optimization with randomized constraint updates provides convergence guarantees without requiring easy projection onto the full feasible region.

title: Randomized Feasibility Methods for Constrained Optimization with Adaptive Step Sizes

abstract: Flow-matching policies have recently emerged as a powerful class of generative models for offline reinforcement learning (RL), capable of capturing complex, multi-modal action distributions from static datasets. However, standard training objectives are largely agnostic to the global properties of the generative path, permitting learned vector fields that are irregular and unstable, which can hinder performance. In this work, we introduce PDE-regularized Q-Learning (PQL), a novel algorithm that addresses this limitation by imposing a principled structure on the entire probability flow. PQL makes two synergistic contributions: first, a partial differential equation based regularizer derived from the continuity equation promotes global smoothness and stability on the flow. Second, to solve the complex optimization problem introduced by this regularizer, we propose a Beta-distributed timestep sampling strategy that focuses learning on the critical trajectory segments where the trade-off between imitation and smoothness is most acute. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that by structuring the generative journey and not just its destination, PQL achieves state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of challenging offline RL tasks.

title: Continuity-Regularized Flow Matching for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Instruction tuning for speech language models (SLMs) is substantially more challenging than for text-based large language models (LLMs), as it requires learning a new modality and a wide range of speech-specific instructions in addition to those supported by text LLMs. Existing SLM training approaches largely replicate the text LLM training paradigm by synthesizing large-scale speech pre-training and instruction-tuning datasets. However, this strategy is difficult to scale, since speech sequences are significantly longer than text sequences. In this paper, we propose SpeechCombine, an instruction-following speech language model trained without any instruction tuning, using only a single round of speech pre-training on as little as 30k hours of speech data. Starting from a text LLM base model, we perform continuous pre-training on speech utterances to obtain a speech-adapted model, and then directly combine its weights with the weight difference between the instruction-tuned and base versions of the text LLM. Our results show that this simple combination strategy not only preserves the knowledge and capabilities of the original text LLM, but also effectively transfers them to the speech domain. These findings suggest a new direction for SLM training that avoids reliance on massive volumes of speech data.

The method starts with a base text language model and continuously pretrains it on speech utterances. The findings suggest that modality adaptation and instruction-following changes can be combined successfully through this weight-based procedure. This offers a direction for speech-model training that reduces reliance on massive speech datasets.
summary.tldr: SpeechCombine transfers text-model instruction-following changes into a speech-adapted model through weight combination, without speech instruction tuning.

title: Unlocking Speech–Text Compositional Powers: Instruction-Following Speech Language Models without Instruction Tuning

abstract: Sequence models typically operate at a fixed temporal or spatial scale and struggle to generalize to substantially longer horizons or higher resolutions without retraining. Existing hierarchical architectures expand receptive fields but rely on scale-specific parameters and lack mechanisms to enforce consistent dynamics across scales. We propose Dynamic Fractal Mamba (DF-Mamba), a recursive state-space model that applies a single shared operator across multiple scales. By sharing parameters across recursion depths and exponentially scaling the effective time step, DF-Mamba achieves an exponentially expanding receptive field while preserving linear computational complexity. A learned content-aware coarse-graining module aggregates representations across scales. Auxiliary reconstruction and cross-scale consistency objectives stabilize recursive training. We evaluate DF-Mamba on long-range time-series forecasting, spatial transcriptomics, and computational pathology. Across all tasks, DF-Mamba consistently outperforms Transformers and flat Mamba baselines while using fewer parameters and maintaining linear-time scalability. Importantly, models trained on short sequences or low-resolution inputs generalize in a zero-shot manner to substantially larger temporal and spatial scales unseen during training. These results demonstrate that recursive parameter sharing provides an effective inductive bias for learning scale-consistent and efficient sequence representations.

paragraphs: Sequence models often learn dynamics at the temporal or spatial scale seen during training, making much longer sequences or higher-resolution inputs difficult to handle. Dynamic Fractal Mamba addresses this by recursively applying one shared state-space operator across multiple scales. The same parameters govern each recursion depth, encouraging related behavior as the scale changes.

The model increases its effective time step exponentially across scales. This expands the receptive field exponentially while retaining linear computational complexity. A learned, content-aware coarse-graining module aggregates representations across scales, while reconstruction and cross-scale consistency objectives help stabilize recursive training. Together, these components combine broad coverage with explicit pressure for coherent representations at different resolutions.

Across these tasks, the model outperforms Transformer and flat Mamba baselines while using fewer parameters. Models trained on short sequences or low-resolution inputs also generalize without additional training to substantially larger unseen scales. The findings support recursive parameter sharing as an effective architectural bias for efficient, scale-consistent representations in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: DF-Mamba shares a recursive state-space operator across scales, enabling efficient modeling and zero-shot generalization to larger temporal and spatial inputs.

title: Dynamic Fractal Mamba: A Neural Renormalization Group Flow for Scale-Invariant Sequence Modeling

abstract: Jailbreak attacks on audio language models (ALMs) optimize audio perturbations to elicit unsafe generations, and they typically update the entire waveform densely throughout optimization. In this work, we investigate the necessity of such dense optimization by analyzing the structure of token-aligned gradients in ALMs. We find that gradient energy is highly non-uniform across audio tokens, indicating that only a small subset of token-aligned audio regions dominates the optimization signal. Motivated by this observation, we propose Token-Aware Gradient Optimization (TAGO), which enables sparse jailbreak optimization by retaining only waveform gradients aligned with audio tokens that have high gradient energy, while masking the remaining gradients at each iteration. Across three ALMs, TAGO outperforms baselines, and substantial sparsification preserves strong attack success rates (e.g., on Qwen3-Omni, $\mathrm{ASR}_{l}$ remains at 86% with a token retention ratio of 0.25, compared to 87% with full token retention). These results demonstrate that dense waveform updates are largely redundant, and we advocate that future audio jailbreak and safety alignment research should further leverage this heterogeneous token-level gradient structure.

paragraphs: Audio jailbreak research often optimizes perturbations across an entire waveform to induce unsafe model responses. This paper asks whether such dense updates are necessary. By examining gradients aligned with audio tokens, the authors find that optimization signal is distributed unevenly: a small subset of token-associated audio regions carries much of the gradient energy.

Token-Aware Gradient Optimization, or TAGO, incorporates that observation into sparse optimization. At each iteration, it retains waveform gradients associated with high-energy audio tokens and masks the others. The method therefore concentrates updates on the regions identified as carrying the strongest optimization signal, directly testing how much of the dense update process is redundant.

Across three audio language models, TAGO outperforms the evaluated baselines while preserving strong attack success under substantial sparsification. In the Qwen3-Omni example, the reported ASR_l is 86% with one-quarter of tokens retained, compared with 87% under full retention. These findings show that dense waveform updates are largely redundant in the evaluated attacks and motivate attention to token-level gradient heterogeneity in both attack research and safety alignment.
summary.tldr: TAGO shows that updating a small subset of high-gradient audio regions can preserve strong jailbreak success across evaluated audio language models.

title: Sparse Tokens Suffice: Jailbreaking Audio Language Models via Token-Aware Gradient Optimization

abstract: Discrete audio tokenizers are fundamental to empowering large language models with native audio processing and generation capabilities. Despite recent progress, existing approaches often rely on pretrained encoders, semantic distillation, or heterogeneous CNN-based architectures. These designs introduce fixed inductive biases that limit reconstruction fidelity and hinder effective scaling. In this paper, we argue that discrete audio tokenization should be learned fully end-to-end using a homogeneous and scalable architecture. Based on this perspective, we propose $\textbf{TAC}$, a Transformer-based audio tokenizer that jointly optimizes the encoder, quantizer, and decoder from scratch for high-fidelity reconstruction of general audio. We show that a simple, fully end-to-end learned tokenizer built from homogeneous, causal Transformer blocks scales gracefully and supports high-fidelity reconstruction across diverse audio domains. Across speech, sound, and music, the proposed tokenizer consistently outperforms prior codecs over a wide range of bitrates, while exhibiting predictable improvements with increased scale. Notably, leveraging TAC’s discrete tokens, we develop the first purely autoregressive TTS model that surpasses prior non-autoregressive and cascaded systems. Furthermore, TAC enables competitive ASR performance without auxiliary encoders. Our findings position TAC as a unified, scalable interface for the next generation of native audio foundation models.

paragraphs: Discrete audio tokenizers turn audio into tokens that language models can process and generate. Existing designs often combine pretrained encoders, semantic distillation, or heterogeneous convolutional components. This paper argues that these choices impose fixed biases that constrain reconstruction quality and scaling, and proposes learning the entire tokenizer together from scratch.

TAC uses a homogeneous architecture of causal Transformer blocks. Its encoder, quantizer, and decoder are jointly optimized to reconstruct general audio faithfully. Across speech, environmental sound, and music, the authors report consistent improvements over prior codecs across a broad range of bitrates, with predictable quality gains as the model scales.

The tokens also support downstream audio tasks. The authors build what they report as the first purely autoregressive text-to-speech model to surpass prior non-autoregressive and cascaded systems. TAC additionally enables competitive speech recognition without auxiliary encoders. These results make the contribution broader than audio compression: the same learned discrete interface supports reconstruction, speech generation, and recognition, providing evidence for its usefulness in native audio foundation models.
summary.tldr: TAC learns a scalable Transformer audio tokenizer end to end, improving reconstruction and supporting strong speech generation and recognition.

title: Scaling Transformers for End-to-End Discrete Audio Tokenization

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures scale Large Language Models via expert specialization induced by conditional computation. In practice, however, expert specialization often fails: some experts become functionally similar, while others functioning as de facto shared experts, limiting the effective capacity and model performance. In this work, we analysis from a spectral perspective on parameter and gradient spaces, uncover that (1) experts share highly overlapping dominant spectral components in their parameters, (2) dominant gradient subspaces are strongly aligned across experts, driven by ubiquitous low-rank structure in human corpus, and (3) gating mechanisms preferentially route inputs along these dominant directions, further limiting specialization. To address this, we propose Spectral-Decoupled MoE (SD-MoE), which decomposes both parameter and gradient in the spectral space. SD-MoE improves performance across downstream tasks, enables effective expert specialization, incurring minimal additional computation, and can be seamlessly integrated into a wide range of existing MoE architectures, including Qwen and DeepSeek.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models gain capacity by routing inputs to different experts, but those experts do not always develop distinct functions. Some become similar to one another, while others effectively act as shared experts. This paper examines that failure of specialization through the spectral structure of parameters and training gradients.

The analysis finds substantial overlap in experts’ dominant parameter components and strong alignment between their dominant gradient subspaces. It attributes the latter to common low-rank structure in human text. Routing adds another reinforcing influence by preferentially directing inputs along dominant directions. Together, these effects help explain why conditional computation may still produce redundant expertise.

Spectral-Decoupled MoE addresses the issue by decomposing both parameters and gradients in spectral space. The authors report improved downstream performance and more effective specialization with minimal additional computation. They also describe compatibility with a broad range of MoE architectures, including Qwen and DeepSeek. The contribution connects a diagnosis of shared dominant directions with a method intended to let expert capacity serve more distinct functions.
summary.tldr: SD-MoE decomposes expert parameters and gradients in spectral space to reduce overlapping behavior and improve specialization and downstream performance.

title: SD-MoE: Spectral Decomposition for Effective Expert Specialization

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown strong promise for robotic task planning, particularly through automatic planning domain generation. However, prior approaches largely treat generated planning domains as planning utilities, which are brittle under imperfect logical states and perception noise, overlooking their potential as scalable sources of reasoning supervision and structured reward signals. At the same time, reasoning LLMs depend on chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision that is expensive to collect for robotic tasks, and reinforcement learning (RL) faces challenges on reward engineering. We propose Self-CriTeach, an LLM self-teaching and self-critiquing framework in which an LLM autonomously generates symbolic planning domains that serve a dual role: (i) enabling large-scale generation of robotic planning problem–plan pairs, and (ii) providing structured reward functions. First, the self-written domains enable large-scale generation of symbolic task plans, which are automatically transformed into extended CoT trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. Second, the self-written domains are reused as structured reward functions, providing dense feedback for reinforcement learning without manual reward engineering. This unified training pipeline yields a planning-enhanced LLM with higher planning success rates, stronger cross-task generalization, reduced inference cost, and resistance to imperfect logical states.

paragraphs: Symbolic planning domains describe the rules used to construct robot task plans. This paper gives automatically generated domains a broader role: they become both a source of training examples and a way to evaluate the model’s behavior. The goal is to reduce reliance on expensive reasoning supervision and manually engineered reinforcement learning rewards.

In Self-CriTeach, a language model writes planning domains that support large-scale generation of problem–plan pairs. The symbolic plans are automatically converted into extended reasoning trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. The same domains are then reused to provide structured, dense feedback during reinforcement learning, linking the model’s teaching material to its critique mechanism.

The resulting training pipeline produces a planning-enhanced model with higher planning success, stronger generalization across tasks, reduced inference cost, and resistance to imperfect logical states. These findings give generated symbolic domains value beyond their immediate use in planning. They can supply reusable supervision and reward structure that improve the language model performing the task.
summary.tldr: Self-CriTeach reuses LLM-generated planning domains as both reasoning supervision and structured rewards to improve robotic task planning.

title: Self-CriTeach: LLM Self-Teaching and Self-Critiquing for Improving Robotic Planning via Automated Domain Generation

abstract: Anonymization is often assumed to protect privacy once explicit identifiers are removed, because re-identification has historically required specialized expertise, tailored algorithms, and manual corroboration. We show that LLM-based agents weaken this barrier: by combining scattered, individually non-identifying cues with public evidence, they reconstruct real-world identities, sometimes even during benign tasks. We evaluate this risk across three settings—classical linkage incidents, a controlled benchmark (InferLink) that varies fingerprint type, task framing, and attacker knowledge, and open-ended human–AI interaction traces. In the sparsest regime of the Netflix Prize deanonymization setting, agents reconstruct 79.2% of identities, against 56.0% for a classical matching baseline; on InferLink, they link individuals even without an explicit re-identification request, and more often once one is given. In redacted human–AI interaction traces, agents further resolve anonymized profiles to specific individuals by corroborating contextual cues with public evidence. These findings suggest that privacy evaluations for agentic systems should measure not only what information is accessed or disclosed, but also what identities can be inferred.

paragraphs: Removing names and other explicit identifiers does not necessarily eliminate the information needed to infer someone's identity. This paper studies how LLM agents combine scattered contextual clues with public evidence to reconnect anonymized records to real people. It examines whether agents lower the expertise and manual effort historically associated with this kind of re-identification.

The evaluation covers classical linkage incidents, a controlled benchmark called InferLink, and open-ended human–AI interaction traces. InferLink varies the kinds of identifying patterns available, the task framing, and the agent's prior knowledge. This lets the authors investigate both explicit attempts to identify someone and identity inference that occurs without such a request.

In the sparsest Netflix Prize setting studied, agents reconstruct 79.2% of identities, compared with 56.0% for a classical matching baseline. They also link people in InferLink without explicit re-identification instructions and resolve anonymized profiles in redacted interaction traces. These findings motivate privacy evaluations that assess identities inferable from available information, alongside information access and disclosure.
summary.tldr: LLM agents can combine weak contextual cues with public evidence to identify anonymized people, sometimes even without an explicit re-identification request.

title: From Weak Cues to Real Identities: Evaluating Inference-Driven De-Anonymization in LLM Agents

abstract: As large language models continue to scale, low-bit weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a practical solution to their memory-efficient deployment. Although block-wise PTQ is capable of matching the full-precision (FP) baseline on basic language modeling and understanding, its quality is degraded for generative tasks—especially at longer responses and extended chains of thought, which is critical in boosting task accuracy. We attribute this shortfall to two factors: (i) the omission of the unembedding layer (the LM head) in block-wise optimization and (ii) the reliance on the mean squared error (MSE) objective. Both factors cause the token probability distribution of the quantized model to misalign with that of the FP model, yielding notable accuracy drops on text generation benchmarks. To rectify the discrepancy, we introduce Logit-aware Final-block Quantization (LFQ), a simple yet effective enhancement to block-wise PTQ that quantizes the final Transformer block by minimizing the cross-entropy between the logits of the FP model and those of its quantized counterpart. By aligning token probabilities at the logit level in the final block, LFQ consistently improves the accuracy of complex generation tasks over state-of-the-art block-wise PTQ across diverse model families, while maintaining parity with FP baselines on language modeling and understanding.

paragraphs: Low-bit weight quantization reduces the memory needed to deploy large language models. However, the authors find that block-wise post-training quantization can preserve basic language modeling and understanding while degrading generative tasks, particularly long responses and extended reasoning. They attribute the gap to optimization that omits the output language-model head and relies on mean squared error.

Both choices can leave the quantized model’s token probabilities misaligned with those of the full-precision model. LFQ addresses that mismatch by changing how the final Transformer block is quantized. It uses a cross-entropy objective based on the full-precision and quantized models’ logits, making agreement in output token probabilities the target of the final-block optimization.

Across diverse model families, LFQ consistently improves complex generation accuracy over state-of-the-art block-wise quantization methods while maintaining parity with full precision on language modeling and understanding. The finding highlights the importance of matching the model’s output distribution when preserving generation quality. The reported generation gains are relative to other quantization methods; full-precision parity is stated for the other task categories.
summary.tldr: LFQ improves low-bit LLM generation by aligning final-block output probabilities with those of the full-precision model.

title: LFQ: Logit-aware Final-block Quantization for Boosting the Generation Quality of Low-Bit Quantized LLMs

abstract: Unsupervised skill discovery (USD) aims to learn diverse behaviors without reward functions, but often results in task-irrelevant or hazardous behaviors due to uniform exploration. Guided skill discovery (GSD) addresses this issue by incorporating human intent to focus exploration on meaningful regions. However, existing GSD methods typically require training additional guidance models, and rely on pre-defined rules or expert demonstration, which can be ineffective under sparse, online-collected human feedback. To overcome this, we propose COLLIE, a GSD framework that leverages dense unsupervised data to construct a semantically coherent skill latent space. This latent space is well-structured, enabling reliable guidance with sparse online feedback. Moreover, its semantic coherence property enables training-free construction of guidance signals, eliminating the need for additional model training beyond skill learning. Theoretical analysis justifies the effectiveness of our training-free guidance signal, while experiments across diverse state-based and pixel-based tasks show that COLLIE learns diverse, human-aligned skills, avoids hazardous behaviors, and achieves superior downstream performance with minimal human feedback.

paragraphs: Learning behaviors without a reward function can produce a diverse collection of skills, but diversity alone does not ensure usefulness or safety. Human guidance can focus exploration on meaningful behaviors. Existing approaches often need a separately trained guidance model, predefined rules, or demonstrations, which can be awkward when people provide only occasional feedback during learning.

COLLIE uses abundant unsupervised data to build a skill representation with coherent semantic structure. This structure makes sparse human feedback useful for directing skill discovery. It also supports constructing guidance signals without training an additional model beyond the skill-learning process itself, reducing the extra machinery needed to incorporate human intent.

The authors provide theoretical justification for this training-free guidance and evaluate it on tasks using both state information and pixels. In those experiments, COLLIE learns varied skills aligned with human preferences, avoids hazardous behaviors, and improves downstream performance with little feedback. The findings connect the organization of the learned skill space to how effectively a small amount of guidance can influence exploration.
summary.tldr: COLLIE organizes learned skills so sparse human feedback can guide useful, safer exploration without a separately trained guidance model.

title: COLLIE: Guiding Skill Discovery in Semantically Coherent Latent Space

abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) promise fast, non-autoregressive text generation, yet existing samplers, which pick tokens to unmask based on model confidence, ignore interactions when unmasking multiple positions in parallel and effectively reduce to slow, autoregressive behavior. We propose the Dilated Unmasking Scheduler (DUS), an inference-only, planner-model-free method that partitions sequence positions into non-adjacent dilated groups and unmasks them in parallel so as to minimize an upper bound on joint entropy gain at each denoising step. By explicitly trading off the number of network calls against generation quality, DUS recovers most of the performance lost under traditional parallel unmasking strategies. Across math (GSM8K, MATH500), code (HumanEval, MBPP), general-knowledge (BBH, MMLU-Pro), and instruction following (IFEval) benchmarks, DUS outperforms confidence-based planners and turns the diffusion-specific quality-speed trade-off into a deterministic, predictable speedup set by the block size $B$, yielding up to $5.8\times$ wall-clock speedup over token-by-token MDLM decoding without modifying the underlying denoiser. Applied as a drop-in post-filter, dilated spacing also improves adaptive samplers. Code is available at https://github.com/omerlux/DUS.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion language models can generate multiple tokens at once, but choosing positions solely by confidence overlooks their interactions. The paper argues that this creates a poor compromise: aggressive parallel generation loses quality, while cautious decoding approaches slow, token-by-token behavior. It proposes changing the unmasking schedule without modifying the underlying model.

The Dilated Unmasking Scheduler divides positions into spaced, non-adjacent groups and unmasks each group in parallel. Its scheduling criterion aims to minimize an upper bound on joint entropy gain at each denoising step. summary.tldr: DUS unmasks spaced token groups in parallel, improving the quality-speed trade-off of masked diffusion decoding without changing the denoiser.

title: Plan for Speed: Dilated Scheduling for Masked Diffusion Language Models

abstract: We formulate the learning of generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models as a Gromov-Wasserstein alignment problem, aiming to map semantically similar VL embeddings to physically similar motion primitives. However, solving this is challenging due to the mathematical heterogeneity between the domains: the semantic space of vision-language is topologically linear and isotropic, while the physical manifold of robotic action is non-Euclidean and anisotropic. As a result, direct regression approaches fail due to the disjoint metric structures of these domains, making standard distance minimization ill-posed. To resolve this incompatibility, we introduce LAST (Lie-algebraic Action Space Tokenizer). LAST reconstructs the action space to establish a more consistent metric alignment between the VL and Action modalities. Specifically, LAST bridges the heterogeneity via two stages: (1) Global Topological Linearization, which linearizes the action manifold through Lie-algebraic mapping, converting trajectories into a fixed-length, physically additive representation; and (2) Local Metric Discretization, where the representation is discretized hierarchically into schemas and whitened residuals, establishing a mathematical isomorphism with the isotropic Euclidean metric. By addressing the structural mismatch globally and locally, LAST enables VLA models with enhanced convergence and generalizability.

paragraphs: LAST addresses how a vision-language-action model should connect semantic similarity with physical similarity between motions. The paper formulates this as a Gromov-Wasserstein alignment problem. Its central difficulty is a mismatch in geometry: vision-language representations are described as linear and isotropic, while robotic action occupies a non-Euclidean, direction-dependent space.

The proposed Lie-algebraic Action Space Tokenizer reconstructs the action representation in two stages. First, it maps trajectories into a fixed-length, physically additive representation through Lie-algebraic linearization. The first stage addresses global structure; the second adjusts local metric structure to align with an isotropic Euclidean geometry.

This reconstruction is intended to make relationships within the action space more compatible with relationships in vision-language embeddings. The paper states that resolving the mismatch enables better convergence and generalization in VLA models. Its main contribution is therefore an action tokenizer designed around the geometry of cross-modal alignment, giving semantic-to-motion learning a more consistent representation on which to operate.
summary.tldr: LAST restructures robotic action representations to align their geometry with vision-language embeddings and improve VLA learning.

title: LAST: Bridging Vision-Language and Action Manifolds via Gromov-Wasserstein Alignment

abstract: Genomic language models (gLMs) achieve strong performance across genomic prediction tasks, but their internal biological representations remain poorly understood. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as an interpretability tool in vision and natural language models, yet their applicability to gLMs remains unexplored. We present a systematic study of SAE-based interpretability for gLMs, introducing a diverse benchmark of human genomic annotations and a suite of genome-tailored interpretability metrics. Using Evo2 as a primary case study, we show that SAE features, particularly those from intermediate layers, are more interpretable than raw model embeddings across 42/55 (76%) of our genomic concept evaluations, with 26 of them having an F1 score greater than 0.7. We further find that interpretability depends on SAE training data properties such as evolutionary proximity and context length. Finally, to organize semantically related genomic concepts learned by an SAE, we develop a graph-based representation method that outperforms the baseline approach of using SAE model weights. We demonstrate how our framework can extend SAEs as a powerful approach for not only better understanding gLMs but also for adopting them in disease-driven genomic explorations.

paragraphs: Genomic language models perform well on prediction tasks, but the biological meaning of their internal representations remains difficult to understand. This paper systematically studies sparse autoencoders as a way to expose those representations. It introduces a benchmark of human genomic annotations and evaluation metrics designed specifically for genomic interpretability.

Using Evo2 as the main case study, the authors compare sparse-autoencoder features with the model's raw embeddings. The learned features are more interpretable in 42 of 55 genomic concept evaluations, or 76%, with particularly strong results from intermediate layers. Twenty-six evaluations achieve F1 scores above 0.7. These results quantify how well the extracted features correspond to the benchmark's biological concepts.

Interpretability also depends on the data used to train the autoencoder, including evolutionary proximity and context length. To organize related concepts, the authors develop a graph-based representation method that outperforms a baseline based on autoencoder weights. Together, these contributions provide tools for examining learned genomic representations and support potential use in disease-oriented genomic exploration.
summary.tldr: Sparse autoencoders expose more interpretable genomic features in Evo2, with results depending on layer choice and training-data properties.

title: Interpreting Genomic Language Models using Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: We formulate the problem of exact unlearning in reinforcement learning, where the goal is to design an efficient framework that enables the removal of any user’s data upon deletion request, i.e., the online learner’s output after unlearning be indistinguishable from what would have been produced had the deleted user never interacted with the learner. For any $\rho >0$, we show that there exists a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that is $\rho$-TV-stable and supports an exact unlearning procedure whose expected computational cost is only a $\rho \sqrt{\ln T}$ fraction of the computational cost of retraining from scratch. We construct such a $\rho$-TV-stable RL algorithm for tabular Markov decision processes (MDPs), which achieves a regret bound of $\mathcal{O}(H^2 \sqrt{SAT} + H^3 S^2 A + {H^{2.5} S^2 A}/{\rho})$, where $S, A, H$, and $T$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, the episode horizon, and the number of episodes, respectively. We also establish a lower bound of $\Omega(H\sqrt{SAT}+{SAH}/{\rho})$ for $\rho$-TV-stable RL algorithms, showing that our algorithm is nearly minimax optimal.

For any $\rho >0$, we show that there exists a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that is $\rho$-TV-stable and supports an exact unlearning procedure whose expected computational cost is only a $\rho \sqrt{\ln T}$ fraction of the computational cost of retraining from scratch. paragraphs: Exact unlearning asks a reinforcement learner to remove a user’s influence so that its resulting output is indistinguishable from the output it would have produced without that user’s interactions. This paper formalizes that requirement for online reinforcement learning and studies how to meet it more efficiently than retraining.

For any positive ρ, the authors establish an RL algorithm with ρ-total-variation stability and an exact unlearning procedure. Its expected computational cost is a ρ√ln T fraction of retraining cost, where T is the number of episodes. The dependence on ρ and T makes the computational comparison conditional on those quantities.

The authors construct a suitable algorithm for tabular Markov decision processes and bound its regret using the numbers of states and actions, episode length, episode count, and ρ. A lower bound for stable algorithms shows near-minimax optimality. Together, these results expose a trade-off: stronger stability can support cheaper deletion, while the regret guarantees include a cost that grows as ρ decreases.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs stable tabular RL algorithms that support exact user-data deletion with quantified computational and regret trade-offs.

title: Exact Unlearning in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Despite rapid advances in text-to-video generation, state-of-the-art generative models still suffer from producing temporally incoherent and unrealistic motion for videos. The key weakness of existing works is that they commonly treat videos as frame sequences and directly adopt Flow Matching (FM) objectives, which are originally designed for images. This practice fails to explicitly model motion priors or temporal dependencies, resulting in suboptimal dynamics that may appear incoherent and unrealistic. To solve this problem, we propose Temporal-aware Flow Matching (TFM), a novel training paradigm that embeds inter-frame constraints into the flow objective, leading to temporally coherent motion modeling in video generation. More specifically, the proposed TFM enforces temporal correlations across frames while retaining the desirable properties of FM, and further introduces a residual-type loss that aligns naturally with this new flow. We theoretically prove that models trained with TFM are able to exhibit remarkably enhanced temporal perception ability. Notably, TFM imposes no additional cost during inference and is applicable to any model using FM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our TFM can significantly improve motion realism across diverse motion types. Generated videos are presented at https://pzrain.github.io/tfm.

paragraphs: A generated video can contain plausible individual frames while showing motion that is inconsistent over time. This paper attributes part of that problem to using image-oriented flow-matching objectives directly on frame sequences. Such objectives do not explicitly capture motion priors or dependencies between frames, leaving temporal behavior under-modeled.

Temporal-aware Flow Matching changes the training objective to include constraints across frames. It enforces temporal correlations while retaining the desirable properties of flow matching, and adds a residual-type loss suited to the modified flow. The approach therefore introduces temporal structure into what the model learns during training.

The authors provide a theoretical result showing that models trained this way can exhibit enhanced temporal perception. Experiments report significant improvements in motion realism across diverse motion types. The method adds no inference cost and is stated to apply to any model using flow matching. This makes the training objective the central intervention: temporal coherence can improve without requiring an additional processing stage when videos are generated.
summary.tldr: Temporal-aware Flow Matching adds inter-frame structure to training, improving generated motion without additional inference cost.

title: Temporal-aware Flow Matching for Video Generation with Temporally Coherent Motion

abstract: Training stability remains a critical bottleneck for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), often manifesting as a trade-off between reasoning plasticity and general capability retention. We identify a root cause as the geometric conflict between plasticity and stability gradients, which leads to destructive interference. Crucially, we argue that deterministic projection methods are suboptimal for GRPO as they overlook the intrinsic stochasticity of group-based gradient estimates. To address this, we propose Probabilistic Conflict Resolution (PCR), a Bayesian framework that models gradients as random variables. PCR dynamically arbitrates conflicts via an uncertainty-aware “soft projection” mechanism, optimizing the signal-to-noise ratio. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PCR significantly smooths the training trajectory and achieves superior performance in various reasoning tasks.

We identify a root cause as the geometric conflict between plasticity and stability gradients, which leads to destructive interference. Crucially, we argue that deterministic projection methods are suboptimal for GRPO as they overlook the intrinsic stochasticity of group-based gradient estimates. To address this, we propose Probabilistic Conflict Resolution (PCR), a Bayesian framework that models gradients as random variables. PCR dynamically arbitrates conflicts via an uncertainty-aware “soft projection” mechanism, optimizing the signal-to-noise ratio. paragraphs: Post-training a language model must balance learning new reasoning behavior with retaining broader capabilities. For Group Relative Policy Optimization, the paper identifies a source of instability in this balance: gradients supporting adaptation and gradients supporting retention can point in conflicting directions, so an update can undermine one objective while advancing the other.

The authors argue that deterministic gradient projections do not adequately account for the randomness inherent in estimates formed from groups of samples. Probabilistic Conflict Resolution instead models gradients as random variables within a Bayesian framework. It uses uncertainty-aware soft projection to arbitrate conflicts dynamically, with the goal of improving the signal-to-noise ratio of the resulting updates.

This changes conflict handling from a decision based only on an estimated direction to one that also accounts for uncertainty in that estimate. Experiments report substantially smoother training trajectories and better performance across reasoning tasks. The findings support treating gradient uncertainty as part of the optimization problem when balancing reasoning plasticity and stability, rather than assuming every observed conflict reflects an equally reliable learning signal.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic Conflict Resolution accounts for gradient uncertainty to reduce destructive interference and improve GRPO reasoning training.

title: On the Plasticity and Stability for Post-Training Large Language Models

abstract: The probabilistic bisection algorithm (PBA) extends the classical binary search to settings with noisy responses, and is a foundational algorithm commonly used in basic problems such as root-finding. Despite its strong empirical success, its theoretical property, particularly the convergence rate, remains unclear. This paper establishes that PBA converges at a geometric rate, providing a rigorous justification for its empirical efficiency. Notably, this rate is optimal in the sense that it matches the performance of classical binary search under noiseless responses. The core of our analysis lies in directly characterizing the dynamics of PBA queries, which had not been examined in the prior literature. We show that the queries oscillate around the truth but steadily draw closer, thus leading to an estimator that rapidly concentrates on the truth. Beyond resolving the long-standing question of PBA’s convergence, our developed techniques offer new tools for analyzing PBA’s dynamics, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Probabilistic bisection extends binary search to situations where responses can be wrong, making it useful for problems such as locating a root with noisy feedback. Although the algorithm has worked well empirically, its convergence speed lacked a clear theoretical account. This paper establishes a geometric convergence rate.

Geometric convergence means that error contracts at an exponential rate as the procedure progresses. The authors characterize this rate as optimal because it matches the rate achieved by classical binary search with noiseless responses. This comparison concerns convergence speed; it does not imply that noise disappears or that the procedures have identical behavior at every step.

The proof directly studies the dynamics of the algorithm’s queries. Those queries move back and forth around the true answer while steadily getting closer, yielding an estimator that rapidly concentrates near the truth. By analyzing this movement, the paper supplies a theoretical explanation for the algorithm’s observed efficiency. The authors also suggest that these analytical techniques may be useful independently for studying probabilistic bisection dynamics.
summary.tldr: The paper proves geometric convergence for probabilistic bisection by showing how its noisy queries oscillate toward the true answer.

title: Probabilistic Bisection Algorithm Provably Achieves Exponential Convergence

abstract: The veracious semantic alignment in autoformalization is significant for formal mathematical reasoning. However, existing evaluations provide only opaque binary verdicts or scalar scores, offering no interpretable insight into where or why translations fail. This opacity severely limits both human understanding and automated system improvement. To bridge this gap, we introduce FormalRx, a comprehensive diagnostic evaluation framework that transforms autoformalization assessment from black-box judgments into actionable feedback. At its core is SCI Error Taxonomy, a hierarchical classification scheme decomposing autoformalization errors into 28 distinct categories with strict priority ordering. Building on this taxonomy, FormalRx provides four critical diagnostic capabilities: alignment verdicts, error categorization, error localization, and correction. We instantiate the framework with a diagnostic model FormalRx-8B, trained on 56,287 synthetically generated samples with fine-grained diagnostic annotations, and release FormalRx-Test as the first fine-grained diagnostic benchmark. FormalRx-8B achieves F1-scores of 0.88 (verdict) and 0.71 (categorization), along with accuracies of 0.75 (localization) and 0.73 (correction), substantially outperforming both general-purpose LLMs and specialized baselines. By connecting evaluation with actionable insights, FormalRx enables systematic diagnosis and improvement of autoformalization systems.

paragraphs: Autoformalization translates mathematical statements into formal representations, making preservation of meaning central to its usefulness. A binary judgment or single score can indicate that a translation failed without explaining the failure. FormalRx addresses that diagnostic gap by organizing evaluation around what went wrong, where it happened, and how the translation could be corrected.

Its SCI Error Taxonomy divides errors into 28 hierarchical categories with a strict priority ordering. The framework uses this structure to provide four outputs: an alignment judgment, an error category, an error location, and a correction. The authors implement these capabilities in FormalRx-8B, trained on 56,287 synthetic examples with detailed diagnostic annotations, and introduce FormalRx-Test as a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark.

FormalRx-8B reports F1 scores of 0.88 for alignment judgments and 0.71 for categorization, plus accuracies of 0.75 for localization and 0.73 for correction. It substantially outperforms the evaluated general-purpose and specialized baselines. These results support evaluating translation quality through actionable diagnosis, giving both human reviewers and automated improvement systems more specific information than an overall correctness score.
summary.tldr: FormalRx diagnoses mathematical autoformalization failures by classifying, locating, and correcting semantic errors.

title: FormalRx: Rectify and eXamine Semantic Failures in Autoformalization

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) improve in mathematical reasoning and formal understanding, a promising approach for automated theorem proving (ATP) is to enable LLMs construct proof sketches, which plan a high-level proof strategy and decompose complex theorems into independently provable subgoals. However, most existing proof sketches are immutable. As a result, any revision typically requires rebuilding the entire sketch, which discards already proved subgoals and bring additional cost. In this paper, we address this limitation by introducing EditableSketch, an editable proof-sketch structure that supports in-place edits for error correction and further subgoal decomposition while preserving previously proved subgoals. Building on EditableSketch, we introduce SketchRefine, a proof-generation framework for ATP by iteratively refining proof sketches through localized, incremental edits. Experiments show that our method not only reduces the cost of the proof process, but also achieves superior performance. For example, our method realizes 76.0% pass rate on FormalMath-Lite (+14.1% vs. DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B). Meanwhile, compared with Hilbert, our method significantly reduces token overhead while achieving comparable performance.

paragraphs: A proof sketch divides a difficult theorem into a high-level strategy and smaller subgoals that can be proved independently. Language models can generate these sketches, but a rigid sketch makes correction expensive. Revising one part may require rebuilding the whole structure and discarding work on subgoals that have already been proved.

EditableSketch makes the proof plan revisable in place. It supports correcting errors and breaking a subgoal into smaller pieces while retaining previously proved subgoals. The accompanying SketchRefine framework repeatedly improves a proof through these localized edits. The approach makes preservation of completed work an explicit part of the proof-generation process.

Experiments report both reduced proof costs and stronger performance. On FormalMath-Lite, the method reaches a 76.0% pass rate, with a reported 14.1% improvement over DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B. Against Hilbert, it achieves comparable performance with substantially lower token overhead. These findings suggest that revisable proof structure can improve the efficiency of automated theorem proving while also helping the system complete more proofs.
summary.tldr: EditableSketch lets theorem-proving systems revise proof plans locally while preserving completed subgoals, reducing cost and improving reported performance.

title: Editable Proof Sketch for Automated Theorem Proving

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often hallucinate by generating factually incorrect or unfaithful content, posing significant risks to their safe use. Detecting such hallucinations is particularly challenging under the zero-source constraint, where no model internals or external references are available, and detection must rely solely on the textual query–answer pair. In this paper, we propose Human-like Criteria Probing for Hallucination Detection (HCPD), a paradigm that emulates the multi-faceted reasoning of human evaluators. Its core is a Human-like Criteria Probing (HCP) mechanism, in which a LLM agent adaptively decomposes its judgment into a weighted set of interpretable criteria and aggregates criterion-specific scores into a final truthfulness measure. To achieve this adaptive capability, we introduce a reward-based alignment scheme using only weak supervision from semantic consistency. At inference, we employ a multi-sampling aggregation strategy to ensure robust decisions while preserving full interpretability. We further provide theoretical analysis supporting the reliability of our approach. Extensive experiments show that HCPD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, offering an effective and explainable solution for zero-source hallucination detection.

paragraphs: Zero-source hallucination detection must judge an answer using only its text and the original query. It has no access to model internals or external references. HCPD addresses this constrained setting by having a language-model agent break its judgment into several interpretable criteria, rather than relying on a single undifferentiated assessment.

The agent adaptively chooses a weighted set of criteria, scores the answer against each one, and combines those scores into a truthfulness measure. A reward-based alignment scheme teaches this adaptation using weak supervision derived only from semantic consistency. At inference, aggregating multiple samples aims to make decisions robust while retaining the criterion-level explanation.

The authors provide theoretical analysis supporting reliability and report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in extensive experiments. The stated contribution is an explainable detector operating under the query–answer-only restriction. Its results support adaptive, multi-criterion judgment as a useful approach when reference-based verification is unavailable, with both the final score and the component assessments remaining interpretable.
summary.tldr: HCPD detects hallucinations from query–answer text alone by combining adaptive, interpretable judgment criteria.

title: Zero-source LLM Hallucination Detection with Human-like Criteria Probing

abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in multimodal reasoning. However, prevailing reinforcement learning (RL) paradigms lack explicit counterfactual enhancement and causal learning mechanisms. This fundamental deficiency results in severe grounding failures, manifesting as a tendency to ignore visual evidence in favor of language priors or exhibiting hallucination drift during long chain-of-thought reasoning. To address this root cause, we propose CounterFactual Policy Optimization (CFPO), a novel framework that enforces causal consistency between visual perception and textual reasoning. CFPO introduces a cross-modal counterfactual enhancement mechanism, which regularizes the policy by maximizing the discrepancy between the model’s predictions and those from a counterfactual state where critical visual cues are suppressed. This approach seamlessly integrates with standard algorithms like GRPO and DAPO without requiring external reward models or additional supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CFPO significantly improves reasoning fidelity, achieving consistent gains of 3.17%-6.25% over standard RL baselines and 1.32%-2.13% over the state-of-the-art perception-aware method (PAPO). Code is available at https://github.com/Raven-July/CFPO.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can produce plausible reasoning while relying too heavily on familiar language patterns and too little on the image. The paper identifies this grounding failure, including drift during long reasoning chains, as a problem with reinforcement learning approaches that lack explicit mechanisms for counterfactual and causal learning.

Counterfactual Policy Optimization, or CFPO, trains with a comparison between the original visual input and a counterfactual state in which critical visual cues are suppressed. Its regularization objective increases the discrepancy between predictions in these two states. The intended effect is to make the model’s reasoning depend more strongly on visual evidence that should matter to the answer.

CFPO integrates with GRPO and DAPO without external reward models or additional supervision. Experiments report consistent gains of 3.17%–6.25% over standard reinforcement learning baselines and 1.32%–2.13% over the perception-aware method PAPO. These results support counterfactual visual interventions as a practical training mechanism for improving reasoning fidelity in the evaluated vision-language models.
summary.tldr: CFPO improves multimodal reasoning by training models to respond differently when critical visual evidence is removed.

title: CFPO: Counterfactual Policy Optimization for Multimodal Reasoning

abstract: Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (MRAG) has emerged as a key paradigm for grounding MLLMs with external knowledge. While query pre-processing (e.g., rewriting) is standard in text-based RAG, existing MRAG pipelines predominantly treat visual inputs as static and immutable, implicitly assuming they are noise-free. However, real-world visual queries are often “imperfect”—suffering from geometric distortions, quality degradation, or semantic ambiguity—leading to catastrophic retrieval failures. To address this gap, we propose V-QPP-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark dedicated to Visual Query Pre-processing (V-QPP). We formulate V-QPP as an agentic decision-making task where MLLMs must autonomously diagnose imperfections and deploy perceptual tools to refine queries. Our extensive evaluation across 46,700 imperfect queries and diverse MRAG paradigms reveals three critical insights: (1) Vulnerability—visual imperfections severely degrade both retrieval recall and end-to-end MRAG performance; (2) Restoration Potential & Bottleneck—while oracle preprocessing recovers near-perfect performance, off-the-shelf MLLMs struggle with tool selection and parameter prediction without specialized training; and (3) Training Enhancement—supervised fine-tuning enables compact models to achieve comparable or superior performance to larger proprietary models, demonstrating the benchmark’s value for developing robust MRAG systems The code is available at https://github.com/phycholosogy/VQQP_Bench

paragraphs: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation uses visual queries to retrieve outside knowledge, but those queries can contain distortions, degraded image quality, or ambiguous content. Many pipelines treat the image as fixed input. V-QPP-Bench examines whether a model can improve retrieval by first diagnosing and correcting imperfections in that input.

The benchmark frames preprocessing as an agent decision task: a multimodal model must choose perceptual tools and predict their parameters to refine the query. Evaluation spans 46,700 imperfect queries and multiple retrieval-augmented generation approaches. This setup tests both recognition of a visual problem and the decisions needed to address it before searching.

The results show that imperfections severely damage retrieval recall and final system performance. Oracle preprocessing restores near-perfect performance, demonstrating substantial recovery potential, but off-the-shelf models struggle with tool and parameter choices. Supervised fine-tuning enables compact models to match or outperform larger proprietary models in the evaluation. These findings identify specialized preprocessing training as a productive route toward more robust visual retrieval.
summary.tldr: V-QPP-Bench tests how agents repair imperfect visual queries and shows that specialized training can substantially improve preprocessing decisions.

title: Fix Before Search: Benchmarking Agentic Visual Query Pre-processing in Multimodal Retrieval-augmented Generation

abstract: The need for developing model evaluations beyond static benchmarking, especially in the post-deployment phase, is now well-understood. At the same time, concerns about the concentration of power in deployed AI systems have sparked a keen interest in "democratic" or "public" AI. In this work, we bring these two ideas together by proposing mechanisms for aggregated individual reporting (AIR), a framework for post-deployment evaluation that relies on individual reports from the public. An AIR mechanism allows those who interact with a specific, deployed (AI) system to report when they feel that they may have experienced something problematic; these reports are then aggregated over time, with the goal of evaluating the relevant system in a fine-grained manner. This position paper argues that individual experiences should be understood as an integral part of post-deployment evaluation, and that the scope of our proposed aggregated individual reporting mechanism is a practical path to that end. On the one hand, individual reporting can identify substantively novel insights about safety and performance; on the other, aggregation can be uniquely useful for informing action. From a normative perspective, the post-deployment phase completes a missing piece in the conversation about "democratic" AI. As a pathway to implementation, we provide a workflow of concrete design decisions and pointers to areas for future research.

paragraphs: This position paper proposes aggregated individual reporting, or AIR, as a way to evaluate AI systems after deployment. People who interact with a particular system could report experiences they consider potentially problematic. Those reports would then be combined over time to support a detailed assessment of the system in actual use.

The proposal joins two concerns: evaluations need to extend beyond static benchmarks, and the public needs a meaningful role in deployed AI. Individual experiences can reveal new information about safety and performance. Aggregation serves a complementary purpose by bringing reports together in a form that can help inform action.

The authors argue that these experiences should become an integral part of post-deployment evaluation. They also treat this phase as a missing element in discussions of democratic AI, since public involvement remains relevant after a system starts operating. To make the proposal actionable, the paper supplies a workflow of design decisions and identifies research questions for implementing reporting mechanisms.
summary.tldr: AIR would aggregate public reports of potentially problematic AI experiences to inform detailed post-deployment evaluation and action.

title: Position: Mechanisms for Aggregated Individual Reporting Should be Established for Post-Deployment Evaluation

abstract: This position paper argues that LLM-based social simulations require clear boundaries to make meaningful contributions to social science. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising capabilities for simulating human behavior, their tendency to produce homogeneous outputs, acting as an "average persona", fundamentally limits their ability to capture the behavioral diversity essential for complex social dynamics. We examine why heterogeneity matters for social simulations and how current LLMs fall short, analyzing the relationship between mean alignment and variance in LLM-generated behaviors. Through a systematic review of representative studies, we find that validation practices often fail to match the heterogeneity requirements of research questions: while most papers include ground truth comparisons, fewer than half explicitly assess behavioral variance, and most that do report lower variance than human populations. We propose that researchers should: (1) match validation depth to the heterogeneity demands of their research questions, (2) explicitly report variance alongside mean alignment, and (3) constrain claims to collective-level qualitative patterns when variance is insufficient. Rather than dismissing LLM-based simulation, we advocate for a boundary-aware approach that ensures these methods contribute genuine insights to social science.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that language-model simulations of human behavior need claims and validation matched to the diversity their research questions require. A model can reproduce an average response while failing to reproduce differences among people. The authors describe an average-persona tendency that limits simulations of social dynamics where those differences matter.

They systematically review representative studies and examine the relationship between matching behavioral means and matching behavioral variation. Although most reviewed papers compare their simulations with ground truth, fewer than half explicitly evaluate variance. Among those that do, most report less variation than human populations. The finding suggests that agreement on averages can coexist with a consequential failure to capture population diversity.

The authors recommend reporting variance alongside mean alignment and making validation more demanding when a question depends on heterogeneity. When simulated variation is insufficient, they advise restricting claims to qualitative patterns at the collective level. Their aim is to define productive boundaries for these methods so that the scope of conclusions follows the evidence.
summary.tldr: LLM social simulations should validate behavioral diversity and restrict their claims when they reproduce averages without sufficient human variation.

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) methods based on least-squares temporal difference (LSTD) have been developed recently and have shown good practical performance. However, the quality of their estimation has not been well elucidated. In this article, we discuss LSTD based policy evaluation from the new viewpoint of semiparametric statistical inference. In fact, the estimator can be obtained from a particular estimating function which guarantees its convergence to the true value asymptotically, without specifying a model of the environment. Based on these observations, we 1) analyze the asymptotic variance of an LSTD-based estimator, 2) derive the optimal estimating function with the minimum asymptotic estimation variance, and 3) derive a suboptimal estimator to reduce the computational burden in obtaining the optimal estimating function.

However, the quality of their estimation has not been well elucidated. In this article, we discuss LSTD based policy evaluation from the new viewpoint of semiparametric statistical inference. In fact, the estimator can be obtained from a particular estimating function which guarantees its convergence to the true value asymptotically, without specifying a model of the environment. Based on these observations, we 1) analyze the asymptotic variance of an LSTD-based estimator, 2) derive the optimal estimating function with the minimum asymptotic estimation variance, and 3) derive a suboptimal estimator to reduce the computational burden in obtaining the optimal estimating function.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation estimates the value of following a particular policy. Least-squares temporal difference methods had shown good practical performance on this task, but the statistical quality of their estimates was less well understood. This paper studies that quality through semiparametric statistical inference, connecting a reinforcement learning procedure to a framework for analyzing estimators.

The authors show that an LSTD-based estimator can be obtained from a particular estimating function. This construction guarantees convergence to the true value asymptotically, without requiring a specified model of the environment. The result concerns what happens as the available information grows, rather than asserting that every estimate from a limited sample is exact.

The paper then analyzes asymptotic variance, which describes the estimator's remaining variability in that large-sample setting. It derives an optimal estimating function with minimum asymptotic estimation variance. Because obtaining that function carries a computational burden, the authors also derive a suboptimal estimator intended to reduce the cost. The contribution therefore links estimation quality with the computation needed to pursue it.
summary.tldr: A statistical analysis of LSTD policy evaluation yields a minimum-asymptotic-variance estimating function and a less costly suboptimal estimator.

title: A semiparametric statistical approach to model-free policy evaluation

abstract: Prediction markets are used in real life to predict outcomes of interest such as presidential elections. In this work we introduce a mathematical theory for Artificial Prediction Markets for supervised classifier aggregation and probability estimation. We introduce the artificial prediction market as a novel way to aggregate classifiers. We derive the market equations to enforce total budget conservation, show the market price uniqueness and give efficient algorithms for computing it. We show how to train the market participants by updating their budgets using training examples. We introduce classifier specialization as a new differentiating characteristic between classifiers. Finally, we present experiments using random decision rules as specialized classifiers and show that the prediction market consistently outperforms Random Forest on real and synthetic data of varying degrees of difficulty.

paragraphs: The paper introduces artificial prediction markets as a mathematical framework for combining classifiers and estimating probabilities. Individual classifiers serve as market participants, and the market provides an aggregate prediction. The authors develop the underlying equations so that this mechanism can be used for supervised learning.

Those equations conserve the total budget, and the authors establish uniqueness of the market price and give efficient algorithms for computing it. Training examples are used to update participants' budgets. The framework also introduces classifier specialization as a distinguishing characteristic, allowing the aggregation scheme to account for specialized participants.

The experiments use random decision rules as specialized classifiers and compare the resulting market with Random Forest. Across the reported real and synthetic datasets of varying difficulty, the prediction market consistently performs better. This is a finding about the evaluated configurations. The contribution combines a formally specified aggregation mechanism, an efficient way to compute its output, and a supervised procedure for adapting the participating classifiers' budgets.
summary.tldr: Artificial prediction markets aggregate specialized classifiers through trained budgets and outperform Random Forest in the reported experiments.

title: Supervised Aggregation of Classifiers using Artificial Prediction Markets

abstract: We present a robust multiple manifold structure learning (RMMSL) scheme to robustly estimate data structures under the multiple low intrinsic dimensional manifolds assumption. In the local learning stage, RMMSL efficiently estimates local tangent space by weighted low-rank matrix factorization. In the global learning stage, we propose a robust manifold clustering method based on local structure learning results. The proposed clustering method is designed to get the flattest manifolds clusters by introducing a novel curved-level similarity function. Our approach is evaluated and compared to state-of-the-art methods on synthetic data, handwritten digit images, human motion capture data and motorbike videos. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, which yields higher clustering accuracy, and produces promising results for challenging tasks of human motion segmentation and motion flow learning from videos.

The proposed clustering method is designed to get the flattest manifolds clusters by introducing a novel curved-level similarity function. Our approach is evaluated and compared to state-of-the-art methods on synthetic data, handwritten digit images, human motion capture data and motorbike videos. paragraphs: The paper assumes that data lie around several manifolds, each with low intrinsic dimensionality. Under this view, the data's meaningful structure can be simpler than its full representation suggests, but different groups may follow different underlying shapes. Robust Multiple Manifold Structure Learning, or RMMSL, aims to estimate and separate those structures.

The method works at two levels. Locally, weighted low-rank matrix factorization efficiently estimates tangent spaces, describing the nearby directions of each manifold. Globally, a robust clustering method uses these local estimates. A new curved-level similarity function guides clustering toward the flattest manifold groups, making geometric structure central to how observations are grouped.

The authors compare RMMSL with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic data, handwritten digits, human motion capture, and motorbike videos. They report higher clustering accuracy and promising results for human motion segmentation and learning motion flow from video. These findings support combining local geometric estimation with global clustering under the multiple low-dimensional manifold assumption, across several evaluated types of data.
summary.tldr: RMMSL combines local tangent-space estimation with curvature-sensitive clustering to recover multiple low-dimensional structures robustly.

title: Robust Multiple Manifold Structure Learning

abstract: In this paper, we propose the distributed tree kernels (DTK) as a novel method to reduce time and space complexity of tree kernels. Using a linear complexity algorithm to compute vectors for trees, we embed feature spaces of tree fragments in low-dimensional spaces where the kernel computation is directly done with dot product. We show that DTKs are faster, correlate with tree kernels, and obtain a statistically similar performance in two natural language processing tasks.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we propose the distributed tree kernels (DTK) as a novel method to reduce time and space complexity of tree kernels. paragraphs: This paper introduces distributed tree kernels as a way to reduce the computational and storage costs of tree-kernel methods. The underlying representations concern fragments of trees, but the proposed method embeds those feature spaces into low-dimensional vector spaces. This gives tree comparisons a compact numerical representation on which kernel computation can operate directly.

The authors provide a linear-complexity algorithm for computing tree vectors. Once those vectors are available, a kernel value is calculated with a dot product. The contribution therefore connects a representation change with a simpler comparison operation: tree-fragment information is carried into vectors, and comparisons are performed in that lower-dimensional space.

The reported results address both efficiency and preservation of useful behavior. Distributed tree kernels are faster, their values correlate with tree-kernel values, and they achieve statistically similar performance on two natural language processing tasks. Correlation does not imply exact reproduction of the original kernel. The evidence instead supports a computationally cheaper representation that retains comparable task performance in the two evaluated applications.
summary.tldr: Distributed tree kernels use compact vectors and dot products to accelerate tree comparisons while retaining statistically similar performance on two NLP tasks.

title: Distributed Tree Kernels
